# Overview

Amnezigo is a declarative configuration generator for **AmneziaWG 2.0, 3.0, and 3.1** networks. You write a single manifest file describing your whole network — one server, any number of clients, and the obfuscation and transport-protection settings they share — and Amnezigo turns it into ready-to-deploy `awg0.conf` files for every peer. The target generation is selected per manifest with `obfuscation.awg_version`; left unset, it defaults to **3.1**.

If you have ever configured AmneziaWG by hand, you know the pain: choosing four S-prefixes, four header ranges, and three junk parameters, then keeping every client's `[Peer]` block inside the server config in sync. Amnezigo replaces that spreadsheet-and-pray workflow with **one file that is the source of truth**.

This page is a gentle tour. It explains what Amnezigo is, introduces the manifest idea, shows what `amnezigo generate` produces, and defines the core concepts you need before reading anything else: **server peer**, **client peer**, the **shared obfuscation profile**, and **per-client CPS**. It is deliberately light on field lists — those live in the [Manifest Reference](/manifest-reference). Read this first; the rest of the docs assume it.

## What Amnezigo Is

Amnezigo is a single Go binary that does one thing well: **read a manifest, write configs**. It is a *generator*, not a daemon — it does not run tunnels, manage keys at runtime, or touch the network. You run it on your laptop, copy the generated files to your machines, and start the AmneziaWG interface yourself.

The same generation logic also ships as an importable Go library: the root package of `github.com/Arsolitt/amnezigo` is the API and the CLI is a thin wrapper around it. The project is GPL-3.0-only. If you would rather drive generation from your own Go program, see [Library API](/library-api).

The CLI exposes four amnezigo commands (plus Cobra's built-in `completion` and `help`):

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `amnezigo generate` | Build `awg0.conf` files from a manifest |
| `amnezigo validate` | Check an existing config for obfuscation problems |
| `amnezigo analyze` | Probe a config's runtime obfuscation characteristics |
| `amnezigo version` | Print the build stamp as `amnezigo <version> (<commit>)` |

`amnezigo version` reports the version and commit stamped into the binary at build time: a release build prints something like `amnezigo 0.4.0 (abc1234)` (the leading `v` of the tag is stripped), while a plain `go build` prints `amnezigo dev (none)`. See [Installation](/installation) for the build paths.

::: tip
Those are the only four amnezigo commands. If an old blog post or fork's README mentions `amnezigo init`, `add`, `edit`, `remove`, `export`, or `list`, it is describing a version that no longer exists — those commands were removed during the refactor to the declarative manifest.
:::

This tour focuses on `generate`, because that is the command you will reach for ninety percent of the time. `validate`, `analyze`, and `version` are covered in [Validation](/validation) and the [CLI Reference](/cli-reference).

## The Declarative Manifest Concept

A **manifest** is a plain JSON (or Jsonnet) file that declares your *entire* network topology in one place. There is no imperative add/remove dance and no hidden state: **the file is the network**. Amnezigo looks for it under one of two default names:

- `amnezigo.json` — plain JSON
- `.amnezigo.jsonnet` — Jsonnet (takes precedence when both exist)

A minimal 3.1 manifest looks like this:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "network": { "mtu": 1280 },
  "obfuscation": { "awg_version": "3.1" },
  "peers": {
    "server": {
      "address": "10.0.0.1/24",
      "endpoint": "vpn.example.com:51820",
      "listen_port": 51820
    },
    "phone": { "address": "10.0.0.2/32" }
  }
}
```

Four things to notice right away, because they surprise people who expect a more conventional schema:

1. **`"version": 1` is required.** The current and only schema version is `1`. Omitting it (or writing any other number) is rejected before anything else runs.
2. **`peers` is a map, not a list.** The map key (`"server"`, `"phone"`) *is* the peer's name — there is no separate `name` field. That name becomes the output directory, so pick something filesystem-safe.
3. **`obfuscation.awg_version` selects the target generation** and may be omitted, in which case the 3.1 default applies. It is the obfuscation field you will reach for most often, because it decides which transport-protection keys the generator is allowed to emit; see [The AWG Version Model](#the-awg-version-model) below.
4. **Most obfuscation values are optional.** Omit a nullable obfuscation field (`s1`–`s4`, the `h1`–`h4` ranges, `jc`, `jmin`, `jmax`) and Amnezigo generates a value for you at generate time. An explicit non-zero value is used verbatim.

::: warning Omitting a value is not the same as setting it to zero
For the S prefixes, omitting the key means "generate a value", and writing an explicit `"s1": 0` does *not* pin zero either: the S fields only preserve non-zero input, so zeros are replaced by generated values. Junk control differs slightly — an explicit `"jc": 0` survives only when `jmin` and `jmax` are explicit as well. Under the default 3.1 header protection there is also a floor: a pinned S value below 12 aborts generation with `header protection requires S1-S4 >= 12 (got S1=3)`, because the header cipher uses the first 12 bytes of the packet as its nonce.
:::

If you want a stable, reproducible profile, pin the fields you care about with legal values:

```json
{
  "obfuscation": {
    "awg_version": "3.1",
    "s1": 18, "s2": 18, "s3": 18, "s4": 18,
    "jc": 8, "jmin": 235, "jmax": 313
  }
}
```

Pinning all four S values equal also keeps the `TRL001` warning quiet, since `RandomTrailers` is on by default under 3.1 and the AWG 3.1 reference wants equal S prefixes. You do not need to memorise the full field list to finish this tour — the [Manifest Reference](/manifest-reference) catalogues every field, and [Manifest Examples](/manifest-examples) has copy-paste topologies. The important idea is the **flow**: you write the manifest once, then run `generate` to materialise it.

## The AWG Version Model

The manifest field `obfuscation.awg_version` selects which AmneziaWG generation the output targets. It accepts exactly three strings — `"2.0"`, `"3.0"`, and `"3.1"` — and may be omitted or left empty, in which case generation defaults to **3.1**. Any other value is rejected before a single config is built:

```text
unsupported awg_version "3" (expected "2.0", "3.0", or "3.1")
```

| Version | What it adds | Transport keys emitted |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `"2.0"` | The classic obfuscation layer: `Jc`/`Jmin`/`Jmax`, `S1`–`S4`, `H1`–`H4`, and the `I1`–`I5` custom packet strings | none |
| `"3.0"` | `HeaderProtectionKey`, `ContentPaddingAddition`, and the five ranges `RekeyAfterTime`, `RekeyTimeout`, `RejectAfterTime`, `KeepaliveTimeout`, `MaxHandshakeAttempts` | the key plus the six ranges |
| `"3.1"` (default) | `RandomTrailers` and `DisableCookies` | all nine |

Selecting a generation is a hard gate in both directions:

- A manifest field that belongs to a newer generation than the selected one is an **error**, not silently ignored: `obfuscation.random_trailers requires awg_version 3.1 or later (got "2.0")`.
- The writer gates emission the same way, so a 2.0 config never carries any 3.x key. Older engine builds reject INI keys they do not know, and targeting 2.0 is what keeps legacy runtimes working.

The 3.x keys are engine features, so a 3.1 config needs a 3.1-capable AmneziaWG userspace; the shipped container image is pinned to `amneziavpn/amneziawg-go:3.1.20260828`.

## Transport Protection (AWG 3.x)

Generation 3.0 introduced a second obfuscation layer on top of the S/H/J parameters, and 3.1 extended it. Under the default 3.1 every generated config carries all nine keys:

| Key | Default | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `HeaderProtectionKey` | generated 44-character base64 | 32-byte ChaCha20 key; encrypts the 4-byte message header at offset S{n}, with the first 12 bytes of the packet as the nonce |
| `ContentPaddingAddition` | `2-10` | uint16 range, written `N` or `N-M` |
| `RekeyAfterTime` | `120-180` | uint16 range |
| `RekeyTimeout` | `5-8` | uint16 range |
| `RejectAfterTime` | `180-240` | uint16 range |
| `KeepaliveTimeout` | `8-12` | uint16 range |
| `MaxHandshakeAttempts` | `16-20` | uint16 range |
| `RandomTrailers` | `on` | receiver classifies packets by size; equal S1–S4 are recommended |
| `DisableCookies` | `on` | disables the 3.1 cookie replies |

Rules worth knowing before you read more:

- Both tunnel ends must use the same `HeaderProtectionKey`; two peers with different keys never complete a handshake.
- The six ranges accept `N` or `N-M`. A range of `{ "min": 0, "max": 0 }` means "disable this key" and the line disappears; a half-zero range such as `{ "min": 0, "max": 10 }` is an error.
- The key is persistent state. `generate` recovers `HeaderProtectionKey` from the previous server config and reuses it, unless you pass `--full-reset` or the key is unset; switching a project from 3.1 to 2.0 and back regenerates it, and clients still configured with the old key stop handshaking until they are re-imported.
- When header protection is active and you leave `h1`–`h4` unset, the H ranges are the WireGuard type-ids `1-1`, `2-2`, `3-3`, `4-4` — the reference configuration, not random ranges. If even one H field is explicit, the other three are generated freely.
- When random trailers are on and all four S values are unset, `generate` draws one value and uses it for `S1=S2=S3=S4`. Pinning any S switches the remaining fields to independent draws, and unequal S values then produce the `TRL001` warning (`RandomTrailers is enabled while S1..S4 differ`).
- Because header protection needs a 12-byte nonce from the S-prefixed area, the S floor of 12 applies whenever the key is present; below 12, generation aborts. With `awg_version: "2.0"`, S values below 12 are legal again.

The full details — every manifest field, the validation codes `HPK001`/`HPK003`/`TRL001`/`TRM001`, and the runtime exposure via `awg show dump` — are in [Transport Protection](/transport-protection). The S/H/J parameters underneath are covered in [Obfuscation](/obfuscation).

## What `amnezigo generate` Produces

When you run:

```shell
amnezigo generate
```

from the directory containing your manifest, Amnezigo performs these steps:

1. **Load** the manifest (resolving Jsonnet first if `.amnezigo.jsonnet` is present).
2. **Find the server peer** and error out unless exactly one peer qualifies.
3. **Reuse or create credentials** — peer keypairs, per-client preshared keys, and the header-protection key, recovered from the previously written output tree when it exists.
4. **Resolve the obfuscation profile** — apply the version gates and per-version defaults, fill unpinned values, enforce the S floor, and pick the H ranges. Unpinned S and J values are re-drawn on every run; H ranges are re-drawn only when at least one `h1`–`h4` field is explicit, and unpinned 3.x ranges fall back to fixed defaults.
5. **Build every config in memory first, then write them all to disk.**

::: warning The build is all-or-nothing, but the write loop is not transactional
All configs are computed in memory before a single file is written, so a *build* failure — a bad `awg_version`, an S below the 12-byte floor, two server peers — aborts the run with nothing written. The write loop itself is a plain per-file `WriteFile` with no temp-file-and-rename, so an I/O error partway through can leave earlier files updated and later ones stale.
:::

The result is **one directory per peer, each containing an `awg0.conf`**:

```text
output/
├── server/awg0.conf   ← server config (contains a [Peer] block for every client)
└── phone/awg0.conf    ← client config for "phone"
```

That is the core output model: **one `awg0.conf` per peer**, in a directory named after the peer's map key. Copy the server's file to your server, and each client's file to its machine. `generate` prints the relative paths and byte sizes of what it wrote, for example (one observed run of this two-peer manifest):

```text
Generated 2 config(s):
  server/awg0.conf (743 bytes)
  phone/awg0.conf (1027 bytes)
```

Treat those byte counts as observations, not constants. The file *list* is fixed by the manifest and by the flags you pass, but the sizes drift between runs because the unpinned S and J values are re-drawn and their digit widths vary — a sample of this fixture produced 1027, 1028, and 1029 bytes. The `I1`–`I4` strings themselves stay byte-identical from run to run, because `quic` is a deterministic template. The output directory itself is not printed; it defaults to `<project>/output`.

Pass `--vpn-links` to also generate an **AmneziaVPN import link** for each client peer. With that flag, every client directory gains an `amnezigo.vpn` file alongside its `awg0.conf`:

```text
output/
├── server/
│   └── awg0.conf          ← server never gets a .vpn file
└── phone/
    ├── awg0.conf
    └── amnezigo.vpn       ← vpn:// import link (--vpn-links only)
```

Each `amnezigo.vpn` file contains a single `vpn://` URL that encodes the client's full config. The link is importable directly by the **AmneziaVPN app** (mobile or desktop) — you scan a QR code or paste the URL and the app configures the tunnel for you. This is distinct from the `awg0.conf` INI file, which targets the standalone AmneziaWG client or kernel module. The server peer never gets a `.vpn` file; only clients do. See [VPN Import Links](/vpn-links) for the full envelope format and usage details.

::: tip Keys are reused by default
The first `generate` creates fresh keys for every peer and bakes them into the configs. On the next run, Amnezigo reads those keys — and the 3.x header-protection key — back out of the output files and reuses them, so re-generating after editing a peer's address does **not** silently rotate everyone's keys. Pass `--full-reset` when you genuinely want all-new material; it rotates every peer keypair, every preshared key, and the header-protection key, invalidating all previously distributed configs.
:::

::: warning Key reuse does not mean config stability
Obfuscation parameters are the exception to reuse: every unpinned S1–S4 and Jc/Jmin/Jmax is re-drawn on each run (H ranges are re-drawn only when at least one `h1`–`h4` field is explicit; unpinned 3.x ranges fall back to their fixed defaults), while the keys stay byte-identical. Configs from different runs are therefore not mutually consistent, and existing clients may need to re-import. Pin the values you care about, or regenerate every peer in one run. [Credentials](/credentials) covers the split in detail.
:::

A generated client config for the default 3.1 profile looks like this. The S values and `Jc`/`Jmin`/`Jmax` below come from one observed run — they are re-drawn on the next run, while the keys, the transport block, and the deterministic `I1`–`I4` strings stay the same:

```ini
[Interface]
PrivateKey = <client private key>
Address = 10.0.0.2/32
DNS = 
MTU = 1280
Jc = 8
Jmin = 235
Jmax = 313
S1 = 18
S2 = 18
S3 = 18
S4 = 18
H1 = 1-1
H2 = 2-2
H3 = 3-3
H4 = 4-4
HeaderProtectionKey = <44-character base64 key>
ContentPaddingAddition = 2-10
RekeyAfterTime = 120-180
RekeyTimeout = 5-8
RejectAfterTime = 180-240
KeepaliveTimeout = 8-12
MaxHandshakeAttempts = 16-20
RandomTrailers = on
DisableCookies = on
I1 = <b 0xc0ff><b 0x00000001><b 0x08><r 8><b 0x00><b 0x00><b 0x0040><b 0x00><b 0x01><t><r 40>
I2 = <b 0xc0ff><b 0x00000001><b 0x08><d><b 0x00><b 0x00><b 0x0020><b 0x01><t><r 20>
I3 = <b 0xc0ff><b 0x00000001><b 0x08><r 8><b 0x00><b 0x00><b 0x0010><b 0x01><t><r 10>
I4 = <b 0xc0ff><b 0x00000001><b 0x08><r 8><b 0x00><b 0x00><b 0x0005><b 0x01><t><r 5>

[Peer]
PublicKey = <server public key>
PresharedKey = <unique per-client PSK>
Endpoint = vpn.example.com:51820
AllowedIPs = 0.0.0.0/0, ::/0
PersistentKeepalive = 0
```

Two rendering details in that excerpt are normal. The client writer always emits a `DNS` line, even when `network.dns` is unset and the value is empty. And every named template fills `I1` through `I4` while leaving the fifth interval empty, so the writer emits no `I5` line here; only the `random` protocol generates all five intervals, and any empty interval is omitted.

Do not try to read the `I1`–`I4` and `Jc`/`S1` lines yet — they are the **obfuscation profile** and the per-client **CPS**, which the next section defines. For now, the takeaway is the shape: one self-contained INI file per peer, ready to hand to the AmneziaWG interface.

## Key Concepts

Before reading any other page, nail down these ideas. Everything else builds on them.

### Server peer vs client peer

Amnezigo has **no `role` field**. Instead, it *infers* each peer's role from two fields:

> A peer is a **server peer** when *both* `endpoint` **and** `listen_port` are set. Every other peer is a **client peer**.

| Role | How it is detected | How many are allowed? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Server peer | `endpoint != ""` **AND** `listen_port != 0` | exactly **one** |
| Client peer | anything else | zero or more |

In the manifest above, `server` has both an endpoint and a listen port, so it is the server; `phone` has neither, so it is a client.

::: warning Both markers are required
A peer with *only* an `endpoint`, or *only* a `listen_port`, is **not** a server — it is a client. Both fields must be set for server detection to fire. And a manifest with zero servers, or with two or more servers, is rejected outright: there must be exactly **one** server peer.
:::

The role determines what gets generated for that peer:

- **Server config** lives at `output/<server-name>/awg0.conf`. It has no `Endpoint` of its own (it *is* the endpoint), listens on its `listen_port`, carries the shared obfuscation profile and transport-protection block, and contains a `[Peer]` block for *every* client.
- **Client config** lives at `output/<client-name>/awg0.conf`. It points at the server via `Endpoint`, carries the client's own address and keys, the same shared profile and transport block, plus per-client CPS, and always gets `AllowedIPs = 0.0.0.0/0, ::/0` (a full tunnel).

### The shared obfuscation profile

AmneziaWG defeats deep-packet inspection by adding "junk" to the WireGuard handshake. Three families of parameters control how much junk, and where:

- **S-prefixes** (`s1`, `s2`, `s3`, `s4`) — magic size prefixes added to each handshake message type.
- **Header ranges** (`h1`–`h4`) — `{ "min", "max" }` ranges for the header bytes.
- **Junk control** (`jc`, `jmin`, `jmax`) — junk packet count and size range.

These are **network-wide**: the server and every client *must* use identical S/H/J values, or the handshake simply fails. That is why they live in one top-level `obfuscation` object in the manifest rather than being scattered per-peer. Amnezigo takes that single profile and stamps it into every generated config, guaranteeing consistency by construction — there is no way for a client to drift out of sync with its server.

::: tip Pin what you care about, randomise the rest
Every S/H/J field is nullable, so you can pin just the values you care about and let Amnezigo fill the rest. Under the default 3.1 header protection the fill rules are not "random everywhere": with all H fields unset the ranges become the fixed reference set `1-1`/`2-2`/`3-3`/`4-4`, and unpinned S values draw from a floor of 12 with one shared value when random trailers are on. The resolved values are written into every generated `awg0.conf`, so you can read them out of the output afterwards and record them.
:::

For the full field-by-field breakdown — including why `h1`–`h4` cannot overlap the WireGuard message type-ids `1`–`4` without header protection — see [Obfuscation](/obfuscation), and for the 3.x layer on top of it, [Transport Protection](/transport-protection).

### Per-client CPS (custom packet strings)

The obfuscation profile above is *shared*, but each client **also** gets its own **custom packet strings** — the `I1`–`I5` slots in the example config (the QUIC template leaves the fifth empty). These strings are **client-only**: they never appear on the server's `[Interface]`. Their shape is chosen per client by a **protocol**: `quic` (the default when the field is empty), `dns`, `dtls`, `stun`, `sip`, `rtp`, and `random`. The protocol is set per-peer (`"protocol": "dns"` on a client).

CPS strings are written in a small tag mini-language — for example `<b 0xc0>` emits fixed bytes, `<r 12>` emits twelve random bytes, `<rc 4>` emits random letters, `<rd 2>` random digits, `<t>` emits a four-byte timestamp, and `<d>` is a runtime passthrough expanded by the AWG 2.0 userspace.

::: tip Named templates are deterministic
For the six named protocol templates, the `I1`–`I5` strings are a pure function of the protocol and the MTU: the same manifest produces byte-identical strings across peers and across runs. The `random` protocol is the exception — it draws a fresh tag sequence each run. On the wire the bytes still differ from config to config, because `<r N>` and `<t>` expand in the engine.
:::

::: warning Not every tag works everywhere
The `<c>` counter tag does **not** exist — it was removed and is rejected by amneziawg-go and all AmneziaVPN clients ("unknown tag"). The `<d>` tag requires the AWG **2.0** userspace; the legacy kernel module rejects it. Stick to `<b>`, `<r>`, `<rc>`, `<rd>`, `<t>`, and `<d>`. Unknown or malformed tags count as zero bytes rather than failing loudly, so a typo shrinks an interval silently.
:::

::: tip The protocol on the *peer* is the one that counts
There is a top-level `obfuscation.protocol` field, but `generate` does **not** read it — it is effectively decorative. The protocol that actually drives a client's CPS is the per-peer `protocol` field, which defaults to `quic` when left empty.
:::

## Where To Go Next

You now have the complete mental model: **manifest → `generate` → one `awg0.conf` per peer**, with a shared obfuscation profile and transport-protection block stamped into every file and per-client CPS layered on top. From here, the natural next steps are:

1. **[Quick Start](/quick-start)** — install the binary and bring up a real server plus one client in five minutes.
2. **[Manifest Reference](/manifest-reference)** — every field, every type, every default, with notes on nullable-vs-zero.
3. **[Manifest Examples](/manifest-examples)** — complete manifests for common topologies (road-warrior, site-to-site, mobile).
4. **[Obfuscation](/obfuscation)** — the S/H/J parameters and the full CPS tag grammar, in depth.
5. **[Transport Protection](/transport-protection)** — the AWG 3.x device layer: the nine keys, per-version defaults, the S floor, and the validation codes.
6. **[CLI Reference](/cli-reference)** — every flag for `generate`, `validate`, and `analyze`.

If you prefer to learn by example, start with [Manifest Examples](/manifest-examples) and copy the topology closest to your setup. If you just want to ship something working right now, start with [Quick Start](/quick-start).

# Quick Start

This guide takes you from zero to a working AmneziaWG 3.1 network in five minutes. You will install Amnezigo, declare a minimal network in `amnezigo.json`, generate per-peer configs, read the output, grow the network, and lint the result.

Amnezigo is a **declarative** generator: you describe the topology you want in a manifest, run one command, and it writes ready-to-use WireGuard/AmneziaWG INI files. There is no imperative add/remove/export flow — the manifest is the single source of truth.

## Prerequisites

- **Go 1.26.1 or newer** — needed to build and install the `amnezigo` binary (`go.mod`).
- **The `amnezigo` binary on your `PATH`.** Install the latest release:

  ```shell
  go install github.com/Arsolitt/amnezigo/cmd/amnezigo@latest
  ```

  This places the binary in `$GOPATH/bin` (typically `$HOME/go/bin`). Make sure that directory is on your `PATH`, then verify the build stamp:

  ```shell
  amnezigo version
  ```

  The output has the shape `amnezigo <version> (<commit>)` — for example `amnezigo 0.4.0 (abc1234)` from a tagged release (release builds strip the leading `v`), or `amnezigo dev (none)` from a plain `go build`. See [Installation](/installation) for prebuilt archives, Docker images, and development builds.

- **An AmneziaWG userspace runtime** (not installed by Amnezigo). The generated configs target the runtime generation selected by `obfuscation.awg_version`, which defaults to `"3.1"` in this release; the legacy kernel module does not understand the 3.x transport-protection keys. You only need the runtime when you actually bring a tunnel up — generating configs needs nothing but the `amnezigo` binary.

::: tip Only four commands exist
Amnezigo has exactly four subcommands: `generate`, `validate`, `analyze`, and `version`. This guide uses all four. If you see references to `init`, `add`, `edit`, `remove`, `export`, or `list` anywhere, those commands were removed — they do not exist.
:::

## Write a Minimal Manifest

In an empty project directory, create `amnezigo.json`. The smallest useful manifest declares a schema version, a network MTU, an AmneziaWG version, and exactly two peers: one **server** and one **client**.

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "network": {
    "mtu": 1280
  },
  "obfuscation": {
    "awg_version": "3.1"
  },
  "peers": {
    "server": {
      "address": "10.0.0.1/24",
      "endpoint": "vpn.example.com:51820",
      "listen_port": 51820
    },
    "phone": {
      "address": "10.0.0.2/32"
    }
  }
}
```

This is the repo fixture `testdata/loader/valid/amnezigo-31.json`, byte for byte. (The repo also ships `testdata/loader/valid/amnezigo.json` — the same network pinned to `"awg_version": "2.0"` with explicit S/H/J values, kept as the 2.0 regression case.)

::: danger Set `network.mtu` explicitly
An omitted `network.mtu` is a known defect, not a shortcut. The emitted configs still say `MTU = 1280`, but CPS generation runs before that default is applied, so the client's `I1`-`I5` all collapse to the bare `<t>` interval and lose their protocol mimicry. Always write `network.mtu` in the manifest — a missing `network` section silently produces degenerate I-packets.
:::

### Annotated, field by field

JSON has no comments, so the block below is a study aid rather than a file to save. If you want comments to live in the manifest, save the same content as `.amnezigo.jsonnet` — Jsonnet is a JSON superset and Amnezigo loads it natively (see [Jsonnet](/jsonnet)).

```jsonnet
{
  // Schema version. MUST be the integer 1. Required — an empty object {}
  // or a missing version fails with "missing or zero version field".
  "version": 1,

  "network": {
    // Per-interface MTU. Set it explicitly: leaving it out degenerates
    // the client's I1-I5 to the bare "<t>" interval.
    "mtu": 1280
  },

  "obfuscation": {
    // Wire generation: "2.0", "3.0" or "3.1". Unset selects the 3.1
    // defaults for this release. 3.1 turns header protection on and adds
    // the nine transport-protection keys to every generated config.
    "awg_version": "3.1",

    // Everything else is optional. S/H/J values left out are drawn from
    // crypto/rand at each run — see "Re-running generate" below.
  },

  "peers": {
    // Peer names are MAP KEYS — there is no "name" field on a peer.
    // The key becomes the output directory name.
    "server": {
      "address": "10.0.0.1/24",            // CIDR, required for every peer
      "endpoint": "vpn.example.com:51820", // host:port — server marker (1 of 2)
      "listen_port": 51820                 // non-zero  — server marker (2 of 2)
    },
    "phone": {
      "address": "10.0.0.2/32"             // clients set address only
    }
  }
}
```

Reference for the fields that matter most in a minimal manifest:

> `version`: int (required) — must be `1`.
> `network.mtu`: int — per-interface MTU. Set it explicitly (see the warning above).
> `obfuscation.awg_version`: string — `"2.0"`, `"3.0"` or `"3.1"`; unset selects the 3.1 defaults.
> `peers.<name>.address`: string (CIDR, required) — e.g. `10.0.0.1/24`.
> `peers.<name>.endpoint`: string — `host:port`; together with a non-zero `listen_port` marks a **server** peer.
> `peers.<name>.listen_port`: int — non-zero; together with `endpoint` marks a **server** peer.

The complete field list lives in [Manifest Reference](/manifest-reference). S/H/J tuning and the CPS tag language are covered in [Obfuscation](/obfuscation), and the nine 3.x keys in [Transport Protection](/transport-protection).

::: warning What makes a peer the server
A peer is the server **only when both** `endpoint` is non-empty **and** `listen_port` is non-zero. A peer with just one of the two is a client. A valid manifest has **exactly one** server peer — zero or more than one is a hard error (`exactly one server peer required, found N`).
:::

::: warning S values are checked against the header-protection floor
With `awg_version: "3.1"` (and any other generation whose profile leaves header protection on), every explicitly pinned S value must be `>= 12`. A manifest that pins `"s1": 3` aborts generation before anything is written:

```text
Error: generating configs: resolve obfuscation: header protection requires S1-S4 >= 12 (got S1=3)
```

Pinning an S to `0` does **not** pin it to zero: an explicit zero S is treated as unset and re-drawn from `crypto/rand`, which also disables the uniform-S path and can trigger the `TRL001` warning. If you want a fixed profile, pin all of `s1`-`s4` to non-zero values.
:::

## Run `amnezigo generate`

From the directory containing `amnezigo.json`:

```shell
amnezigo generate
```

`generate` with no flags reads `./amnezigo.json` (or `./.amnezigo.jsonnet`) and writes to `./output`. It loads the manifest, builds a full set of configs in memory, then writes them and prints one summary line per file:

```shell
Generated 2 config(s):
  server/awg0.conf (743 bytes)
  phone/awg0.conf (1027 bytes)
```

For a default run the number of config files equals the number of peers (with `--peer` the server is always included and only selected clients are written; `--vpn-links` adds one `amnezigo.vpn` per client). Each line shows the path **relative to the output directory** plus the file size in bytes, and the sizes are observations rather than constants — they drift by a byte or two between runs because generated key and parameter values differ in length.

If resolution or validation emits findings during generation, a `Warnings: N` block follows the file list and the command still exits 0:

```shell
Generated 2 config(s):
  server/awg0.conf (743 bytes)
  phone/awg0.conf (1027 bytes)

Warnings: 1
[WARNING TRL001]  (key=RandomTrailers): RandomTrailers is enabled while S1..S4 differ; the AWG 3.1 reference recommends equal S values to avoid packet-type misclassification
```

This particular warning appears when you pin unequal S prefixes while `RandomTrailers` is on. Warnings never change the exit code; use `amnezigo validate --strict` if you want them to fail a pipeline.

### Useful flags

| Flag | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `--project` | current working directory | project directory containing the manifest |
| `--output` | `<project>/output` | output directory for generated configs |
| `--full-reset` | `false` | regenerate **all** credentials: every peer keypair, every PSK, and the header-protection key |
| `--dry-run` | `false` | compute configs without writing files; prints `Dry run — no files written` |
| `--peer` | (none) | generate only the named client peers (repeatable); the server config is always generated |
| `--jpath` | (none) | extra Jsonnet library search paths |
| `--vpn-links` | `false` | also emit an AmneziaVPN `vpn://` import link for each client peer |

::: warning `--dry-run` is a file-list preview, not a key preview
Credentials are resolved before the write step is skipped. On a project that already has `output/`, a dry run reads the persisted keys and does not rotate them, so it is safe. On a **fresh** project the dry run computes brand-new keys in memory and writes nothing; the following real run generates a *different* key set, and the dry run never prints the config bodies it built anyway. `--dry-run` shows which files would be written and their approximate sizes — never the key material the next real run will persist.
:::

::: tip Generate AmneziaVPN import links
Add `--vpn-links` to also emit a `vpn://` import link (`amnezigo.vpn`) for each client peer, ready to paste into the AmneziaVPN app:

```shell
amnezigo generate --vpn-links
```

The run then reports three files — the extra one is a client-only artifact (an observed run printed `phone/amnezigo.vpn (1352 bytes)`; the size varies):

```shell
Generated 3 config(s):
  server/awg0.conf (743 bytes)
  phone/awg0.conf (1027 bytes)
  phone/amnezigo.vpn (1352 bytes)
```

The server peer never gets a `.vpn` file. See [VPN Import Links](/vpn-links) for the envelope format and app import walkthrough.
:::

## Understand the Output

After the run above, your project looks like this:

```text
your-project/
├── amnezigo.json
└── output/
    ├── server/
    │   └── awg0.conf      # [Interface] + one [Peer] block per client
    └── phone/
        └── awg0.conf      # client [Interface] (with I1-I5) + server [Peer]
```

One directory per peer, each named after the manifest map key, each holding a single `awg0.conf`. The **server** config carries the server's `[Interface]` and a `[Peer]` section for every client. Each **client** config carries the client's own `[Interface]` and a single `[Peer]` pointing at the server.

Here is the generated `output/server/awg0.conf` (a real first run; yours will differ because keys and unpacked parameters are randomly generated):

```ini
[Interface]
PrivateKey = sA7LpOtZJydB5iInEAAUmBjwZZx5ILb1Fe+Z3DxKRGM=
PublicKey = dpSeRIK19rRT0EoY4TOOY6uMB63QMq82nTizThXcNDM=
Address = 10.0.0.1/24
ListenPort = 51820
MTU = 1280
Jc = 5
Jmin = 565
Jmax = 695
S1 = 30
S2 = 30
S3 = 30
S4 = 30
H1 = 1-1
H2 = 2-2
H3 = 3-3
H4 = 4-4
HeaderProtectionKey = B0YSRUqub6BMguRznhvTYFxtEpHzNlPm1pO7JjI45xo=
ContentPaddingAddition = 2-10
RekeyAfterTime = 120-180
RekeyTimeout = 5-8
RejectAfterTime = 180-240
KeepaliveTimeout = 8-12
MaxHandshakeAttempts = 16-20
RandomTrailers = on
DisableCookies = on
#_ClientToClient = false
#_TunName = awg0

[Peer]
#_Name = phone
PublicKey = QEaMGaN802IjxoSYnuGau+LPqsaD0LLvooxGyHwLx3w=
PresharedKey = BPMWg06swhgjzeCoRQHaZQq2s+XljjWGh7B/lxIMu94=
AllowedIPs = 10.0.0.2/32
```

A few things to notice:

- The 2.0 block (`Jc`/`Jmin`/`Jmax`, `S1`-`S4`, `H1`-`H4`) is followed by the **nine AWG 3.x transport-protection keys**: `HeaderProtectionKey`, `ContentPaddingAddition`, `RekeyAfterTime`, `RekeyTimeout`, `RejectAfterTime`, `KeepaliveTimeout`, `MaxHandshakeAttempts`, `RandomTrailers`, `DisableCookies`. See [Transport Protection](/transport-protection) for what each does, and [Output Format](/output-format) for the exact key order.
- The 3.1 defaults are visible in the output: `ContentPaddingAddition = 2-10`, `RekeyAfterTime = 120-180`, `RekeyTimeout = 5-8`, `RejectAfterTime = 180-240`, `KeepaliveTimeout = 8-12`, `MaxHandshakeAttempts = 16-20`, `RandomTrailers = on`, `DisableCookies = on`, and a 44-character base64 `HeaderProtectionKey` that is identical in the server and client configs.
- With header protection on and no explicit H ranges, the header ranges are the plain WireGuard type-ids: `H1 = 1-1`, `H2 = 2-2`, `H3 = 3-3`, `H4 = 4-4`.
- With random trailers on and no explicit S values, **one** random S is drawn and reused for all four prefixes (`S1 = S2 = S3 = S4`, each `>= 12`), because trailer classification is size-based. Pin S values if you need a specific padding profile.
- `#_`-prefixed lines are **metadata comments** — Amnezigo's own bookkeeping (tunnel name, peer name). WireGuard ignores them; Amnezigo reads them back on the next run when reusing credentials.
- The client's `AllowedIPs` in the server config is the client's own `/32` address (`10.0.0.2/32`).

::: tip The client config is the fuller one
The client's `phone/awg0.conf` additionally contains the `I1`-`I5` custom packet strings and a `[Peer]` block with the server's `Endpoint` and a full-tunnel `AllowedIPs = 0.0.0.0/0, ::/0` route:

```ini
[Interface]
PrivateKey = 0G4wsohXEWnSIt3tw6pIPAsOmOJCoyo3YVcdMQKTZXY=
Address = 10.0.0.2/32
DNS = 
MTU = 1280
Jc = 5
Jmin = 565
Jmax = 695
S1 = 30
S2 = 30
S3 = 30
S4 = 30
H1 = 1-1
H2 = 2-2
H3 = 3-3
H4 = 4-4
HeaderProtectionKey = B0YSRUqub6BMguRznhvTYFxtEpHzNlPm1pO7JjI45xo=
ContentPaddingAddition = 2-10
RekeyAfterTime = 120-180
RekeyTimeout = 5-8
RejectAfterTime = 180-240
KeepaliveTimeout = 8-12
MaxHandshakeAttempts = 16-20
RandomTrailers = on
DisableCookies = on
I1 = <b 0xc0ff><b 0x00000001><b 0x08><r 8><b 0x00><b 0x00><b 0x0040><b 0x00><b 0x01><t><r 40>
I2 = <b 0xc0ff><b 0x00000001><b 0x08><d><b 0x00><b 0x00><b 0x0020><b 0x01><t><r 20>
I3 = <b 0xc0ff><b 0x00000001><b 0x08><r 8><b 0x00><b 0x00><b 0x0010><b 0x01><t><r 10>
I4 = <b 0xc0ff><b 0x00000001><b 0x08><r 8><b 0x00><b 0x00><b 0x0005><b 0x01><t><r 5>

[Peer]
PublicKey = dpSeRIK19rRT0EoY4TOOY6uMB63QMq82nTizThXcNDM=
PresharedKey = BPMWg06swhgjzeCoRQHaZQq2s+XljjWGh7B/lxIMu94=
Endpoint = vpn.example.com:51820
AllowedIPs = 0.0.0.0/0, ::/0
PersistentKeepalive = 0
```

The `I1`-`I5` values are CPS tag strings; the server config never carries them. They are recomputed for every client on every run, but they are **deterministic for named protocol templates** — the same `peers.<name>.protocol` plus the same `network.mtu` yields byte-identical strings across peers and across runs. Only a peer with `peers.<name>.protocol: "random"` draws a fresh tag sequence each run. On the wire the bytes still differ, because `<r N>` and `<t>` expand at runtime. There is no `I5` line above because the built-in templates leave the fifth interval empty; the writer skips empty I-values, so a missing `I5` is expected, not a truncation bug. The tag language (`<b>`, `<r>`, `<t>`, `<d>`, `<rc>`, `<rd>`, and the silently rejected `<c>`) is documented in [Obfuscation](/obfuscation).

`DNS = ` is emitted empty because `network.dns` is unset — set it in the manifest for a usable resolver list, or edit the client config before importing it.
:::

### Using the `vpn://` import link

When you generate with `--vpn-links`, each client directory contains an `amnezigo.vpn` file with a single `vpn://` URL. This link encodes the full client config — keys, endpoint, obfuscation params, and CPS tags — in a compressed base64url envelope that the **AmneziaVPN app** can import directly:

1. Open the `amnezigo.vpn` file and copy the entire `vpn://...` line.
2. In the AmneziaVPN app, add a new configuration and paste the link.
3. The app decodes the envelope and configures the tunnel automatically.

::: warning vpn:// links are for the AmneziaVPN app, not standalone AmneziaWG
The `vpn://` envelope uses an AmneziaVPN-specific format. The standalone AmneziaWG client and kernel module cannot import these links — for those, use `awg0.conf` directly. See [VPN Import Links](/vpn-links).
:::

## Re-running generate

By default, `generate` reuses the credentials already present under `output/`: it recovers each peer's private key from that peer's own `output/<name>/awg0.conf`, and the server's keypair and the header-protection key survive unchanged. Verified by re-running the fixture: `PrivateKey`, `PublicKey`, `PresharedKey`, and `HeaderProtectionKey` were byte-identical before and after, including across a `--dry-run`.

Only the **keys** are stable. Every obfuscation value left unset in the manifest is re-drawn from `crypto/rand` on each run: `S1`-`S4`, `Jc`/`Jmin`/`Jmax`, and the H ranges whenever no header-protection key applies (under header protection with all H unset they are the constant `1-1`/`2-2`/`3-3`/`4-4`). Six consecutive runs of the fixture above produced `Jmin`-`Jmax` junk ranges `311-995`, `545-682`, `487-591`, `507-572`, `677-703`, `355-866` and S values `31`, `31`, `21`, `17`, `22`, `23`. A re-run therefore does **not** reproduce the file bytes, and a previously distributed client config can silently stop matching the regenerated server config.

::: danger Re-running generate is not a no-op
Keys and PSKs are reused, but unpacked obfuscation parameters are re-drawn every run — so only configs written by the *same* run are mutually consistent. To make re-runs byte-stable, pin `s1`-`s4`, `h1`-`h4`, and `jc`/`jmin`/`jmax` in the manifest. Remember also that `output/` **is** the credential store: deleting it silently generates a brand-new key set on the next run.
:::

::: warning Want everything fresh? Use `--full-reset`
`amnezigo generate --full-reset` ignores all persisted credentials and regenerates every peer keypair, every PSK, **and the header-protection key**. Use it deliberately — every client config changes and must be redistributed. `--peer` does not protect against this: the shared header-protection key rotates no matter which clients you asked for.
:::

### Generating for a single client

`--peer phone` limits the client set to the named peers, but the server config is always regenerated, so for this manifest the output still contains two files:

```shell
Generated 2 config(s):
  server/awg0.conf (743 bytes)
  phone/awg0.conf (1027 bytes)
```

A `--peer` value that matches no manifest peer is ignored without a warning: `generate --peer nobody` prints the summary header plus a single file line (`Generated 1 config(s):` then `server/awg0.conf`) and exits 0. See [CLI Reference](/cli-reference) for the full flag and exit-code matrix.

## Add Another Peer

Growing the network is just editing the manifest. Add a second client — say `laptop`:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "network": { "mtu": 1280 },
  "obfuscation": { "awg_version": "3.1" },
  "peers": {
    "server": { "address": "10.0.0.1/24", "endpoint": "vpn.example.com:51820", "listen_port": 51820 },
    "phone":  { "address": "10.0.0.2/32" },
    "laptop": { "address": "10.0.0.3/32" }
  }
}
```

Re-run the same command:

```shell
amnezigo generate
```

An observed run produced three files and a new directory:

```shell
Generated 3 config(s):
  server/awg0.conf (909 bytes)
  laptop/awg0.conf (1027 bytes)
  phone/awg0.conf (1027 bytes)
```

```text
output/
├── laptop/
│   └── awg0.conf
├── phone/
│   └── awg0.conf
└── server/
    └── awg0.conf
```

The `laptop` peer appears in the server config as a new `[Peer]` block with `AllowedIPs = 10.0.0.3/32`, and gets its own directory. The existing `phone` peer keeps exactly the same `PrivateKey` it had before — you can verify it directly, since the value is byte-identical across the two runs:

```shell
grep '^PrivateKey' output/phone/awg0.conf
```

Because the default protocol template is named (`quic`), `phone` and `laptop` receive identical `I1`-`I5` strings from the same run — the disguise is a property of the protocol profile, not of the peer. Only a peer with `peers.<name>.protocol: "random"` gets its own fresh tag sequence.

## Lint and Profile the Result

`generate` mutates the filesystem; `validate` and `analyze` are read-only. Lint the server config first:

```shell
amnezigo validate output/server/awg0.conf
```

A freshly generated 3.1 config is clean, and the command exits 0:

```shell
✓ output/server/awg0.conf: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 info
```

`validate` is designed for server configs: it strict-parses the file, so a *client* config reports `KEY001` warnings for its client-only keys (`I1`-`I4`, `Endpoint`, `PersistentKeepalive`) plus a hard `FLD001` error for the missing `ListenPort`, exiting 1. Validate the server config, or expect those findings on a client. Add `--strict` to make warnings fail the exit code, and `--output json` for machine-readable findings — details in [Validation](/validation).

`analyze` profiles the packet shape. It reads `./awg0.conf` by default, so point it at the generated file:

```shell
amnezigo analyze --config output/server/awg0.conf
```

```shell
=== AmneziaWG Config Analysis ===

MTU: 1280 | Port: 51820 | Peers: 1 | Protocol: random

--- Handshake Sizes ---
  Init:      S1=30 + 148 = 178 bytes
  Response:  S2=30 + 92 = 122 bytes
  Cookie:    S3=30 + 64 = 94 bytes
  Transport: S4=30 + 32 = 62 bytes

--- Junk Packets ---
  Count: 5 (Jc) | Range: [565..695] | Width: 131 B

--- Header Ranges ---
  H1: [1..1] (width 1)
  H2: [2..2] (width 1)
  H3: [3..3] (width 1)
  H4: [4..4] (width 1)

--- I-Packets (per peer) ---
  Peer "phone":
    i1=116  i2=94  i3=79  i4=146  i5=72 bytes

--- Wire Ordering ---
  1. i1 -> i2 -> i3 -> i4 -> i5
  2. junk x 5
  3. Handshake Init

--- Findings ---
  [info] RISK005: padded Cookie (94) is within ±4 B of raw WG size 92 — may confuse naive DPI
  [info] RISK005: padded Transport (62) is within ±4 B of raw WG size 64 — may confuse naive DPI

Note: I-packet sizes are freshly generated from config parameters and may differ on each run.
```

Two behaviors matter here:

- **Findings do not fail the command.** `analyze` exits 0 even when the report lists `RISK` findings; only a config-load failure or an invalid `--output` value makes it exit 1. Parse `--output json` in CI instead of trusting the exit status.
- **The report regenerates I-packets.** `analyze` recomputes I-packet sizes from the config's parameters using its own `--protocol` flag (default `random`), so the sizes it prints are not necessarily the `I1`-`I5` stored in the file, and its protocol line says nothing about the template that produced them.

::: warning `analyze --seed` is a shipping defect
`--seed` is accepted, and the help text presents it as making the report reproducible, but the seeded reader is never read by the analysis code — two runs with the same seed still produce different output. Do not rely on `--seed` for reproducibility.
:::

## Next Steps

You now have a generated 3.1 network. Where to go from here:

- **Learn the 3.x layer you just emitted** — [Transport Protection](/transport-protection) explains the nine keys, their defaults, and the gates the resolver applies.
- **Tune obfuscation deliberately** — [Obfuscation](/obfuscation) covers the S/H/J knobs, the CPS tag language, and the protocol templates; [Presets](/presets) documents seven named profiles, but there is no `--preset` flag and no manifest field: copy the preset's obfuscation values into `obfuscation.*`, its MTU into `network.mtu`, and its cover protocol into `peers.<name>.protocol` by hand (`obfuscation.mtu` and `obfuscation.protocol` do not exist and are silently ignored), or reproduce the preset in Jsonnet.
- **Read the field list** — [Manifest Reference](/manifest-reference) documents every manifest key and its defaults; [Manifest Examples](/manifest-examples) has more topologies.
- **Switch to Jsonnet** for comments, variables, and shared profiles stored as `.amnezigo.jsonnet` — see [Jsonnet](/jsonnet). No Jsonnet libraries ship with the repo; `lib/` is a user convention, and `--jpath` points at whatever you create.
- **Generate `vpn://` import links** — `amnezigo generate --vpn-links` writes an `amnezigo.vpn` file per client, ready for the AmneziaVPN app; the envelope format is in [VPN Import Links](/vpn-links).
- **Gate a pipeline** — [Validation](/validation) covers `validate`/`analyze` output formats and exit codes; [CLI Reference](/cli-reference) lists every flag.
- **Understand credential lifecycle** — [Credentials](/credentials) details key and parameter reuse, `--full-reset`, and how `output/` acts as the credential store.
- **Check the sharp edges** — [Gotchas](/gotchas) collects open defects such as the omitted-MTU collapse and the ineffective `analyze --seed`.

The manifest is the source of truth: change it, re-run `amnezigo generate`, and the `output/` tree reflects your new topology.
---
url: /installation
---
# Installation

Amnezigo is a single static binary — a declarative AmneziaWG **2.0/3.0/3.1** configuration generator (default 3.1). It exposes exactly four subcommands: `generate`, `validate`, `analyze`, and `version`. There are no `init`, `add`, `edit`, `remove`, `export`, or `list` commands.

::: warning
Amnezigo only *generates* `awg0.conf` files. It does not install, enable, or manage an AmneziaWG runtime, set up network interfaces, or bring tunnels up/down. Running the generated configs requires an AmneziaWG engine matching the manifest's `obfuscation.awg_version` — see [Transport Protection](/transport-protection) for the version model and runtime requirements.
:::

This page walks through every supported install method and verifies the binary at the end.

## Requirements

Amnezigo is written in Go and ships as a single binary with no runtime file dependencies.

> **Go toolchain**: `>= 1.26.1` — declared by the `go 1.26.1` directive in `go.mod`.

| Requirement | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Go | 1.26.1 or newer (only needed for `go install` and build-from-source) |
| Module path | `github.com/Arsolitt/amnezigo` |
| Binary entry point | `cmd/amnezigo/main.go` → calls `cli.Execute()` |
| AmneziaWG runtime | AmneziaWG userspace (`amneziawg-go`) matching the selected `obfuscation.awg_version` — `"2.0"`, `"3.0"`, or `"3.1"` (default `"3.1"`); required to actually run generated configs |
| Docker | Only for the container image; the runtime base and the published images are **amd64-only** (see [Run via Docker](#run-via-docker)) |

::: tip
You only need the Go toolchain to *build* the binary. Once built, `amnezigo` is self-contained and can be copied to any machine of the same OS/architecture — no Go install required on the target.
:::

## Install via `go install`

The fastest path. This downloads, compiles, and installs the binary into your Go bin directory in one step:

```shell
go install github.com/Arsolitt/amnezigo/cmd/amnezigo@latest
```

The binary lands at `$(go env GOPATH)/bin/amnezigo` (typically `~/go/bin/amnezigo`). That directory must be on your `PATH` for the shell to find it. Add it once:

```shell
export PATH="$PATH:$(go env GOPATH)/bin"
```

::: tip
Persist the `PATH` export by appending it to your shell rc (`~/.bashrc`, `~/.zshrc`, etc.) so it survives new terminals.
:::

Pin a specific version by replacing `@latest` with a tag or commit, for example:

```shell
go install github.com/Arsolitt/amnezigo/cmd/amnezigo@v1.0.0
```

::: warning
`go install` (like a plain `go build`) does not stamp a version, so the installed binary reports `amnezigo dev (none)` from `amnezigo version`. Install a release binary or use `make build` when the exact revision matters (see [Verify the Install](#verify-the-install)).
:::

## Prebuilt release binaries

Every tagged release attaches raw, statically linked executables — there is no archive to extract. Download the asset for your OS from the [releases page](https://github.com/Arsolitt/amnezigo/releases):

| Asset | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `amnezigo-linux-amd64` | Linux x86-64 executable. |
| `amnezigo-darwin-amd64` | macOS x86-64 executable (runs on Apple Silicon through Rosetta 2). |
| `checksums.txt` | SHA-256 checksums for every asset. |
| `amnezigo-licenses_<version>.tar.gz` | `LICENSE`, `NOTICE`, and the `licenses/` attribution bundle (GPL-3.0 plus third-party notices). |

```shell
# replace <tag> with the release tag, e.g. v0.4.0
curl -LO https://github.com/Arsolitt/amnezigo/releases/download/<tag>/amnezigo-linux-amd64
curl -LO https://github.com/Arsolitt/amnezigo/releases/download/<tag>/checksums.txt
sha256sum -c --ignore-missing checksums.txt
chmod +x amnezigo-linux-amd64
sudo mv amnezigo-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/amnezigo
```

Use `amnezigo-darwin-amd64` instead of `amnezigo-linux-amd64` on macOS.

::: warning
The release matrix is **amd64-only** — there are no arm64 binaries. On Apple Silicon, `amnezigo-darwin-amd64` runs under Rosetta 2, or build from source for a native arm64 binary.
:::

## Build from Source

Building from source is useful for development, for reproducible local builds, or when you want to pass custom build flags.

1. Clone the repository:

   ```shell
   git clone https://github.com/Arsolitt/amnezigo.git
   cd amnezigo
   ```

2. Build the development binary with the project Makefile:

   ```shell
   make build
   ```

   The binary is written to `bin/amnezigo` (`BIN_DIR` defaults to `bin`), and `make build` injects a version stamp via `-ldflags`: `VERSION` defaults to `git describe --tags --always --dirty` and `COMMIT` to `git rev-parse --short HEAD`. Invoke it directly as `./bin/amnezigo --help`, or move it onto your `PATH`:

   ```shell
   sudo mv bin/amnezigo /usr/local/bin/
   ```

::: tip
`make clean` removes both `bin/` and `dist/`. A bare `go build -o mydir/amnezigo ./cmd/amnezigo/` works too, but produces an unstamped binary that reports `amnezigo dev (none)` — `make build` exists precisely to avoid that.
:::

### Stripped static binary

The production `Dockerfile` builds with CGO disabled and the strip flags `-ldflags="-s -w"`, producing a smaller static binary. Use the same flags for a distribution-ready local build:

```shell
CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 go build -ldflags="-s -w" -o build/amnezigo ./cmd/amnezigo/
```

::: tip
`CGO_ENABLED=0` produces a fully static binary with no libc dependency, ideal for `FROM scratch` or minimal base images. `-s -w` strips the symbol table and DWARF debug info to shrink the file size. This output path (`build/amnezigo`) mirrors the container build stage; the development output is `bin/amnezigo`.
:::

## Run via Docker

Amnezigo ships a multi-stage `Dockerfile` that builds the binary and packages it on top of the AmneziaWG userspace image.

### What the Dockerfile does

```dockerfile
# Stage 1 — builder
FROM golang:1.26-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
ARG VERSION=dev
ARG COMMIT=none
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux go build \
    -ldflags="-s -w -X github.com/Arsolitt/amnezigo/internal/buildinfo.Version=${VERSION} -X github.com/Arsolitt/amnezigo/internal/buildinfo.Commit=${COMMIT}" \
    -o ./build/amnezigo ./cmd/amnezigo/

# Stage 2 — runtime
FROM amneziavpn/amneziawg-go:3.1.20260828
COPY --from=builder /app/build/amnezigo /usr/local/bin/amnezigo
ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/local/bin/amnezigo"]
```

| Stage | Base image | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Builder | `golang:1.26-alpine` | Compiles a static binary with CGO disabled; the version/commit stamp defaults to `dev`/`none` and can be overridden with `--build-arg VERSION=… --build-arg COMMIT=…` |
| Runtime | `amneziavpn/amneziawg-go:3.1.20260828` | AmneziaWG userspace base image (Alpine 3.19, amd64-only). It already ships bash, the ca-certificates bundle, and the `awg` tools, so the build adds **no package layer**. The binary lands at `/usr/local/bin/amnezigo`, which is also the image ENTRYPOINT. |

### Build the image

Both the runtime base image and the published images are amd64-only, so the platform must be explicit on arm64 hosts (Docker then runs the result through Rosetta/containerd emulation):

```shell
docker build --platform linux/amd64 -t amnezigo .
```

`make image` runs exactly this command (the `--platform` flag is already pinned in the target).

### Run amnezigo inside the container

The image sets `ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/local/bin/amnezigo"]`, so subcommands are passed straight to `docker run` — no `--entrypoint` workaround is needed. To generate configs into your working directory, mount it as a volume, set it as the working directory (`generate` writes to `<project>/output` by default), and pass:

```shell
docker run --rm \
  --user $(id -u):$(id -g) \
  -v "$(pwd):/work" \
  -w /work \
  amnezigo generate
```

Generated files appear under `./output/`. Replace `generate` with `validate`, `analyze`, or `version` to run another subcommand.

::: danger
Neither Dockerfile declares a `USER`, deliberately: the CLI reads and writes configs in the mounted working directory. Without `--user $(id -u):$(id -g)`, every file `generate` writes into your project comes out **owned by root** and is awkward to edit or delete afterwards. Always pass the flag when the mounted directory belongs to you.
:::

The published image is `ghcr.io/arsolitt/amnezigo:<version>` (built by GoReleaser from `cmd/amnezigo/Dockerfile`; same entrypoint, and it ships `NOTICE`, `LICENSE`, and `licenses/` under `/usr/share/doc/amnezigo/`):

```shell
docker run --rm --user $(id -u):$(id -g) ghcr.io/arsolitt/amnezigo:<version> version
```

### Container tag rules

Release tags map to image tags with the leading `v` stripped: tag `v1.0.0` publishes `ghcr.io/arsolitt/amnezigo:1.0.0`, and a stable release also updates `:latest`. Prereleases (`vX.Y.Z-rc.N`) are version-tagged only — `:latest` always points at the newest stable release.

::: warning
The runtime stage is pinned to `amneziavpn/amneziawg-go:3.1.20260828`. Generated Amnezigo configs target the generation selected by `obfuscation.awg_version` (default `"3.1"`); the `<d>` CPS tag in particular is a userspace feature (AWG 2.0 or newer) that the legacy kernel module rejects. Keep the engine version aligned with the configured target. See [Obfuscation](/obfuscation) for the CPS grammar.
:::

## Verify the Install

Confirm the binary is reachable and reports the expected identity:

```shell
amnezigo --help
amnezigo version
```

`amnezigo version` prints `amnezigo <Version> (<Commit>)`. The values depend on how the binary was built:

| Build | Example output | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Release binary (GoReleaser) | `amnezigo 0.4.0 (abc1234)` | The version is the release tag with its leading `v` stripped; commit is `{{ .ShortCommit }}`. |
| `go install` / plain `go build` | `amnezigo dev (none)` | Defaults of the `internal/buildinfo` variables; intended for unstamped builds, not a sign of a broken binary. |
| `make build` | `amnezigo v0.3.0-5-g81451b7-dirty (81451b7)` | Stamped from `git describe --tags --always --dirty`, so non-tag commits carry commit distance and a possible `-dirty` suffix — and keep the `v`. |

The same commit can therefore print different strings depending on the build method; library callers can read the same values from `internal/buildinfo.Version` and `internal/buildinfo.Commit` (see [Library API](/library-api)).

The root command's short description is **"AmneziaWG v3.1 Configuration Generator"**, and its `--help` text begins `Declarative AmneziaWG v3.1 configuration generator.` It lists exactly four subcommands:

| Subcommand | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `generate` | Build server and client AmneziaWG configs from a manifest |
| `validate` | Check an existing config against AWG size invariants |
| `analyze` | Heuristic analysis of an obfuscation config for weaknesses |
| `version` | Print the build's version and commit stamp |

If you built from source rather than installing to your `PATH`, invoke the binary by path instead:

```shell
./bin/amnezigo --help
```

You are now ready to write a manifest and run `amnezigo generate`. The binary does not need a manifest to be present for `version` or `--help`; for the manifest format start with [Manifest Reference](/manifest-reference) and the [Quick Start](/quick-start).

## Release Artifacts & Development Tooling

Releases are tag-driven: `vX.Y.Z` publishes a stable GitHub release plus image tags `:X.Y.Z` and `:latest`; `vX.Y.Z-rc.N` publishes a pre-release with the image tag `:X.Y.Z-rc.N` only. In every case the tag's leading `v` is stripped for the container tag.

Every release attaches:

| Asset | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `amnezigo-linux-amd64`, `amnezigo-darwin-amd64` | Raw static executables. The release matrix is **amd64-only** — there are no arm64 binaries. |
| `checksums.txt` | SHA-256 checksums for every asset. |
| `amnezigo-licenses_<version>.tar.gz` | `LICENSE`, `NOTICE`, and the `licenses/` attribution bundle. |
| `ghcr.io/arsolitt/amnezigo:<version>` (container) | The release image, linux/amd64. |

Local development uses the toolchain pinned in `mise.toml` (Go 1.26.8, golangci-lint 2.14.0, GoReleaser 2.18.1):

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `mise install` | Install the pinned tool versions. |
| `make build` / `make test` / `make test-race` / `make test-e2e` | Build the CLI (→ `bin/amnezigo`) and run the unit, race, and Docker-backed e2e suites. |
| `make lint` / `make fmt` | Lint and format with the golden `golangci-lint` config (`.golangci.yaml`). |
| `make notice` (`go run ./hack/noticegen`) | Regenerate `NOTICE` and `licenses/` from the module graph. |
| `make snapshot` | Build every release artifact locally (`goreleaser release --snapshot --clean`). |
| `make image` | Build the from-source container image (the target already pins `--platform linux/amd64`). |
| `make clean` | Remove `bin/` and `dist/`. |
| `mise exec -- goreleaser check` | Validate `.goreleaser.yaml`. |

::: tip
`make test-e2e` self-skips when a reachable Docker daemon or a container able to open `/dev/net/tun` is unavailable — a skipped run proves nothing about the container path, but it is not a failure either. `NOTICE` and `licenses/` are generated and CI-enforced: dependency changes require a warm module cache plus `go run ./hack/noticegen`, and CI skips its jobs entirely for docs-only or README-only changes.
:::
---
url: /manifest-reference
---
# Manifest Reference

The manifest is amnezigo's single declarative input: one JSON document — `amnezigo.json`, or `.amnezigo.jsonnet`, which takes precedence — that declares the whole network. `amnezigo generate` reads it and emits INI configs; `amnezigo validate` and `amnezigo analyze` read the *generated* INI, not the manifest.

The root object has exactly four keys: `version`, `network`, `obfuscation` and `peers`. The manifest is deliberately data-only — there is no `preset` field, no computed value and no crypto material. Randomness, version gating and defaults are all resolved by the generate pipeline, so an unpinned manifest produces different obfuscation parameters on every run.

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "network": { "mtu": 1280, "dns": ["1.1.1.1", "1.0.0.1"] },
  "obfuscation": { "awg_version": "3.1" },
  "peers": {
    "server": { "address": "10.0.0.1/24", "endpoint": "vpn.example.com:51820", "listen_port": 51820, "main_iface": "eth0" },
    "phone":  { "address": "10.0.0.2/32", "keepalive": 25, "protocol": "quic" },
    "laptop": { "address": "10.0.0.3/32" }
  }
}
```

Worked manifests are on [Manifest Examples](/manifest-examples); the AWG 3.x layer in depth is on [Transport Protection](/transport-protection).

## Top-Level Fields

> `version`: `int` — **required**. JSON schema version; must be exactly `1`. No `omitempty`, so `{}` decodes to `0` and is rejected.
> `network`: `NetworkConfig` — optional shared interface settings. No `omitempty`.
> `obfuscation`: `ObfuscationManifest` — optional obfuscation profile. No `omitempty`.
> `peers`: `map[string]PeerManifest` — **required** topology map. No `omitempty`.

| Field | Go type | Required | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `version` | `int` | yes | — | Schema version; must be `1`. |
| `network` | `NetworkConfig` | no | zero value | Interface MTU and client DNS. |
| `obfuscation` | `ObfuscationManifest` | no | zero value | Obfuscation profile, including the ten AWG 3.x transport-protection fields. |
| `peers` | `map[string]PeerManifest` | yes | — | Peer name → peer object. Exactly one peer must be the server. |

All four fields lack `omitempty`, so they always serialize; only `version` and `peers` must actually be present.

### Manifest versioning

| `version` | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `0` or absent | error: `<path>: missing or zero version field` |
| `1` | accepted — the only supported schema |
| anything else | error: `<path>: unsupported schema version <N> (expected 1)` |

- `<path>` is the manifest file path (so a Jsonnet manifest must emit `version: 1` in its output object, not a Jsonnet-level version).
- The check lives in the loaders (`validateManifestVersion`). A `Manifest` built in Go with `Version: 0` is accepted by `Generate` — only real file loading enforces `1`.
- The JSON **schema** version is independent of the AWG **protocol** target: `version: 1` says nothing about `obfuscation.awg_version`.

### Unknown keys

Unknown JSON keys are silently ignored at every level of the document, both top-level and nested. A typo in a field name therefore does not fail loading and future schema fields do not break older binaries — but it also produces no warning, so verify spellings against this page.

### Helper methods on `*Manifest`

| Method | Returns | Behaviour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ServerPeer()` | `(name string, count int)` | Counts peers for which `IsServer()` is true. `generate` calls this method and requires `count == 1`; with `count > 1` the returned name is one of the servers, arbitrary because of map iteration order, so check the count first. |
| `ServerPeerName()` | `string` | Returns the sole server's name and **panics** with `ServerPeerName: expected exactly 1 server peer, found <N>` otherwise. Use `ServerPeer()` in validation code. |
| `PeerNames()` | `[]string` | All peer names, sorted alphabetically. The pipeline does not call it; it sorts its own peer-name slices to the same order. |

## `network`

`NetworkConfig` is global because the MTU belongs to the interface, not the peer, and DNS applies to every client.

> `network.mtu`: `int` — JSON key `mtu`. Per-interface MTU shared by the server and every client. `0` or absent means "unset" in the manifest.
> `network.dns`: `[]string` — JSON key `dns`. Upstream resolvers for **client** configs only.

| Field | JSON key | Type | Required | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| MTU | `mtu` | `int` | no | `0` in the manifest; resolves to `1280` in the emitted configs |
| DNS | `dns` | `[]string` | no | `nil` |

- `dns` is joined with `", "` into the clients' `DNS =` line. The server config never contains a `DNS` line, because the pipeline never populates DNS on the server interface.
- Client configs always emit a `DNS =` line, empty when `network.dns` is unset.
- The `1280` default is applied by the generate pipeline when building each config, not by the loader.

::: danger Omitting `network.mtu` degrades client I1-I5
Both config builders default the *emitted* MTU to `1280`, but the client path generates I1-I5 from `manifest.Network.MTU` **before** applying that default. With the manifest value `0`, `calculateMaxISize` goes negative, every template fails and all five I-packets fall back to the bare `<t>` interval (4 bytes), while the emitted client INI still reads `MTU = 1280`. This is a shipping defect, not intended behaviour: set `network.mtu` explicitly. The server path defaults first and is unaffected.
:::

## `obfuscation`

`ObfuscationManifest` carries the shared obfuscation profile. Every field is optional. S/H/J parameters are pointers so that an absent key means "generate a value"; the AWG 3.x parameters reuse the pointer convention with a version default instead. Every field is resolved by the generate pipeline in `resolveObfuscation`.

::: warning No `preset` field
There is no `preset` key in the schema and no `--preset` flag. Presets live in Go code and are copy-by-value only, so take the value sets from [Presets](/presets) and paste the numbers into `obfuscation.*` (or compute them in Jsonnet). The old imperative `init`/`add`/`edit`/`remove`/`export`/`list` commands no longer exist either; the CLI has exactly four subcommands — `generate`, `validate`, `analyze` and `version`.
:::

### S, H and J parameters

| JSON key | Go type | `nil` (absent) | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `s1`, `s2`, `s3` | `*int` | generated in `[12, 65)` with header protection, `[0, 65)` without | S-prefix lengths 1–3. |
| `s4` | `*int` | generated in `[12, 33)` with header protection, `[0, 33)` without | Capped lower than S1–S3. |
| `h1`–`h4` | `*HeaderRange` | generated (see [H ranges](#h-ranges)) | Header ranges, `{"min": uint32, "max": uint32}`. |
| `jc` | `*int` | generated in `[0, 11)`, retried until non-zero | Junk packet count. |
| `jmin`, `jmax` | `*int` | generated in `[64, 1024]` with `jmin < jmax` | Junk sizes; must not collide with the padded/raw WireGuard packet sizes. |
| `protocol` | `string` | — | **Dead configuration.** Parsed and stored, never read by `generate`. The per-peer `protocol` field is the active selector. |

The four AWG-padded handshake sizes — `S1+148`, `S2+92`, `S3+64`, `S4+32` — must be pairwise distinct (six comparisons; `S1+56 != S2` is only one of them). Independent generated draws are retried (up to 1000 attempts) until the invariant holds; the uniform-S draw needs no retry, because the four padded sizes stay pairwise distinct for any single value of `S`.

```json
"obfuscation": {
  "s1": 30, "s2": 35, "s3": 20, "s4": 12,
  "h1": { "min": 100, "max": 5000000 },
  "h2": { "min": 10000000, "max": 200000000 },
  "h3": { "min": 400000000, "max": 800000000 },
  "h4": { "min": 1000000000, "max": 2100000000 },
  "jc": 5, "jmin": 250, "jmax": 750
}
```

### S-prefix floor under header protection

With header protection active, every S value must be `>= 12`, because the header cipher encrypts the 4-byte message header at offset `S<n>` using a ChaCha20 nonce made from the first 12 bytes of the packet. A violating explicit value aborts generation before any file is written:

```text
header protection requires S1-S4 >= 12 (got S<N>=<value>)
```

Generated values start at 12 in that mode. Under `awg_version: "2.0"` or `header_protection: false` the floor is skipped and S values below 12 are legal. Pinned S values are otherwise used verbatim — the pipeline does not re-draw them and does not enforce the padded-size invariant during generation, so a hand-picked set that collides is only reported later by `validate`/`analyze` (see [Validation](/validation)).

### Uniform S

When `random_trailers` is in effect and **all four** `s1`–`s4` keys are absent, one value is drawn in `[12, 33)` (or `[0, 33)` without header protection, retried to stay non-zero) and applied to `S1 = S2 = S3 = S4`, because the AWG 3.1 receiver classifies packet types by size. Setting any one of the four keys — including an explicit `0`, which is otherwise regenerated — disables the shortcut, the other three fall back to independent draws, and `validate` then warns `TRL001` (`RandomTrailers is enabled while S1..S4 differ; ...`).

### H ranges

`HeaderRange` is `{"min": <uint32>, "max": <uint32>}` with lowercase JSON keys. Resolution depends on the whole set:

- Header protection active **and all four H keys absent**: the fixed reference set is used — `H1 = 1-1`, `H2 = 2-2`, `H3 = 3-3`, `H4 = 4-4`. The 4-byte message type is encrypted, so the WireGuard type-ids 1–4 are no longer observable and the usual avoidance rule does not apply.
- Otherwise the missing ranges are generated: non-overlapping, `Min >= 5`, `Max <= 2147483647`, span `>= 10000000`, and never intersecting the type-ids 1–4. The shortcut is all-or-nothing, so a lone `"h1": {"min": 1, "max": 1}` does **not** imply `2-2`/`3-3`/`4-4` for the rest — the other three become large generated ranges.
- Explicit H values are used verbatim. Mixing an explicit range with generated ones can produce overlapping ranges; amnezigo's own validation does not detect overlap (only `Max < Min` and, without header protection, the type-id rule), and the engine rejects it at `awg setconf` time with `headers must not overlap`.

H ranges are always written in INI as the two-part `Min-Max` form, even when `Min == Max`.

### Junk parameters

`jc`, `jmin` and `jmax` are all-or-nothing when pinned:

- **All three present**: copied verbatim, including an explicit `"jc": 0`. No collision check runs.
- **Any one absent**: the missing fields are generated and a zero `jc` is replaced — `pickNonZero` keeps a non-zero explicit value, and the enclosing loop retries (up to 100 attempts) until `jc != 0`, so `"jc": 0` behaves like "unset" in this case.

### AWG 3.x transport protection

Ten fields configure the AWG 3.0/3.1 device-level transport protection. Nil selects the version default; the version gates are hard errors, not silent ignores.

| JSON key | Go type | Default | Minimum `awg_version` | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `awg_version` | `string` | `""` selects `"3.1"` | — | Target protocol generation. |
| `header_protection` | `*bool` | `true` (3.0/3.1) | `"3.0"` | `false` removes `HeaderProtectionKey` from the output and lifts the S `>= 12` floor. |
| `content_padding` | `*U16Range` | `{2, 10}` | `"3.0"` | Content-padding addition range. |
| `rekey_after_time` | `*U16Range` | `{120, 180}` | `"3.0"` | Rekey-after-time seconds. |
| `rekey_timeout` | `*U16Range` | `{5, 8}` | `"3.0"` | Rekey timeout seconds. |
| `reject_after_time` | `*U16Range` | `{180, 240}` | `"3.0"` | Reject-after-time seconds. |
| `keepalive_timeout` | `*U16Range` | `{8, 12}` | `"3.0"` | Keepalive timeout seconds. |
| `max_handshake_attempts` | `*U16Range` | `{16, 20}` | `"3.0"` | Maximum handshake attempts. |
| `random_trailers` | `*bool` | `true` under 3.1, always `false` below | `"3.1"` | Append random trailers to packets. |
| `disable_cookies` | `*bool` | `true` under 3.1, always `false` below | `"3.1"` | Disable cookie replies. |

`awg_version` accepts exactly `""`, `"2.0"`, `"3.0"` and `"3.1"`. Any other value — including a plausible `"3"` — fails with:

```text
unsupported awg_version "<value>" (expected "2.0", "3.0", or "3.1")
```

The field is a JSON string; a non-string value fails during JSON parsing instead. The CLI wraps resolution errors as `generating configs: resolve obfuscation: ...`, so scripts matching the raw message must allow that prefix.

#### Version gates

A 3.x field present in the manifest under a lower target version is rejected, even when its value would be harmless:

```text
obfuscation.<field> requires awg_version <version> or later (got "<got>")
```

- `header_protection`, `content_padding`, `rekey_after_time`, `rekey_timeout`, `reject_after_time`, `keepalive_timeout` and `max_handshake_attempts` require 3.0.
- `random_trailers` and `disable_cookies` require 3.1.
- The gate triggers on the field's **presence**, not its value: `"header_protection": false` with `"awg_version": "2.0"` is still an error.
- Only the first offending field is reported, checked in the order above.

#### Range semantics

A nil range field selects the version default; an explicit `{"min": 0, "max": 0}` disables the corresponding engine key, so the writer omits it and the engine keeps its own default. Invalid ranges fail with:

| Condition | Error |
| --- | --- |
| Exactly one bound is zero | `obfuscation.<field>: bounds must both be zero or both non-zero (got <min>-<max>)` |
| `max < min` | `obfuscation.<field>: max (<max>) is below min (<min>)` |

The six ranges are resolved only for `awg_version` 3.0 and above.

::: warning `header_protection: false` does not disable the other 3.x keys
It only removes the `HeaderProtectionKey` line. The six ranges and the 3.1 booleans are still emitted, and the H ranges switch from the fixed `1-1`…`4-4` set to large generated ranges.
:::

::: tip Header-protection persistence
Under 3.0/3.1 the header-protection key is generated once and persisted inside the emitted server config (`output/<server>/awg0.conf`), so 3.1 output depends on the previous run; `--full-reset` rotates it. A run that emits no key (2.0, or `header_protection: false`) drops the persisted state, so the next 3.x run generates a new key and previously distributed client configs stop handshaking. See [Credentials](/credentials).
:::

### Range types

#### `U16Range`

Inclusive `uint16` range used by the six 3.x range parameters.

| Field | JSON key | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Min` | `min` | `uint16` | Lower bound (inclusive). Values above 65535 do not fit and fail JSON unmarshalling. |
| `Max` | `max` | `uint16` | Upper bound (inclusive). |

- The zero value `{0, 0}` is the **disabled/unset sentinel**: `IsZero()` returns `true` and the key is omitted from the emitted INI.
- A missing bound decodes to `0`, so `{}` and `{"min": 0}` both mean the disabled `{0, 0}` state — they do **not** select the version default. To keep the default, omit the field entirely.
- A single non-zero bound is invalid: `{"min": 5}` fails with `obfuscation.<field>: bounds must both be zero or both non-zero (got 5-0)`.
- `String()` renders `N` when `Min == Max` and `N-M` otherwise, and the writer uses that rendering for the INI value.

```json
"content_padding": { "min": 2, "max": 10 }
```

#### `HeaderRange`

Inclusive `uint32` pair used by H1–H4 (see [H ranges](#h-ranges)).

| Field | JSON key | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Min` | `min` | `uint32` | Lower bound (inclusive). |
| `Max` | `max` | `uint32` | Upper bound (inclusive). |

```json
"h1": { "min": 100, "max": 5000000 }
```

### Pointer and nil semantics

Pointer fields exist to distinguish "the user wrote a value" from "the key is absent". That distinction is preserved for S/H/J presence, but it is **not** a pinning mechanism for a zero S value:

| Pointer type | `nil` (absent) | Explicit value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `*int` — `s1`–`s4` | generated | pinned only if non-zero; an explicit `0` is **regenerated** like a missing value, though it still disables the uniform-S shortcut |
| `*int` — `jc`, `jmin`, `jmax` | generated for the missing fields; a zero `jc` is replaced | all three explicit: copied verbatim, including `jc: 0`; otherwise the explicit non-zero values are kept and zero/missing ones regenerated |
| `*HeaderRange` — `h1`–`h4` | generated; fixed `1-1`…`4-4` under header protection when all four are nil | pinned range, used verbatim |
| `*U16Range` — the six 3.x ranges | version default | pinned range; `{0, 0}` disables the key; mixed zero bounds and `max < min` are errors |
| `*bool` — `header_protection`, `random_trailers`, `disable_cookies` | version default | overrides the default |
| `*int` — peer `keepalive` | `PersistentKeepalive = 0` (off) | `PersistentKeepalive = <value>` |

::: danger An explicit `"s1": 0` is not a pin
`fillMissingSPrefixes` only preserves non-zero S values (`pickNonZero`), so `"s1": 0` asks for a generated value rather than pinning zero. A preset or manifest that documents `s1: 0` as "disabled" is misleading — under header protection the drawn value starts at 12 and can never be 0. The JSON decode still yields a non-nil pointer, and that presence is what disables the uniform-S shortcut; the value itself is replaced.
:::

### Helper methods on `*ObfuscationManifest`

| Method | Returns | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `HasAnyValue()` | `bool` | `true` when any of the eleven S/H/J pointers (`S1`–`S4`, `H1`–`H4`, `Jc`, `Jmin`, `Jmax`) is non-nil. It deliberately ignores every 3.x field, so `false` does not mean "fully random generation" under 3.x. The pipeline does not call it; it reads each field directly. |
| `ToSharedObfuscation()` | `ServerObfuscationConfig` | Projects only the S/H/J pointers; `Version` stays at its zero value and every 3.x field is dropped, so the result is not a resolvable 3.x config. Callers must resolve 3.x fields through the pipeline. |

## `peers`

`peers` is a map: each key is a peer name and the name **is** the output directory (`output/<peer>/awg0.conf`), so keep names filesystem-safe. There is no `name` field inside a peer object.

> `peers`: map of peer-name → peer object — **required**. Exactly one peer must be the server.

| Field | JSON key | Go type | Required | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
