Share this URL with the AmneziaVPN app user — they paste it into the app's import
dialog or scan it as a QR code.

### Flag reference

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `--vpn-links` | `bool` | `false` | No | Generate AmneziaVPN `vpn://` import links for each client peer |

**Source:** `internal/cli/generate.go:47`

When set, `Generate` is called with `GenerateOptions.VPNLinks = true`. See
[CLI Reference](/cli-reference) for the complete `generate` flag list.

## Compatibility Caveat

::: warning AmneziaVPN app only
`vpn://` import links work **only** with the AmneziaVPN app (Android, iOS,
desktop). They do **not** work with the standalone AmneziaWG client,
`amneziawg-go`, or the kernel module.
:::

The envelope format — `vpnEnvelope`/`vpnContainer`/`vpnAwgConfig`/`vpnLastConfig`
JSON, `qCompress` encoding, base64url — is AmneziaVPN-specific. It was
reverse-engineered from the app's `containersModel`/`importController` and
`Wireguard.kt:parseConfigData()`. No other client implements this import format.

| Consumer | `vpn://` link | `awg0.conf` |
|---|---|---|
| AmneziaVPN app (mobile/desktop) | Import directly | Import via file |
| Standalone AmneziaWG client | Does not work | Use directly |
| `amneziawg-go` userspace | Does not work | Use directly |
| Kernel module (`amneziawg-linux-kernel-module`) | Does not work | Use directly |

**If you need standalone AmneziaWG or kernel module deployment**, use the
generated `awg0.conf` file directly. See [Output Format](/output-format) for the
INI layout.

For more compatibility pitfalls, see [Gotchas](/gotchas).
---
url: /cli-reference
---
# CLI Reference

Amnezigo ships a single `amnezigo` binary with exactly four project subcommands: `generate`, `validate`, `analyze`, and `version`. There are no global flags and no other project commands — cobra additionally registers its built-in `completion` and `help`, which show up in `--help` output but are not part of the documented surface.

## Global (`amnezigo`)

```shell
amnezigo [subcommand] [flags]
```

The root command's short description is **AmneziaWG v3.1 Configuration Generator** (its `--help` opens with `Declarative AmneziaWG v3.1 configuration generator.`). Running bare `amnezigo` — or with `-h`/`--help` — prints the help text and exits `0`. There is no root-level `--version` flag; `amnezigo version` is the only way to read the build stamp.

| Subcommand | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `generate` | Read a manifest and write per-peer AmneziaWG configs. |
| `validate` | Run every generator-enforced invariant check against an existing config. |
| `analyze` | Run heuristic weakness analysis on a server config; purely informational. |
| `version` | Print the build's version and commit stamp. |

::: warning
Legacy commands mentioned in older docs (`init`, `add`, `edit`, `remove`, `export`, `list`) and the `Manager` API do **not** exist — they were removed. The four commands above are the complete surface.
:::

### Error and exit behavior

There are two distinct failure paths, and they look different on stderr:

| Path | Output | Exit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Success | Command's own output only. | `0` |
| `validate` lint failure with errors (or warnings under `--strict`) | Findings and summary only — **no** `Error:` line and **no** usage block. | `1` via `exitFn(1)` (`os.Exit`) |
| CLI-level error: unreadable file, invalid `--output`, wrong argument count, unknown command | cobra prints `Error: <msg>` followed by the usage block, then `Execute` writes `Error: <msg>` a second time to stderr. The message appears **twice**. For an unknown command the first block is just `Error: unknown command "bogus" for "amnezigo"` plus `Run 'amnezigo --help' for usage.` — no usage/flags list. | `1` |

A failed lint deliberately bypasses cobra so that machine-readable output is not polluted by usage text — but it also means deferred cleanup does not run. Scripts that grep stderr for `Error:` will not see a signal for a failed lint; use the exit code instead.

```text
amnezigo validate awg0.conf --output xml
Error: unknown --output format "xml" (want: text|json)
Usage:
  amnezigo validate <config> [flags]

Flags:
  -h, --help            help for validate
      --output string   Output format: text|json (default "text")
      --quiet           Suppress summary line; print findings only
      --strict          Treat warnings as errors for exit code

Error: unknown --output format "xml" (want: text|json)
```

## amnezigo generate

Reads `amnezigo.json` or `.amnezigo.jsonnet` from the project directory and produces one AmneziaWG config per peer into the output directory.

```shell
amnezigo generate [--project DIR] [--output DIR] [--full-reset] [--dry-run] [--peer NAME]... [--jpath DIR]... [--vpn-links]
```

Arguments: none (`NoArgs`).

### Flags

| Flag | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--project` | current dir | no | Project directory containing the manifest. |
| `--output` | `<project>/output` | no | Output **directory** for generated configs (`validate`/`analyze` reuse this flag name for the output *format*). |
| `--full-reset` | `false` | no | Regenerate all credentials instead of reusing them from a previous run. |
| `--dry-run` | `false` | no | Compute configs without writing any files. |
| `--peer` | none | no | Generate only specific peers; repeatable. The server peer is always included regardless of this filter. |
| `--jpath` | `<dir>/lib` (jsonnet only) | no | Jsonnet library search paths. |
| `--vpn-links` | `false` | no | Generate AmneziaVPN `vpn://` import links for each client peer. |

`--peer` and `--jpath` are cobra `StringSlice` flags: they accept repetition and comma-separated values, so `--peer laptop,phone` equals `--peer laptop --peer phone`.

### Behavior

1. Resolves the project directory (`--project`, default `os.Getwd()`; failure wraps as `getting working directory: <err>`) and the output directory (`--output`, default `<project>/output`).
2. Loads the manifest (`.amnezigo.jsonnet` takes precedence over `amnezigo.json`; failure wraps as `loading manifest: <err>`).
3. Runs `Generate()`. With `--dry-run`, prints `Dry run — no files written` before the file list.
4. Prints `Generated N config(s):` followed by one line per file: `  <RelPath> (<bytes> bytes)`.
5. Prints a warnings block if there are any findings.
6. Exits `0` — warnings never change the exit code.

The output directory itself is never printed; the destination is implicit in `--output` / `<project>/output`. On a first run the directory is created with mode `0750` and files with mode `0600`.

### Output format

`N` counts every `FileOutput`, including `amnezigo.vpn` links added by `--vpn-links` (see [VPN Links](/vpn-links)). With `--dry-run` the sizes are still computed and printed — only the write step is skipped. The INI layout of the written files is documented in [Output Format](/output-format).

```text
Generated 3 config(s):
  server/awg0.conf (743 bytes)
  phone/awg0.conf (1027 bytes)
  phone/amnezigo.vpn (1370 bytes)

Warnings: 1
[WARNING TRL001]  (key=RandomTrailers): RandomTrailers is enabled while S1..S4 differ; the AWG 3.1 reference recommends equal S values to avoid packet-type misclassification
```

The warnings block is emitted only when there is at least one finding: a blank line, then `Warnings: <N>` where `N` is `len(result.Findings)` (the label always says `Warnings:` — it is not a severity filter), then one `Finding.OneLine()` line per finding.

Findings produced inside `Generate` come from validating the in-memory server config, so their `Location` is empty and `OneLine()` renders a **double space** after the closing bracket (`[WARNING TRL001]  (key=RandomTrailers): ...`), unlike `validate` findings which carry the file path and line. Only the server config is re-parsed: client configs are never validated by `generate`, so point `amnezigo validate` at an individual client config to close that gap.

### Errors

Failures are wrapped so that the CLI prefix identifies the stage:

| Stage | Wrapped message |
| --- | --- |
| Project resolution | `getting working directory: <err>` |
| Manifest load | `loading manifest: <err>` |
| Generation | `generating configs: <err>` |

Nested causes are appended after the prefix, e.g. `generating configs: resolve obfuscation: obfuscation.random_trailers requires awg_version 3.1 or later (got "2.0")` or `generating configs: resolve obfuscation: unsupported awg_version "3" (expected "2.0", "3.0", or "3.1")`. Pattern-matching on the raw library message therefore has to allow the CLI prefix.

### Exit codes

| Code | Condition |
| --- | --- |
| `0` | Manifest loaded and configs generated — even when warnings were printed. |
| `1` | Manifest load error, generation error, or a flag/argument error. |

::: tip
`--peer` filters **clients only**. The server config is always generated and always counted, and a name that matches no peer is silently ignored (`--peer nobody` prints `Generated 1 config(s):` and exits `0`) — check spelling if a config you expected is missing. Credential resolution is not limited by the filter: keys are still loaded for every persisted peer.
:::

::: tip
`--jpath` applies only to `.amnezigo.jsonnet` manifests and **replaces** the default `<project>/lib` rather than appending to it — a manifest importing from `lib/` breaks as soon as `--jpath` points elsewhere, unless `<project>/lib` is listed too. Relative `--jpath` values resolve against the process working directory, not the manifest directory; when two search directories contain the same file, the **last** one wins. No Jsonnet library ships with amnezigo.
:::

::: warning
`--full-reset` is a fleet-wide operation: it rotates every peer key pair, every pre-shared key, and the header-protection key, so all previously distributed client configs must be re-provisioned. `--dry-run` computes fresh keys in memory and discards them, so a later real run writes different keys than the ones the dry run reported.
:::

::: warning
Key reuse does not mean config stability. Re-running `generate` without `--full-reset` keeps credentials but re-draws every unpinned S/H/J parameter, so previously distributed client configs can become inconsistent with the rewritten server config. `--peer <one>` makes this worse: it rewrites the server config with newly resolved parameters while leaving every other client config stale. See [Gotchas](/gotchas).
:::

### Examples

```shell
amnezigo generate
amnezigo generate --project ~/vpn/prod --output ./out
amnezigo generate --dry-run
amnezigo generate --full-reset
amnezigo generate --peer laptop --peer phone
amnezigo generate --peer laptop,phone
amnezigo generate --project ./myproj --jpath ./jsonnet-lib
amnezigo generate --vpn-links
```

## amnezigo validate

Runs every check the generator enforces (size collisions, header ranges, required fields, deprecated tags) against an existing config file.

```shell
amnezigo validate <config> [--output text|json] [--strict] [--quiet]
```

Arguments: exactly one — the path to a config file (`ExactArgs(1)`).

### Flags

| Flag | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--output` | `text` | no | Output **format**: `text` or `json`. Any other value is an error. |
| `--strict` | `false` | no | Treat warnings as errors for the exit code. |
| `--quiet` | `false` | no | Suppress the summary line; print findings only. Ignored with `--output json`. |

### Behavior

The config is always parsed in **strict mode** (`ParseServerConfigWithOptions` with `Strict: true`), so unknown INI keys and raw `<c>` tags are collected as warnings (`KEY001` / `CPS001`) even without `--strict`. The resulting findings are then emitted in the requested format.

`validate` has no notion of client vs. server. Pointed at a client config it strict-parses it as a server config: client-only keys (`I1`-`I5`, `Endpoint`, `PersistentKeepalive`) become `KEY001` warnings and the missing `ListenPort` becomes a `FLD001` error. That is expected — `validate` is designed for the server config.

### Finding codes

| Code | Severity | Trigger |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `FLD001` | error | A required `[Interface]` field (`PrivateKey`, `Address`, `ListenPort`) is missing. |
| `PSC001` | error | Two S-padded handshake sizes collide. |
| `PSC002` | error | The junk range contains a padded or raw WG size. |
| `PSC003` | error | An I-packet length equals a padded size. **Library-only:** `ValidateServerConfig` passes no I-packet sizes, so the CLI never emits this code today. |
| `PSC000` | error | Unclassified packet-size error fallback; no reachable emission path — the validator only ever returns the classified collision kinds. |
| `JNK001` | error | `Jmin > Jmax`; can be reported twice for the same config. |
| `HDR001` | error | An H range contains WG type-ids 1..4 while no header-protection key is set. **Library-only from the CLI:** the parser rejects such a range first, so the user sees a single `PSE001`. |
| `HDR002` | error | An H range has `Max < Min`. **Library-only from the CLI:** the parser rejects it first, so the user sees a single `PSE001`. |
| `HPK001` | error | A header-protection key is present but some S prefix is below 12. |
| `HPK003` | error | The header-protection key is not 44-char base64 of 32 bytes. **Library-only from the CLI:** the parser aborts first, so the user sees a single `PSE001`. |
| `TRL001` | warning | `RandomTrailers` is enabled while S1..S4 are not all equal. |
| `TRM001` | error | A 3.x uint16 range is inverted or half-zero. |
| `KEY001` | warning | Unknown INI key in `[Interface]`/`[Peer]`; emitted by the strict parser, not the validator. |
| `CPS001` | warning | A raw `<c>` tag literal appears in the file; emitted by the strict parser. |
| `PSE001` | error | Structural parse failure — the only finding for that file. |

`PSE001` pre-empts the semantic codes: when parsing aborts (malformed header-protection key, a non-numeric value where a range/bool is expected, an H range containing WG type-ids without a key, an inverted H range) the file never reaches `ValidateServerConfig`, so you get exactly one `PSE001` finding carrying the parser message with only `location.file` set. That is why `HPK003`, `HDR001`, `HDR002`, and `PSC003` cannot be produced by the CLI even though the library defines them.

```text
amnezigo validate bad.conf
[ERROR PSE001] bad.conf: invalid HeaderProtectionKey "not-base64!!!": must be 44-char base64 of 32 bytes
✗ bad.conf: 1 errors, 0 warnings, 0 info
```

The invariants behind these codes — the size-collision rule, the S floor, header-range rules, and the 3.x transport gates — are detailed in [Validation](/validation).

### Output formats

**Text** — one line per finding via `Finding.OneLine()`, with a non-empty `Detail` indented two spaces, then a summary line (suppressed by `--quiet`):

```text
[<SEVERITY> <CODE>] <file>:<line> (key=<key>): <message>
✓/✗ <path>: E errors, W warnings, I info
```

The line and `(key=...)` segments are omitted when empty, and the summary marker is `✓` when there are no errors, `✗` otherwise.

**JSON** — a single indented object; `findings` is never `null` (a clean result is `[]`). `--quiet` has no effect here:

```json
{
  "file": "<path>",
  "findings": [],
  "summary": { "errors": 0, "warnings": 0, "info": 0 }
}
```

### Exit codes

| Code | Condition |
| --- | --- |
| `0` | No errors, and no warnings unless `--strict` is set. |
| `1` | At least one error, OR any warning when `--strict` is set. Exits through `exitFn(1)`, printing no `Error:` line and no usage block. |
| `1` | CLI-level error (`open "<path>": ...`, `unknown --output format "<v>" (want: text|json)`, `accepts 1 arg(s), received N`). Printed twice with the usage block in between. |

::: warning
`--strict` does not change which findings are reported — it only changes the exit code so that warnings also fail the run. Info-level findings never affect the exit code.
:::

### Examples

```shell
amnezigo validate /etc/amnezia/awg0.conf
amnezigo validate awg0.conf --output json
amnezigo validate awg0.conf --strict --quiet
amnezigo validate output/myserver/awg0.conf --strict
```

## amnezigo analyze

Runs heuristic analysis on a server config, reporting potential weaknesses (`RISK001`-`RISK009`) and profiling handshake sizes, junk parameters, header ranges, and I-packet distributions. Output is informational; the command never fails on findings.

```shell
amnezigo analyze [--config PATH] [--protocol random|quic|dns|dtls|stun|sip|rtp] [--peer NAME] [--output text|json] [--samples N] [--seed N]
```

Arguments: none (`NoArgs`).

### Flags

| Flag | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | `awg0.conf` | no | Server config file path. |
| `--protocol` | `random` | no | Obfuscation protocol to profile: `random`, `quic`, `dns`, `dtls`, `stun`, `sip`, `rtp`. |
| `--peer` | `""` (all) | no | Analyze only this peer. |
| `--output` | `text` | no | Output **format**: `text` or `json`. |
| `--samples` | `0` | no | Number of samples for distribution analysis. `0` = snapshot only. |
| `--seed` | `0` | no | Accepted, and documented by the help text as a reproducibility control — see below. `0` = `crypto/rand`. |

### Snapshot vs. samples

- `--samples 0` (default) emits a **snapshot only**: static profiling of sizes, junk parameters, and header ranges, plus any `RISK` findings. No I-packet distribution is computed.
- `--samples N` (N > 0) additionally generates `N` sample I-packets and reports their size/field distribution under each peer.

`analyze` regenerates I-packets from protocol, MTU, and S prefixes; it does not read the `I1`-`I5` strings stored in the file. The reported sizes are therefore a model of the config, not the config's actual values, and the report ends with a `Note:` line saying so.

### `--seed` does not make output reproducible (defect)

::: danger
`--seed N` is **not implemented**. The CLI builds a seeded `math/rand/v2` PCG reader and assigns it to `AnalyzeOptions.Rand`, but no code path reads that field — I-packet generation goes to `crypto/rand` (in the default `random` protocol). Two runs of `amnezigo analyze --config <cfg> --output json --samples 5 --seed 42` on the same file produce different distributions, so the help text's promise of "reproducible output" (and the flag's own description) is wrong. There is no workaround short of pinning the analysis in your own harness.
:::

`--seed 0`, the default, is documented as `crypto/rand` and is likewise non-reproducible. The non-determinism comes from the default `random` protocol, whose tag generator draws from `crypto/rand` regardless of `--seed`. With a named protocol (`--protocol quic`, `dns`, ...) the snapshot and `Distribution` blocks are identical across runs, and a config with no peers to sample has no I-packet generation at all.

### Output formats

**Text** (`FormatText`) contains, in order: a `=== AmneziaWG Config Analysis ===` header, a `MTU: <n> | Port: <n> | Peers: <n> | Protocol: <p>` line, `--- Handshake Sizes ---`, `--- Junk Packets ---`, `--- Header Ranges ---`, `--- I-Packets (per peer) ---` (only when peers exist), `--- Wire Ordering ---`, an optional `--- Findings ---` block formatted `  [<severity>] <code>: <message>`, and a final `Note: <sample_note>` line. With `--samples N` each peer also gets a `Distribution (N samples)` block with min/max/mean/median per `i1`-`i5`.

**JSON** (`FormatJSON`) is a two-space-indented object with the top-level keys `peers`, `findings`, `ordering`, `sample_note`, `config`, `handshake`, `headers`, `junk`.

```text
  [warning] RISK001: junk range [100..150] contains raw WG size 148 — junk packets may be misclassified
```

### Exit codes

| Code | Condition |
| --- | --- |
| `0` | Success — **even when findings are reported**. |
| `1` | Config load error (`failed to load server config: <err>`) or invalid `--output` value (`invalid output format "<v>": must be text or json`); both are cobra errors, printed twice with the usage block. |

::: warning
Because findings never fail the command, a CI gate must parse `--output json` rather than trust the exit status. `--config` defaults to `awg0.conf` relative to the current working directory, not to the generated `output/<server>/awg0.conf` — either `cd` into the server directory or pass the full path. The report's `RISK` severity words in text output are lowercase (`[warning]`), unlike `validate`'s uppercase `Finding.OneLine()` rendering.
:::

::: tip
All seven accepted protocol values — `random`, `quic`, `dns`, `dtls`, `stun`, `sip`, `rtp` — are accepted. The six named values force a specific named template with a distinct leading-byte signature; `random` (the default) instead runs the random-tag generator, producing a fresh tag sequence per I-packet with tag types drawn from `b`/`r`/`rc`/`rd`/`t`. Note that this is `analyze`'s own protocol choice: the manifest's `obfuscation.protocol` field is never read by the pipeline, and `peers.<name>.protocol` is what selects a template during generation.
:::

### Examples

```shell
amnezigo analyze --config output/myserver/awg0.conf
amnezigo analyze --config awg0.conf --output json
amnezigo analyze --protocol quic --peer laptop --samples 100
amnezigo analyze --config awg0.conf --samples 50 --seed 42
amnezigo analyze --config awg0.conf --protocol dns --samples 0
```

## amnezigo version

Prints the build stamp baked in at compile time via `-ldflags -X` (see `internal/buildinfo`). The format is:

```text
amnezigo <Version> (<Commit>)
```

* `<Version>` — the release version with the tag's leading `v` stripped (tag `v0.4.0` → `0.4.0`), a GoReleaser snapshot version, or `dev` for a plain `go build` / `go run`.
* `<Commit>` — the short commit hash the binary was built from, or `none` for an unstamped build.

```shell
amnezigo version                 # amnezigo 0.4.0 (abc1234)  — release binary
go run ./cmd/amnezigo version    # amnezigo dev (none)
```

No flags beyond `-h`/`--help`; arguments: none (`NoArgs`); always exits `0`. The same commit reports differently depending on how the binary was built: GoReleaser stamps the tag without its leading `v` (`0.4.0`), while `make build` stamps `git describe --tags --always --dirty` (e.g. `v0.3.0-5-g81451b7-dirty`). The source Dockerfile runs no git command: it only bakes in the `VERSION`/`COMMIT` build args (`ARG VERSION=dev`, `ARG COMMIT=none`), so a plain `docker build` without `--build-arg` yields `amnezigo dev (none)`.
---
url: /credentials
---
# Credential Reuse & Rotation

Amnezigo re-resolves obfuscation parameters on every `generate` run — unpinned S-prefixes and junk are drawn fresh, while other unset fields fall back to fixed defaults or generated ranges — but it deliberately **reuses cryptographic keys, preshared keys, and the AWG 3.x header-protection key** recovered from your previous output. The output tree itself is the key store. This page covers how material is generated, how it is recovered and reused, what `--full-reset` rotates, and which parts of a config change anyway.

::: warning Key reuse does not mean configs are stable
Only the credentials are reused. Unpinned S-prefixes and junk (`Jc`/`Jmin`/`Jmax`) are drawn fresh from `crypto/rand` on every run; unpinned header ranges are drawn fresh too, except under AWG 3.x header protection with all four H fields unset, where they resolve to the fixed `1-1`/`2-2`/`3-3`/`4-4` ranges. So a re-run against an unpinned manifest rewrites the server config with values the already-deployed client configs do not carry, and those tunnels break until the clients are re-imported. CPS `I1`-`I5` strings are recomputed but deterministic for named protocol templates; only `protocol: random` redraws them. Pin every obfuscation field if you need a re-run to leave deployed clients in sync.
:::

## How Keys Are Generated

All material is 32 bytes encoded as base64 `StdEncoding` (44 characters). Four functions in `keys.go` generate or derive it:

> `GenerateKeyPair() (privateKey, publicKey string)` — X25519 keypair, base64 `StdEncoding`, 44 characters each. Applies WireGuard clamping (`priv[0] &= 248; priv[31] &= 127; priv[31] |= 64`) before scalar multiplication.

> `DerivePublicKey(privateKey string) string` — re-derives the public key from a base64 private key. Same clamping. 44-char output.

> `GeneratePSK() string` — 32 random bytes, base64-encoded, 44 characters.

> `GenerateHeaderProtectionKey() string` — 32 random bytes, base64-encoded, 44 characters. This is the AWG 3.0+ device-level header-protection key: a symmetric ChaCha20 key, **not** a Curve25519 scalar, so it is deliberately **not** clamped.

Each **peer** gets its own X25519 keypair. Each **client** additionally gets a unique PresharedKey (PSK) protecting that client's tunnel to the server. The server gets a keypair only — never a PSK. The header-protection key is **device-wide**: one shared value emitted into the server config and every client config.

::: warning
`GenerateKeyPair`, `DerivePublicKey`, `GeneratePSK`, and `GenerateHeaderProtectionKey` **panic** on failure (broken `crypto/rand`, invalid base64, or a non-32-byte private key). `DerivePublicKey` panicking on bad input is the one to watch for: a hand-edited invalid `PrivateKey` in an existing client config raises `crypto: invalid base64 private key` or `crypto: private key must be 32 bytes` and **crashes the next `generate`**. The recover-guarded `tryDerivePublicKey` wrapper is used only by the credential scanner during recovery — the pipeline's reuse path calls raw `DerivePublicKey`, so the bad key is not regenerated, it aborts the run.
:::

## Reuse Across Runs

Before generating, the pipeline calls `LoadCredentials(outputDir, serverPeerName)` to read whatever material already exists on disk. It returns **empty credentials, not an error**, when the output directory does not exist at all (the first-run path); only read or parse failures other than "file does not exist" are errors.

Material is recovered from the previously generated INI files, not from a separate state file:

| Material | Recovered from | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Server `PrivateKey`, `PublicKey` | `output/<server>/awg0.conf` → `[Interface]` | Both halves are reused verbatim, including an empty `PublicKey` — the public key is never re-derived. |
| Per-peer `PrivateKey` | **Each client's own** `output/<peer>/awg0.conf` → `[Interface]` | A client secret is never stored in the server config; this is the only source. |
| Per-peer `PublicKey` | Server config → `[Peer]` sections | Recorded, but never trusted: the resolved client public key is always re-derived from its private key. |
| Per-peer `PresharedKey` | Server config → `[Peer]` sections | The fallback scan reads it from the client's own config instead. |
| Header-protection key | Server config → `[Interface] HeaderProtectionKey` | A normal (non-`#_`) INI key; recoverable only from the server config. |

Reuse is decided per peer by `resolvePeerCredentials`:

- the **server** path reuses when `!fullReset && persisted.Server.PrivateKey != ""` — `PrivateKey` and `PublicKey` are copied verbatim;
- the **client** path reuses when `!fullReset && persisted.Peers[name].PrivateKey != ""` — `PrivateKey` and `PresharedKey` are copied, and the public key is **always** re-derived with `DerivePublicKey`;
- the **header-protection key** is reused when `!fullReset && persisted.HeaderProtectionKey != ""`.

Anything else is generated fresh.

The recovery path (`loadPeersFromServer` → `extractClientCredentials`) is a lightweight line-by-line INI scanner, not a full client parser. It reads `PrivateKey` from `[Interface]` and `PresharedKey` from `[Peer]`, skips ordinary `#` comments, but reads `#_` metadata lines. `PublicKey` is then **re-derived from the recovered `PrivateKey`** rather than trusted from disk — this guarantees the public key always matches the private key.

::: danger Peer private keys come from the CLIENT config, never the server copy
The server config's `[Peer]` section historically carried a `#_PrivateKey` metadata line. On reload this value is **deliberately ignored** — it is a stale server-side copy. The peer's real `PrivateKey` is read from its own `output/<peer>/awg0.conf`. This is pinned by `TestLoadCredentials_PeerPrivkeyFromClientConfig` and prevents a "keys rotate on every generate" bug. If a client config is missing, that peer's `PrivateKey` is empty and a fresh keypair and PSK are generated on the next run.
:::

**Fallback path:** if the server config itself is missing (but per-peer output directories exist), `LoadCredentials` scans the output subdirectories and recovers `PrivateKey`/`PresharedKey` directly from each client config; unreadable configs are skipped, and only entries with a non-empty `PrivateKey` are recorded — which is why a lost client config silently rotates that peer's keypair and PSK. It **cannot** recover the server keypair or the header-protection key — the next run generates both fresh, so the server identity and the device key change and every client must re-import.

A peer present in the manifest but with **no existing client config** gets an empty `PrivateKey`, so the pipeline generates a fresh keypair and PSK for it. Recovery also depends on peer names: a server `[Peer]` block without a `#_Name` comment cannot be matched to a manifest entry, so it is skipped and that peer's keypair and PSK are **regenerated on that run** — the rewritten server config restores the `#_Name` comment, so reuse resumes on the following run. Renaming a peer has the same effect — the new name has no persisted entry, and the old `output/<oldname>/awg0.conf` is orphaned.

::: danger Losing the server config's `PublicKey` line silently breaks every client
The server reuse path copies the persisted public key verbatim and checks only that `PrivateKey` is non-empty. If the `PublicKey` line is lost or empty, the next run writes `PublicKey = ` (an empty value) into every client's `[Peer]`, writes no `PublicKey` line into the server `[Interface]`, and still exits 0 with no finding. The state is sticky — later runs keep copying the empty value. `--full-reset`, deleting the server config (the fallback regenerates the server keypair), or deleting the output tree restore a working public key.
:::

## Header-Protection Key

AWG 3.0 header protection encrypts the packet header (hiding the WireGuard message type-ids) with a device-wide ChaCha20 key. Generation, storage, and reuse mirror the peer keys, with one extra failure mode: a run whose output contains no key drops it from the persisted state.

| Stage | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Emission | `HeaderProtectionKey = <44-char base64>` in the server `[Interface]` and in every client `[Interface]`; only when header protection is on and the target version is 3.0+. |
| Recovery | `LoadCredentials` reads the server config's line into `PersistedCredentials.HeaderProtectionKey`. |
| Reuse | Kept when `!fullReset && persisted.HeaderProtectionKey != ""`; otherwise `GenerateHeaderProtectionKey()` runs. |
| Disabled | With `header_protection: false` (or an `awg_version` below 3.0) the field stays empty and no line is emitted. |

The key rotates — and every already-distributed client config stops handshaking, because mismatched keys never complete a handshake — when:

- you run `generate --full-reset`;
- the server config is missing, so the fallback scan runs and never sets `HeaderProtectionKey`;
- the **previous run emitted no key** (`awg_version: "2.0"`, or `header_protection: false`) — nothing is recovered the next time 3.x header protection is enabled, so a fresh key is generated (a 3.1 → 2.0 → 3.1 sequence rotates it);
- you delete `output/` or the server config.

::: danger A corrupt `HeaderProtectionKey` blocks `generate`
The parser validates the line as 44-char base64 decoding to exactly 32 bytes. A hand-edited value aborts credential loading — and therefore the whole run, before anything is written — with:

```text
load credentials: load server config for credentials: invalid HeaderProtectionKey "notbase64": must be 44-char base64 of 32 bytes
```

There is no fallback to regeneration: fix the line or remove the file before the next run. `--full-reset` does not bypass this — credentials are loaded before the flag is consulted, so the run still aborts. Other malformed values the parser validates — the AWG 3.x range and boolean keys — are equally fatal; unparseable legacy numerics (`ListenPort`, `MTU`, `Jc`, `S1`-`S4`) are silently ignored, and unknown keys only warn in strict parses.
:::

The key is also stored in **plaintext** — it is a normal INI key, not `#_` metadata — in the server config and in every client config, so any reader of a client config can decrypt header-protected packet headers, on top of the private key and PSK the file already exposes. Treat every client config, and every `vpn://` link, as a secret. See [Transport Protection](/transport-protection) and [VPN Links](/vpn-links).

## The `--full-reset` Flag

```shell
amnezigo generate --full-reset
```

When `--full-reset` is set, `resolvePeerCredentials` ignores all persisted state and generates fresh material for every peer:

- a new server keypair via `GenerateKeyPair()`;
- a new client keypair via `GenerateKeyPair()` for each client;
- a new unique PSK via `GeneratePSK()` for each client;
- a new device-wide header-protection key via `GenerateHeaderProtectionKey()`.

Because the server key, every PSK, and the device key all change, `--full-reset` is a fleet-wide re-provisioning action: every client config must be redistributed. It is all-or-nothing — there is no per-peer reset flag. See [CLI Reference](/cli-reference).

::: tip `--full-reset` is a credentials reset, not an obfuscation reset
Obfuscation is re-resolved from the manifest on every run (`resolveObfuscation`): explicit manifest values are preserved, and unset (`null`) fields are re-drawn or fall back to fixed defaults — this happens **regardless** of `--full-reset`. The flag forces only the regeneration of keys, PSKs, and the header-protection key.
:::

Because a PSK protects a specific keypair relationship, PSKs are regenerated alongside the keys — no flag rotates only the server key. Deleting just the server config does effectively that: the fallback scan preserves each client's private key and PSK while the server keypair (and the header-protection key) is regenerated — but every client still has to re-import.

## Server vs Client Material

The distinction is enforced in `resolvePeerCredentials`:

| Role | Keypair | PresharedKey | Recovered from |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Server peer | Yes | **No** (never) | `output/<server>/awg0.conf` `[Interface]` |
| Client peer | Yes | Yes — unique per client | Keypair from own `output/<peer>/awg0.conf`; PSK from server `[Peer]` |

> `PeerCredentials` (per peer): `PrivateKey` (base64 X25519), `PublicKey` (base64 X25519, derived from `PrivateKey`), `PresharedKey` (base64 32-byte PSK; empty for the server).

> `PersistedCredentials`: `Peers` (`map[name]PeerCredentials` — only peers found in the existing output are present), `Server` (`PeerCredentials`, keypair only; zero-value on first run), and `HeaderProtectionKey` (`string` — the AWG 3.x device key, empty when absent or when the target version predates 3.x).

> `EmptyCredentials() *PersistedCredentials` — constructor returning an initialized (empty, non-nil) `Peers` map and zero-value `Server`/`HeaderProtectionKey`. It is used on the first run and when `OutputDir` is empty; `--full-reset` does not call it, but suppresses reuse of whatever was loaded.

The server is identified the same way as everywhere else: the single peer whose `endpoint != ""` **and** `listen_port != 0` (both required). There is at most one server peer.

## Practical Workflows

### Re-run `generate` safely

After editing obfuscation values, adding/removing a peer, or changing endpoints, just re-run:

```shell
amnezigo generate
```

Existing peers keep their keypairs, PSKs, and the header-protection key (recovered from `output/`) — but only the credentials are reused. Every unpinned S-prefix and junk value is re-drawn (header ranges too, unless all four H fields are unset under header protection), so the rewritten server config can disagree with already-deployed client configs; pin those fields if you need a re-run to leave deployed clients in sync. CPS `I1`-`I5` strings are not persisted and are recomputed per client, but named protocol templates are deterministic for the same protocol and MTU — identical strings are reproduced across runs; only `protocol: random` draws a fresh tag sequence per run (on-wire bytes still differ because `<r N>`/`<t>` expand in the engine). See [Obfuscation](/obfuscation).

### Add a peer without rotating others

Add the new peer to `peers` in `amnezigo.json`, then:

```shell
amnezigo generate
```

The new peer has no existing `output/<newpeer>/awg0.conf`, so its `PrivateKey` is empty after `LoadCredentials` — the pipeline generates a fresh keypair and PSK **only for it**. All existing peers are reused verbatim, and the header-protection key is unchanged. The server config gains a new `[Peer]` block; existing client configs do not depend on the peer list, so with every obfuscation field pinned they come out identical — with an unpinned manifest the re-drawn S-prefix and junk values (plus freshly drawn header ranges unless all four H fields are unset under header protection) invalidate the configs already in the field (see above).

::: tip Use `--peer` to generate selectively
`--peer` (repeatable; the server is always included) limits which client configs are written. It does not change credential recovery — keys are still reused for everyone — it just controls which files land on disk.
:::

### Force a full rotation

```shell
amnezigo generate --full-reset
```

Every keypair, every PSK, and the header-protection key are regenerated. **Every config must be redeployed** — old client configs will no longer authenticate against the new server keypair, and the old header-protection key no longer matches.

### Remove or rename a peer

Deleting a peer from the manifest does **not** delete its `output/<peer>/` directory. The orphaned client config (and its recovered credentials) is simply unused on subsequent runs. The directory persists on disk in case you want the keys for migration — remove it manually if you want the material gone. **Renaming** a peer is a remove plus an add as far as reuse is concerned: the new name has no client config, so it gets a fresh keypair and PSK, while the old directory is orphaned.

### Preview without writing

```shell
amnezigo generate --dry-run
```

`--dry-run` computes everything, prints the file list (with byte counts), and writes nothing. Credential loading still happens, so an existing server config under `output/` is read and its keys are reused in what you see. Any **freshly generated** keys — a first run with no output tree — are discarded: the next real run writes different keys, and there is no way to preview the exact material it will use.

## Deleting `output/` Loses Reuse State

::: danger
Credential reuse depends entirely on the contents of `output/`. **Deleting `output/` (or any peer's `output/<peer>/awg0.conf`) destroys the recovered-key state** — the next `generate` run treats it as a first run and generates fresh keys for the server and every missing peer, even without `--full-reset`.

Specifically: removing the whole `output/` directory regenerates the server keypair, **all** client keypairs/PSKs, and the **header-protection key**. Removing a single client's `output/<peer>/awg0.conf` regenerates that peer's keypair **and PSK** (the old PSK is still readable in the server config's `[Peer]` section, but credential reuse is gated on a non-empty persisted `PrivateKey`, so a fresh PSK is drawn too). Removing the **server config** triggers the fallback scan, which recovers client private keys and PSKs from client configs but **cannot** recover the server keypair or the header-protection key — the server and the device key both change and every client must be redeployed.

There is no separate key store to restore from; if you want reuse to keep working, treat `output/` as state, not a disposable build artifact.
:::
---
url: /jsonnet
---
# Jsonnet Manifests

AmneziaWG configs are repetitive: the same obfuscation shape, network, and
endpoint pattern repeat across peers and environments. Instead of hand-copying
`amnezigo.json` for every deployment, you can author the manifest as a
[Jsonnet](https://jsonnet.org/) template. Jsonnet is a strict superset of JSON
that adds variables, functions, comprehensions, conditionals, and imports, then
evaluates down to plain JSON that the loader consumes exactly like a hand-written
manifest.

This page covers when to reach for Jsonnet, how the loader picks between the two
manifest filenames, how library imports are resolved, and a concrete reuse
pattern drawn from the project's own test fixtures.

## Why Jsonnet

A static JSON manifest is fine for one server and a couple of clients, but it
forces you to duplicate values that are logically shared. Jsonnet earns its keep
in three situations:

**Computation.** Variables, arithmetic, and functions let you derive fields
instead of repeating them. Compute a subnet once and reuse it; build a peer's
`address` from an index; share one obfuscation block across every peer.

**Reuse.** A `.libsonnet` library encodes a network, a preset, or a peer
template once and `import`s it everywhere. Updating the shared value updates
every manifest that imports it — no find-and-replace.

**Environment-specific manifests.** Jsonnet conditionals and imports let one
template produce different output for staging vs. production, or for a laptop
vs. a phone, without forking the file. Comprehensions mass-generate peers — the
test suite builds a 100-peer manifest from a single comprehension.

::: tip
Jsonnet is opt-in. If your manifest is small and stable, plain `amnezigo.json`
is perfectly fine. Reach for Jsonnet when you find yourself copy-pasting peer
blocks or maintaining near-duplicate manifests per environment.
:::

Whatever Jsonnet produces, the loader treats it as a normal manifest: the
evaluated JSON is parsed into the same `Manifest` struct and validated against
the same schema. There is no "Jsonnet mode" downstream — `generate` cannot tell
the difference, and `validate`/`analyze` never see a manifest at all (they
operate on already-generated configs).

## File Precedence

The loader discovers a manifest by looking for two fixed filenames, in order:

| Filename | Format | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `.amnezigo.jsonnet` | Jsonnet (evaluated by the VM) | Auto-discovered first; **leading dot is required** |
| `amnezigo.json` | Plain JSON | Used only when no Jsonnet file is present |

`amnezigo generate` (and the loader it calls) scans the project directory and
picks the first match:

1. `.amnezigo.jsonnet` — if it exists, evaluate it with the Jsonnet VM.
2. `amnezigo.json` — otherwise, parse it as plain JSON.

When **both** files sit in the same directory, the Jsonnet file wins. This is
deliberate: you can keep a checked-in `amnezigo.json` for reference or for tools
that only read JSON, while `.amnezigo.jsonnet` is the source of truth at
generation time.

::: warning
The Jsonnet file must be named **exactly** `.amnezigo.jsonnet` (with the leading
dot) to be auto-discovered. `generate` only ever looks for that filename and
`amnezigo.json`; a file named `amnezigo.jsonnet` (no dot) is **not**
discovered. Only the Go API's `LoadManifestFromFile` given an explicit path
will evaluate it — and that routing is a **case-sensitive** suffix check: only
a path ending in exactly `.jsonnet` goes through the Jsonnet VM.
`Manifest.Jsonnet` or `backup.jsonnet.bak` is parsed as JSON and fails.
:::

## `jpath` & Library Imports

Jsonnet's `import` and `importstr` statements pull in other files. To keep
imports reproducible without flags, Amnezigo gives the VM a default library
search path.

**Default jpath.** When you do not pass `--jpath`, the loader resolves imports
against `<manifestDir>/lib` — a `lib/` directory sitting next to the manifest
file (`<project>/lib` for `generate`, the manifest file's parent directory for
`LoadManifestFromFile`). This lets you write `import 'network.libsonnet'` and
have it just work, with no extra flags.

**`--jpath` flag.** The `generate` command accepts a repeatable `--jpath` flag
that overrides the default:

| Flag | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--jpath` | `<project>/lib` | no | Jsonnet library search paths. Repeat the flag or pass a comma-separated list. Entries are searched **last-to-first**, so when duplicate filenames exist the **last** directory listed wins. |

```shell
amnezigo generate --project ./my-vpn --jpath ./jsonnet/libs --jpath ./vendor
```

When `--jpath` is supplied, the default `<project>/lib` is **not** added
automatically — the flag fully replaces the default, not appends to it. List
every directory you need, including `lib/` if you still want it searched.

::: warning Relative `--jpath` values resolve against the working directory
jpath strings are handed to the importer verbatim, so `--jpath lib` means
`<current working directory>/lib`, not `<project>/lib`. Use absolute paths in
scripts and CI (`--jpath "$PWD/jsonnet/libs"` or `--jpath "$(pwd)/lib"`) when
the process working directory is not guaranteed.
:::

::: warning Import resolution order
Imports resolve **relative to the importing file's own directory first**, then
the jpath entries — which are tried from the last entry to the first. An
`import 'network.libsonnet'` inside `./my-vpn/.amnezigo.jsonnet` is found in
`./my-vpn/` itself **before** any jpath entry is searched. Because duplicate
lookups resolve last-to-first, the **last** directory listed wins; to layer an
override directory on top of a base one, put the override last. To import a
library outside both locations, pass its directory via `--jpath`.
:::

**`import` vs `importstr`.** Use `import 'file.libsonnet'` for Jsonnet/JSON
data — the imported file is parsed and merged as a value. Use
`importstr 'file.txt'` for raw text (for example, embedding a base64 key blob)
when you want the literal bytes, not a parsed structure.

**No external inputs.** The VM is `google/go-jsonnet` configured with a
`FileImporter` over the resolved jpath entries and nothing else: no external
variables and no top-level arguments are registered, and no native functions
are installed. `std.extVar('x')` therefore fails at evaluation with
`RUNTIME ERROR: Undefined external variable: x`, `std.native('x')` evaluates to
`null` rather than erroring, and the CLI exposes no `--ext-str`, `--ext-code`,
`--tla-str`, or `--tla-code` flags — `--jpath` is the only Jsonnet knob.
Everything a template needs must be inline, computed, or imported.

**Imports are not sandboxed.** `JPaths` only adds search locations; it does not
restrict what a template may read. Absolute import paths and `../` traversal are
both allowed, so a Jsonnet manifest from an untrusted source can read any file
the process can read. Review manifests you did not author.

**Nothing ships under `lib/`.** Amnezigo bundles no Jsonnet libraries: there is
no committed `lib/` directory and no `presets.libsonnet`. The default
`<manifestDir>/lib` path is a user-created convention — the directory and every
library inside it are yours.

## Reuse Pattern

The canonical reuse pattern lives in the project's own test fixture
(`testdata/loader/valid-jsonnet-with-lib/`). It splits the manifest into a tiny
`.amnezigo.jsonnet` that imports a shared `network.libsonnet` from `lib/`.

Directory layout:

```text
my-vpn/
├── .amnezigo.jsonnet
└── lib/
    └── network.libsonnet
```

`lib/network.libsonnet` — a plain Jsonnet object exporting the shared network
block:

```jsonnet
{
  mtu: 1420,
  dns: ['1.1.1.1', '8.8.8.8'],
}
```

`.amnezigo.jsonnet` — imports the library with `local net = import ...`, then
spreads it into the manifest:

```jsonnet
local net = import 'network.libsonnet';
{
  version: 1,
  network: net,
  obfuscation: {
    protocol: 'quic',
    s1: 30, s2: 35, s3: 20, s4: 12,
    h1: { min: 100, max: 5000000 },
    h2: { min: 10000000, max: 200000000 },
    h3: { min: 400000000, max: 800000000 },
    h4: { min: 1000000000, max: 2100000000 },
    jc: 5, jmin: 250, jmax: 750,
  },
  peers: {
    server: {
      address: '10.0.0.1/24',
      endpoint: 'vpn.example.com:51820',
      listen_port: 51820,
    },
  },
}
```

Because `network.libsonnet` lives under the default `<manifestDir>/lib`, this
generates with no flags:

```shell
amnezigo generate --project ./my-vpn
```

The same pattern scales to obfuscation presets. Presets are **Go data** in
`presets.go` (`lan-conservative`, `home-balanced`, `mobile-aggressive`,
`stealth-paranoid`, `standard-1420`, `low-overhead`, `test-minimal`) — the
manifest has no `preset` field and the CLI has no `--preset` flag, so a Jsonnet
file cannot import a preset by name. Copy the numbers by hand into your own
library; a `.libsonnet` object is the natural home for them:

```jsonnet
// lib/presets.libsonnet — the built-in `mobile-aggressive` preset, copied by hand
{
  mobileAggressive: {
    s1: 60, s2: 60, s3: 50, s4: 24,
    h1: { min: 50, max: 10000000 },
    h2: { min: 50000000, max: 500000000 },
    h3: { min: 700000000, max: 1200000000 },
    h4: { min: 1500000000, max: 2147000000 },
    jc: 8, jmin: 500, jmax: 1000,
    content_padding: { min: 2, max: 10 },
    random_trailers: true,
    disable_cookies: true,
  },
}
```

```jsonnet
local presets = import 'presets.libsonnet';
{
  version: 1,
  network: { mtu: 1280, dns: ['1.1.1.1'] },
  obfuscation: { awg_version: '3.1' } + presets.mobileAggressive,
  peers: {
    server: {
      address: '10.0.0.1/24',
      endpoint: 'vpn.example.com:51820',
      listen_port: 51820,
      protocol: 'dns',
    },
    // ... client peers ...
  },
}
```

Presets carry an `MTU` and a default protocol that are not part of the
`obfuscation` block, so copying a preset also means copying those two values by
hand (`mobile-aggressive` uses MTU 1280 and the `dns` protocol). All presets
target AWG 3.1 and keep S1-S4 at or above the header-protection floor of 12.
Presets that enable random trailers with unequal S values (including
`mobile-aggressive`) make `generate` print the non-fatal `TRL001` warning
(`[WARNING TRL001]`); generation continues.

::: tip
Keep one library per concern: `network.libsonnet`, `presets.libsonnet`, a
`peers.libsonnet` with a function that emits a peer given a name and address.
Comprehensions then turn a list of names into a full `peers` map in one
expression.
:::

## Errors & Debugging

The loader reports Jsonnet problems through three different wrappers: Jsonnet
VM failures as `evaluate jsonnet <path>: ...`, output-shape failures as
`parse jsonnet output from <path>: ...`, and schema-version failures as a bare
`<path>: ...`. The failure modes worth knowing:

**Schema validation still applies.** Jsonnet output is JSON-parsed into the
`Manifest` struct and version-checked. A template that emits
`{ version: 99 }` is rejected just like a JSON manifest would be:

```text
<path>: unsupported schema version 99 (expected 1)
```

A template that omits `version` entirely fails with `missing or zero version
field`. The evaluated JSON must be a valid manifest, regardless of how it was
produced.

**The top level must be an object.** The manifested value is unmarshalled into
the `Manifest` struct, so a template that evaluates to an array, string, or
number fails with:

```text
parse jsonnet output from <path>: json: cannot unmarshal array into Go value of type amnezigo.Manifest
```

A top-level function fails earlier, at evaluation, with `RUNTIME ERROR: Missing
argument: <name>` (`Top-level function call`). Always manifest an object. The
struct is also strictly typed: a number where a string is expected fails with
`json: cannot unmarshal number into Go struct field PeerManifest.peers.address of type string`.

**Syntax errors.** A malformed Jsonnet file yields a `go-jsonnet` error that
includes the offending file and line number. Read the file:line prefix first —
it points directly at the broken expression.

**Missing external variables.** Since no ext vars or TLAs are registered,
`std.extVar('name')` fails at evaluation with a multi-line `RUNTIME ERROR:
Undefined external variable: <name>` trace. (`std.native('name')` is quieter:
it returns `null` because no native functions exist.) There is no flag to
define ext vars; pass the value through an import instead.

**Failed imports.** An `import` whose target cannot be found anywhere fails with
go-jsonnet's `couldn't open import "nonexistent.libsonnet": no match locally or
in the Jsonnet library paths`. The `jsonnet-import-error` fixture imports
`nonexistent.libsonnet` to exercise this path. If you see it, check that the
file exists either next to the importing file, or **under a jpath entry**
(default `<manifestDir>/lib`, or one of your `--jpath` directories).

::: warning
`obfuscation.protocol` is **decorative** — it does not drive I-packet
generation. Only per-peer `peers[].protocol` (defaulting to `quic`) selects the
I1–I5 template. Setting `obfuscation.protocol: 'quic'` in a Jsonnet template is
harmless, but it will not change the generated config. Set `protocol` on each
peer if you want per-protocol shaping.
:::
---
url: /obfuscation
---
# Obfuscation Parameters

Amnezigo generates the complete obfuscation block — size prefixes (`S1`–`S4`), header ranges (`H1`–`H4`), junk parameters (`Jc`/`Jmin`/`Jmax`) and client-only custom packet strings (`I1`–`I5`) — and, from `awg_version` `"3.0"` onward, the transport-protection block that encrypts the message header and pads transport packets. `obfuscation.awg_version` defaults to `"3.1"`, so a manifest that never mentions a version gets the full 3.x key set; `"2.0"` is the opt-in legacy mode that emits S/H/J only.

The generated values must satisfy the **size-classification invariant** (`ValidatePacketSizes` in `validation.go`):

1. The four S-padded handshake sizes `S1+148`, `S2+92`, `S3+64`, `S4+32` are **pairwise distinct**.
2. No I-packet byte length equals any of the four padded sizes.
3. The junk range `[Jmin..Jmax]` (inclusive) excludes all four padded sizes **and** the four raw WireGuard message sizes `148, 92, 64, 32`.

The mnemonic `S1+56 != S2` is only the Init-vs-Response pair (`148 − 92 = 56`) of leg 1, not the whole rule.

::: warning Who enforces which leg — `generate` is not the enforcer
The CLI `generate` pipeline never calls `ValidatePacketSizes` and has no panic path; it only re-parses the server config it just wrote and appends findings — and when that re-parse fails, the parse error is dropped and no findings are appended at all, so `generate` can exit 0 on a config that `validate` immediately rejects. Legs 1 and 3 are enforced by the generator functions and reported reactively by `validate` (`PSC001`, `PSC002`, `JNK001`). Leg 2 is enforced **only** by the library helper `GenerateConfig`, which threads `PaddedSizes(...)` into CPS generation and re-checks with `ValidatePacketSizes`; the pipeline calls `GenerateCPS`, whose forbidden set is empty, and `validate` passes `nil` I-packet sizes, so a CLI-generated I-packet that collides with a padded size is never reported by either command. See the [Byte-Budget Constraints](#byte-budget-constraints) section.
:::

## How AmneziaWG Defeats DPI

A passive DPI box fingerprints vanilla WireGuard along several independent axes. AWG breaks each one with a dedicated knob — the invariants above exist so the knobs do not collide with each other on the wire.

| DPI signal | What vanilla WG leaks | AWG countermeasure | Parameter |
|---|---|---|---|
| Handshake initiation is the first large UDP packet to a fixed port | The 148-byte initiation stands out as the session opener | Bury it behind `Jc` random-length junk packets | `Jc`, `Jmin`, `Jmax` |
| Message type byte is `{1,2,3,4}` at offset 0 | The first 4 bytes identify the WG message type | Replace with a random value drawn from a wide range; from 3.0, encrypt the header entirely under `HeaderProtectionKey` | `H1`–`H4` |
| Fixed handshake sizes 148 / 92 / 64 | A size histogram reveals the WG handshake | Pad each message with `Sn` random bytes | `S1`, `S2`, `S3` |
| Fixed keepalive/transport size 32 | Steady-state data has a recognizable length floor | Pad every transport packet (the bulk of real traffic) | `S4` |
| Statistical/timing shape of a VPN flow | Packet cadence and size distribution look like a tunnel | Prepend 1–5 cover packets mimicking a real UDP protocol so DPI buckets the flow as permitted; 3.1 adds random trailers and suppresses cookie replies | `I1`–`I5` + `protocol` |

**Why the invariants exist — receive-side classification.** The AWG receiver (`DeterminePacketTypeAndPadding` in `amneziawg-go` `device/receive.go`) classifies every inbound packet by two checks: its length must equal `Sn + baseSize` — or, with `RandomTrailers` on (the 3.1 default), be at least that size — **and** its first 4 bytes must fall inside that type's `Hn` range; the first message type that matches wins. If two padded sizes coincided, or a junk/I-packet length matched a padded size whose random header happened to land in-range, the receiver would misclassify. Amnezigo's generators draw values that avoid this, and `validate` reports configs that violate it.

From AWG 3.0 the header substitution is backed by a cipher: the 4-byte message type is encrypted, so the type byte no longer appears on the wire in the clear, and 3.1 adds trailer-based padding and cookie suppression. That device layer — `HeaderProtectionKey`, the six uint16 ranges, `RandomTrailers`, `DisableCookies`, their version gates and the INI emission rules — is covered in [Transport Protection](/transport-protection). This page covers the 3.x layer only where it constrains the S/H/J/CPS parameter values: the S ≥ 12 floor, the `H1..H4 = 1-1..4-4` reference set, and the trailer-driven uniform S.

**S4 is the high-leverage pad for size-based fingerprinting.** `S1`–`S3` pad only the handshake (which fires roughly every two minutes); `S4` pads *every transport-data packet* — the overwhelming majority of bytes in a real session. Raising `S4` is the single most effective way to blur steady-state size fingerprinting, at the cost of `S4` extra bytes per packet (~`S4`/MTU throughput overhead). If bandwidth is constrained, lower `S4` first; if a censor is profiling data-plane sizes, raise it.

## Choosing the AWG Version

`obfuscation.awg_version` pins the target engine generation. Unset selects `"3.1"`; any other value fails with `unsupported awg_version "3" (expected "2.0", "3.0", or "3.1")` (the CLI wraps it as `generating configs: resolve obfuscation: ...`).

| `awg_version` | Meaning | Flags default | Emitted 3.x keys |
|---|---|---|---|
| `"2.0"` | legacy S/H/J + I1-I5 | header protection off | none |
| `"3.0"` | adds the header-protection key and the six uint16 ranges | `header_protection: true`; `random_trailers` and `disable_cookies` false | `HeaderProtectionKey` plus the six ranges |
| `"3.1"` | adds trailers and cookie suppression | all three `true` | the 3.0 set plus `RandomTrailers`/`DisableCookies` |

The version gates are **presence-based, not value-based**: a field the target version cannot express is rejected even when its value is a no-op. `header_protection: false` under `"2.0"` is still an error.

| Fields | Minimum `awg_version` |
|---|---|
| `header_protection`, `content_padding`, `rekey_after_time`, `rekey_timeout`, `reject_after_time`, `keepalive_timeout`, `max_handshake_attempts` | `"3.0"` |
| `random_trailers`, `disable_cookies` | `"3.1"` |

```text
obfuscation.<field> requires awg_version <min> or later (got "<have>")
obfuscation.header_protection requires awg_version 3.0 or later (got "2.0")
obfuscation.random_trailers requires awg_version 3.1 or later (got "3.0")
```

## S1–S4 — Size Prefixes

Each WireGuard handshake message carries a small prefix of `Sn` random bytes. The AWG-aware peer strips `Sn` before handing the message to the inner WireGuard implementation; a vanilla WireGuard peer rejects the oversized packet. The four prefixes map one-to-one onto the four WireGuard message types:

| Field | WireGuard message | Raw WG size | Padded size |
|---|---|---|---|
| `s1` | MessageInitiation | 148 | `S1 + 148` |
| `s2` | MessageResponse | 92 | `S2 + 92` |
| `s3` | MessageCookieReply | 64 | `S3 + 64` |
| `s4` | MessageTransport | 32 | `S4 + 32` |

> `s1`: int (nullable pointer) — prefix length for MessageInitiation
> `s2`: int (nullable pointer) — prefix length for MessageResponse
> `s3`: int (nullable pointer) — prefix length for MessageCookieReply
> `s4`: int (nullable pointer) — prefix length for MessageTransport

**Generator ranges** (`generator.go`), with `minS = 0` when header protection is off and `minS = headerProtectionNonceSize = 12` when it is on:

| Field | Range without HP (inclusive) | Range under HP (inclusive) | Constant |
|---|---|---|---|
| `s1`, `s2`, `s3` | `[0, 64]` | `[12, 64]` | `sPrefixRangeMax = 65` (drawn via `crypto/rand` `[minS, max)`) |
| `s4` | `[0, 32]` | `[12, 32]` | `s4RangeMax = 33` |

The library generators retry (up to `sMaxAttempts = 1000`) until the four padded sizes are pairwise distinct, then panic if they cannot find a valid combination. The manifest pipeline is different: it loops at most 100 times and returns whatever it has, with no panic path.

::: danger Header protection requires S1–S4 ≥ 12
The AWG 3.x header cipher encrypts the 4-byte message header at offset `S{n}` with a nonce made from the first 12 bytes of the S-prefix, so **every** S value must be at least 12 whenever a `HeaderProtectionKey` is present. The floor applies to generated values (`minS = 12`) and to explicit manifest values alike: `{"s3": 8}` under 3.1 aborts generation with

```text
header protection requires S1-S4 >= 12 (got S3=8)
```

and `generate` exits 1 writing nothing. On an already-written config the same condition is the `HPK001` error. Under `awg_version: "2.0"` or `header_protection: false` the floor check is skipped and S < 12 stays legal (the S-prefix range starts at 0).
:::

::: warning A fixed `S1` still triggers S2–S4 regeneration
A pinned explicit `s1` is kept verbatim, and `s2`–`s4` are drawn; the merged set is **not** re-checked during resolution, so a collision between the pinned value and a generated one is reported by `validate` as `PSC001` rather than repaired. The library helper `GenerateSPrefixesWithS1(minS, fixedS1)` is the variant that does draw S2–S4 against the fixed S1 across all six padded pairs; `GenerateConfig` uses it, the manifest pipeline does not. Pin all four S values for stable output.
:::

::: tip Uniform S under 3.1 trailers
When `random_trailers` is on (the 3.1 default) **and all four S manifest fields are nil**, resolution calls `GenerateUniformSPrefixes(minS)`: one draw in `[minS, 33)` copied into `S1=S2=S3=S4`, because the 3.1 receiver classifies packets by size and the reference recommends equal S values under trailers. The padded sizes stay pairwise distinct anyway — `148+S`, `92+S`, `64+S` and `32+S` differ by construction for any `S`. Under header protection the draw is `12`–`32`; with header protection off the draw may be `0`, which counts as unset and is redrawn, so the effective minimum is `1`. Pinning even one S disables the uniform path, and unequal pinned S with trailers enabled produces the `TRL001` **warning** (never an error) — four of the seven built-in [presets](/presets) do exactly that.
:::

## H1–H4 — Header Ranges

WireGuard's first on-wire byte is a message type-id ∈ `{1, 2, 3, 4}` (Initiation, Response, Cookie Reply, Transport). AmneziaWG replaces it with a pseudo-random header byte drawn from `H1`–`H4` — one range per message type. The manifest loader does **not** validate `H` ranges itself; a written config carrying a forbidden range aborts parsing, so `amnezigo validate` reports a single structural error with code `PSE001` and the parse message — `invalid H1: header range [1-1] contains forbidden WG type-id(s) in [1..4]`, or `invalid H2: invalid header range: Max (3) < Min (500)` for a reversed range. (`HDR001`/`HDR002` exist in `ValidateServerConfig` but are unreachable from the CLI: the file never parses.)

| Field | Default | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `h1` | `{1,1}` under HP when all H are unset; generated otherwise | no | Header window for MessageInitiation |
| `h2` | `{2,2}` under the same condition | no | Header window for MessageResponse |
| `h3` | `{3,3}` under the same condition | no | Header window for MessageCookieReply |
| `h4` | `{4,4}` under the same condition | no | Header window for MessageTransport |

> `h1`, `h2`, `h3`, `h4`: `{min, max}` object (nullable pointer) — both fields are `uint32`

**The `[1..4]` ban is waived under header protection.** `ValidateHeaderRange` itself always rejects a range intersecting the WG type-ids, but both the validator and the parser suppress that rejection when a `HeaderProtectionKey` is present (only the structural `Max >= Min` check remains). With the header encrypted, `H1 = 1-1` … `H4 = 4-4` is the legitimate 3.x reference configuration. Without header protection a range containing `[1..4]` would let genuine WireGuard traffic reach the peer and defeat the obfuscation, so an explicit such range aborts parsing — `validate` reports it as the structural error `PSE001` — and generated ranges never intersect `[1..4]`.

**The `H=1..4` default is a pipeline shortcut, not a general rule:**

- Header protection on **and all four H fields nil** → the reference set `{1,1}`, `{2,2}`, `{3,3}`, `{4,4}` via `standardHeaderRanges()`.
- Header protection on **and at least one H explicit** → that value is used verbatim and every nil H is filled from one `GenerateHeaderRanges()` call, so the other three are wide random ranges, not `2-2`/`3-3`/`4-4`.
- Header protection off → every nil H is filled from `GenerateHeaderRanges()` (all four when all are nil); explicit H values are still written verbatim, so a pinned `h1: {1,1}` survives generation and only fails at validate/parse time. Generated ranges never contain `[1..4]`.

**Generator bounds** (`GenerateHeaderRanges`):

| Property | Value | Constant |
|---|---|---|
| Minimum `Min` | `5` | `headerMinValue` (structurally above the `[1..4]` window) |
| Maximum `Max` | `2147483647` (`int32` max) | `headerMaxValue` |
| Minimum span (`Max − Min`) | `10000000` | `headerMinRange` |
| Non-overlap | yes — sorted by `Min`, `Max_i < Min_{i+1}` (touching ranges are rejected) | `headerRangesValid` |
| Retry budget | `1000` attempts, then `panic("failed to generate non-overlapping header ranges after 1000 attempts")` | `headerMaxAttempts` |

The generator returns the four ranges **sorted by `Min`** and retries by drawing a whole new set, never by nudging bounds. Overlap is a generation-time rule only: `validate` has no overlap check at all, so an explicit range that overlaps a generated (or another explicit) range passes amnezigo validation and is rejected by the engine when the config is applied (`headers must not overlap`).

Header ranges are always written two-part: a single-value range appears as `H1 = 1-1`, never `H1 = 1`; the parser only accepts the two-part form.

```json
{
  "obfuscation": {
    "h1": { "min": 100000000,  "max": 200000000 },
    "h2": { "min": 300000000,  "max": 400000000 },
    "h3": { "min": 500000000,  "max": 600000000 },
    "h4": { "min": 700000000,  "max": 800000000 }
  }
}
```

## Jc / Jmin / Jmax — Junk Parameters

AmneziaWG emits `Jc` junk packets before each real handshake message, each between `Jmin` and `Jmax` bytes long. The goal is to drown out the size signature of real handshake messages. To prevent a junk packet from impersonating a handshake packet, `[Jmin..Jmax]` (inclusive) must exclude the four padded sizes **and** the four raw WireGuard sizes.

| Field | Default | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `jc` | random in `[0, 10]`, retried until non-zero | no | Number of junk packets sent before each handshake message |
| `jmin` | random in `[64, 1024]` | no | Inclusive lower bound on junk packet size |
| `jmax` | random in `[64, 1024]` | no | Inclusive upper bound on junk packet size (`> jmin`) |

> `jc`: int (nullable pointer)
> `jmin`: int (nullable pointer)
> `jmax`: int (nullable pointer)

**Forbidden sizes for `[Jmin..Jmax]`** (`junkRangeOK` in `generator.go`):

| Set | Values | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| AWG-padded handshake sizes | `S1+148`, `S2+92`, `S3+64`, `S4+32` | A junk packet this size would be indistinguishable from a real handshake message |
| Raw WireGuard sizes | `148, 92, 64, 32` | A junk packet this size would leak the underlying WG message length |

::: danger Junk range boundary is INCLUSIVE
`jmin` or `jmax` equal to a forbidden size **is** a collision. `ValidatePacketSizes` checks `f >= jmin && f <= jmax`. The generator (`GenerateJunkParamsWithForbidden`) retries up to `junkMaxAttempts = 1000` to find a clean range; the legacy `GenerateJunkParams()` (no collision avoidance) is retained only for backward compatibility and is not used by the pipeline.
:::

::: warning When collisions are not checked at all
`fillMissingJunk` short-circuits when `jc`, `jmin` and `jmax` are **all** explicit and copies them verbatim — no collision check, no repair; the violation surfaces only through `validate` (as `PSC002`/`JNK001`). An explicit `"jc": 0` is treated as unset and replaced by a non-zero draw unless `jmin` and `jmax` are also explicit, because the generator can draw `Jc = 0`. The pipeline retries junk generation at most 100 times; a generator error (`failed to generate non-colliding junk range after 1000 attempts`, `junkMaxAttempts`) aborts generation outright.
:::

The generator draws `Jmin, Jmax ∈ [64, 1024]` (`junkMinValue = 64`, `junkRangeSize = 961 = 1024 − 64 + 1`), swaps them if `Jmin > Jmax`, and bumps `Jmax = Jmin + 1` if they are equal.

## AWG 3.x Transport Parameters

These ten manifest fields cover the device layer. This section documents the manifest/INI parameter surface; the engine semantics (what the header cipher protects, how trailer classification works, key persistence across runs) live in [Transport Protection](/transport-protection).

| Manifest field | Type | Resolved default | Version gate | INI key |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `awg_version` | string | `"3.1"` (`DefaultAWGVersion`) | — | selects the emitted key set |
| `header_protection` | `*bool` | `true` for `>= 3.0` | 3.0 | `HeaderProtectionKey` |
| `content_padding` | `*U16Range` | `2-10` | 3.0 | `ContentPaddingAddition` |
| `rekey_after_time` | `*U16Range` | `120-180` | 3.0 | `RekeyAfterTime` |
| `rekey_timeout` | `*U16Range` | `5-8` | 3.0 | `RekeyTimeout` |
| `reject_after_time` | `*U16Range` | `180-240` | 3.0 | `RejectAfterTime` |
| `keepalive_timeout` | `*U16Range` | `8-12` | 3.0 | `KeepaliveTimeout` |
| `max_handshake_attempts` | `*U16Range` | `16-20` | 3.0 | `MaxHandshakeAttempts` |
| `random_trailers` | `*bool` | `true` for `3.1`, `false` for `3.0` | 3.1 | `RandomTrailers` (`on`/`off`) |
| `disable_cookies` | `*bool` | `true` for `>= 3.1` | 3.1 | `DisableCookies` (`on`/`off`) |

> `awg_version`: string — one of `"2.0"`, `"3.0"`, `"3.1"`; anything else is an error
> `header_protection`: bool (nullable) — controls whether a `HeaderProtectionKey` is generated; a false value under 2.0 is still a version-gate error
> `content_padding`, `rekey_after_time`, `rekey_timeout`, `reject_after_time`, `keepalive_timeout`, `max_handshake_attempts`: `{min, max}` with `uint16` bounds (nullable) — `nil` takes the default; an explicit `{0,0}` disables the key (it is omitted from the INI)
> `random_trailers`: bool (nullable) — 3.1 only
> `disable_cookies`: bool (nullable) — 3.1 only

`U16Range` serializes as `{"min": N, "max": M}`, renders as `N` when `Min == Max` and `Min-Max` otherwise, and has two error classes:

```text
obfuscation.<field>: bounds must both be zero or both non-zero (got 0-5)
obfuscation.<field>: max (2) is below min (5)
```

The nine INI key spellings are defined once in `transport_keys.go` and shared by writer, parser and validation. Emission is gated by the resolved `Version`:

- Below AWG 3.0 (including `"2.0"`): nothing — `writeTransportProtectionKeys` returns immediately, so a 2.0 config looks exactly like a legacy S/H/J config.
- 3.0 and above: `HeaderProtectionKey` only when non-empty, then the six ranges in the fixed order `ContentPaddingAddition`, `RekeyAfterTime`, `RekeyTimeout`, `RejectAfterTime`, `KeepaliveTimeout`, `MaxHandshakeAttempts`, each only when non-zero.
- 3.1: `RandomTrailers` and `DisableCookies` are always emitted, spelled `on`/`off`.

A hand-built `ServerObfuscationConfig` with a zero-value `Version` therefore emits none of the nine keys even when its 3.x fields are populated. All presets are 3.1 data by construction (`ToServerObfuscation` hardcodes `AWG31`).

The defaults produce this block in a 3.1 config (the full `[Interface]` layout is in [Output Format](/output-format)):

```ini
HeaderProtectionKey = <44-char base64>
ContentPaddingAddition = 2-10
RekeyAfterTime = 120-180
RekeyTimeout = 5-8
RejectAfterTime = 180-240
KeepaliveTimeout = 8-12
MaxHandshakeAttempts = 16-20
RandomTrailers = on
DisableCookies = on
```

`HeaderProtectionKey` is a 32-byte `crypto/rand` key, base64 StdEncoding (44 characters), deliberately not clamped, persisted across runs and reused unless `--full-reset` (see [Credentials](/credentials)). Header protection is switched by the key being present, not by a separate boolean, and the key's lifecycle has a sharp edge: a run that emits no key (a 2.0 manifest, or `header_protection: false`) drops it from the persisted state, so the next 3.x run generates a new one and every client still holding the old key stops completing handshakes.

## CPS I1–I5 — Custom Packet Strings (Client-Only)

The five custom packet strings (`I1`–`I5`) are templates for the five padding intervals AmneziaWG inserts around a handshake. They are generated **per client peer** and **never appear in the server config** — the server's `ServerObfuscationConfig` has no `I1`–`I5` fields.

`I1`–`I4` are populated from the peer's `protocol` template (or random tags). `I5` is **empty for named templates** (`quic`/`dns`/`dtls`/`stun`/`sip`/`rtp`); `random` fills all five.

A CPS string is a concatenation of tags drawn from this fixed grammar:

| Tag | Meaning | Size / Range |
|---|---|---|
| `<b 0xHEX>` | Literal hex bytes (a missing `0x` prefix is added automatically) | `len(HEX) / 2` bytes |
| `<r N>` | `N` random bytes (any value) | `N` bytes |
| `<rc N>` | `N` random **letters** from `[a-zA-Z]` (52 letters, lowercase first) | `N` bytes |
| `<rd N>` | `N` random **digits** (`0`–`9`) | `N` bytes |
| `<t>` | `uint32` Big-Endian Unix timestamp | exactly `4` bytes |
| `<d>` | Data passthrough — the engine reuses a value from an earlier I-packet position at emit time | `0` bytes at generation time |
| anything else | unsupported/unknown tag, including `<c>` and the engine-only `ds`/`dz` | `0` bytes |

**Byte accounting is lenient.** `CPSLength` — the same oracle used by generation-time validation — counts unknown tags as 0 bytes, and numeric parse failures inside a tag become 0 (`strconv.Atoi` errors are ignored), so `<r abc>` counts as 0. A malformed or unsupported tag shrinks the interval instead of failing validation. The engine's 3.1 parser accepts `ds` and `dz`, but no amnezigo code path recognises or emits them: a hand-written `<dz 32>` silently disappears from every size calculation. amnezigo implements exactly `b`, `t`, `r`, `rc`, `rd` and `d`.

::: danger There is NO `<c>` tag — do not use it
The legacy `<c>` (counter) tag is **kernel-only** and is rejected by `amneziawg-go` and **all** AmneziaVPN clients (iOS, Android, Windows, macOS) with `unknown tag`. `BuildCPSTag("c", ...)` returns the empty string (the same sentinel as any unknown tag); `CPSLength` treats any stray `<c>` as 0 bytes. Amnezigo never emits `<c>`. If you hand-edit a client config and add one, `validate` reports `CPS001`.
:::

::: warning `<rc>` is letters only — not alphanumeric
The widely-cited Habr article on AWG 2.0 incorrectly claims `<rc>` draws from `[a-zA-Z0-9]`. The actual alphabet (source: `amneziawg-go` `device/obf_randchars.go`) is the 52 ASCII letters, lowercase first. For a mixed letter+digit field, concatenate: `<rc 4><rd 2>` produces 4 letters followed by 2 digits.
:::

::: tip `<d>` requires a userspace AWG runtime
`<d>` is a runtime-passthrough marker that only makes sense inside a multi-interval template where an earlier interval produces the value being reused (e.g. QUIC's I2 reuses I1's DCID via `<d>`). The legacy `amneziawg-linux-kernel-module` rejects `<d>` with `unknown tag`. Amnezigo's Dockerfile pins `amneziavpn/amneziawg-go:3.1.20260828` (userspace) so generated configs work out of the box.
:::

::: tip I1–I5 determinism
Named templates are recomputed per client but are deterministic: the same protocol (and the same MTU/S1 budget, which only matters when clipping is triggered) yields identical strings across peers and across runs. A fresh tag sequence per run happens only for `protocol: random`. The on-wire bytes still differ from any two peers' configs because the engine expands `<r N>`/`<rc N>`/`<rd N>`/`<t>` at emit time; the tag literals in the config are the fingerprint, not the values.
:::

**Generated CPS examples** (rendered tag shapes — values inside `<r>`/`<rc>`/`<rd>` are filled by the AmneziaWG receiver at emit time):

```ini
# QUIC I1 — long-header Initial with random DCID, timestamp, random payload
I1 = <b 0xc0ff><b 0x00000001><b 0x08><r 8><b 0x00><b 0x00><b 0x0040><b 0x00><b 0x01><t><r 40>

# QUIC I2 — DCID chained from I1 via <d>
I2 = <b 0xc0ff><b 0x00000001><b 0x08><d><b 0x00><b 0x00><b 0x0020><b 0x01><t><r 20>

# DNS I1 — query with <rc>-filled labels (e.g. "www.example.com")
I1 = <r 2><b 0x0100><b 0x0001><b 0x0000><b 0x0000><b 0x0000><b 0x03><rc 3><b 0x07><rc 7><b 0x03><rc 3><b 0x00><b 0x0001><b 0x0001>
```

## Protocols

The peer's `protocol` field selects the I1–I4 template. Empty `protocol` defaults to `quic`. `random` fills all five intervals with standalone random tags (it does **not** pick a named template). Any other **unrecognized** value is not rejected: the template lookup's default branch picks one of the six named templates (`quic`/`dns`/`dtls`/`stun`/`sip`/`rtp`) uniformly at random, so a typo yields a plausible but unexpected protocol shape. Each named template populates `I1`–`I4` and leaves `I5` empty. `ListProtocols()` returns the seven names sorted alphabetically: `dns`, `dtls`, `quic`, `random`, `rtp`, `sip`, `stun`.

The top-level `obfuscation.protocol` is **decorative** — `generate` does not read it. Only the per-peer `protocol` drives I-packet generation.

| Protocol | Mimics | Leading bytes | Characteristic tags | Notable behavior |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `quic` | QUIC Long-Header Initial (RFC 9000) | `0xC0` long-header form | `<b>` for header fields, `<r>` for DCID/payload, `<t>` in payload, `<d>` in I2 (DCID reuse) | I2 chains I1's DCID via `<d>` |
| `dns` | DNS standard query (RFC 1035) | random transaction ID first, flags `0x0100` | `<r>` transaction ID, `<rc>` for query-name labels | I3 uses `<rd>` for an all-digit "domain" |
| `dtls` | DTLS 1.2 ClientHello (RFC 6347) | `0x16` ContentType=Handshake, then `fefd` | `<b>` for record/handshake headers, `<t>` + `<r 28>` for the 32-byte Random | I1 carries a realistic cipher-suite list |
