| `stun` | STUN Binding Request (RFC 5389) | `0x0001` message type | `<b 0x2112a442>` magic cookie, `<r 12>` transaction ID | I2 adds a PADDING attribute |
| `sip` | SIP OPTIONS request over UDP (RFC 3261) | ASCII `"OPTIONS "` (`0x4f...`) | `<rc>` for user/host tokens, `<rd>` for CSeq digits | No `<t>` (timestamp), no `<r>` — pure ASCII |
| `rtp` | RTP media packet (RFC 3550) | `0x80` V=2 first byte | `<b>` for fixed header (V/PT), `<r>` for seq/SSRC/payload, `<t>` for 32-bit timestamp | Binary-only (no `<rc>`/`<rd>`); PT=0 (PCMU/G.711 μ-law) |
| `random` | (none — standalone intervals) | none | 3–6 tags drawn from `{b, r, rc, rd, t}`, at most one `<t>` | Fills all five intervals; never emits `<d>` |

**Measured template budgets** (`CPSLength` over the rendered templates, before any MTU clipping; `I5` is empty and contributes 0 bytes for all six):

| Protocol | I1 | I2 | I3 | I4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `quic` | 65 | 36 | 34 | 29 |
| `dns` | 33 | 22 | 20 | 19 |
| `dtls` | 73 | 67 | 67 | 67 |
| `stun` | 20 | 24 | 20 | 20 |
| `sip` | 312 | 203 | 140 | 87 |
| `rtp` | 92 | 52 | 36 | 20 |

The budgets are consequences of the template definitions, not an invariant — they are not monotonic (STUN I2 is larger than I1). The SIP source comment quotes `~360/~240/~170/~120`; those numbers are approximate and must not be quoted as exact — the measured values above are `312/203/140/87`. The RTP comment (`~92/~52/~36/~20`) matches the rendered lengths.

Rendered examples (`CPSLength` in parentheses):

```text
quic I1 = <b 0xc0ff><b 0x00000001><b 0x08><r 8><b 0x00><b 0x00><b 0x0040><b 0x00><b 0x01><t><r 40>  (65 B)
stun I1 = <b 0x0001><b 0x0000><b 0x2112a442><r 12>  (20 B)
rtp  I1 = <b 0x8000><r 2><t><r 4><r 80>  (92 B)
sip  I1 = <b 0x4f5054494f4e53><b 0x20><b 0x7369703a><rc 8>...  (312 B)
```

**`random` tag selection** (`generateRandomTags` in `cps.go`): 3–6 tags per interval (`minTagCount = 3`, `maxTagCount = 6`); `<b>` payload length 4–16 bytes (`minByteLen = 4`, `maxByteLen = 16`); `<r>`/`<rc>`/`<rd>` sizes 5–40 (`minSize = 5`, `maxSize = 40`); at most one `<t>` per interval. `<d>` is excluded from random mode — it has no chaining context there.

Each named protocol's leading bytes are deliberately distinct (`QUIC 0xC0`, `DTLS 0x16`, `STUN 0x0001`, `SIP "OPTIONS "`), so the template picked for an unrecognized protocol string is visible in the resulting packet shapes.

## Byte-Budget Constraints

Every I-packet must satisfy two hard constraints enforced by `cpsAcceptable` (`cps.go`):

1. **MTU fit** — its calculated byte length must be **strictly less than** `maxISize` (an interval whose length equals the budget is rejected).
2. **No size collision** — its calculated byte length must not equal any of the four padded handshake sizes (`S1+148`, `S2+92`, `S3+64`, `S4+32`) — *when a forbidden set is threaded through*.

The per-I budget is:

```text
maxISize = MTU − reserve(49) − handshakeSize(149) − S1
```

| Constant | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `reserve` | `49` | IP header (20 or 40) + UDP header (8) + 1 byte margin |
| `handshakeSize` | `149` | Fixed WireGuard handshake size (`148 + 1` margin) |
| `maxISize` | `MTU − 49 − 149 − S1` | Maximum I-packet byte length |

With the default MTU `1280` and `S1 = 0`, `maxISize = 1082`; with `S1 = 32` it is `1050`. Raise `S1` and the budget shrinks dollar-for-dollar.

**Fallback ladder** (`buildAndValidateCPS` / `generateSimpleI`):

1. Generate the template / random tags.
2. If the result does not fit or collides with a padded size, drop trailing tags one at a time.
3. If still colliding, perturb by appending `<t><rd N>` for `N ∈ [1..8]`.
4. Last resort: bare `<t>` (4 bytes) — always fits and never collides with a padded size (the smallest padded size is `S4+32 ≥ 32`).

::: danger Constraint 2 is only real on the library path
`GenerateConfig` passes `PaddedSizes(S1,S2,S3,S4)` into CPS generation and then re-checks the produced interval lengths with `ValidatePacketSizes`, panicking with `GenerateConfig: produced invalid sizes: %v` if the invariant is broken. The `generate` pipeline instead calls `GenerateCPS(protocol, mtu, s1, jc)` — whose fourth argument is ignored and whose forbidden set is hardcoded empty — so CLI-emitted I1-I5 are never sized against the padded handshake sizes and neither `generate` nor `validate` reports a collision (`validate` passes `nil` I-packet sizes, making `PSC003` unreachable). A manifest can therefore silently emit an I-packet whose length equals a padded size — e.g. `S3 = 1` makes the padded cookie reply `65` bytes, the same as the default QUIC I1. Use the library [`GenerateConfig`](/library-api) path, or re-check emitted intervals with `ValidatePacketSizes`, if you need the stronger guarantee.
:::

::: warning Tiny MTU collapses every interval to `<t>`
If `maxISize ≤ 0` (e.g. very large `S1` combined with a small MTU), every interval falls back to bare `<t>` (4 bytes) — five identical 4-byte I-packets. Named-template intervals are shrunk tag-by-tag before this fallback; `random` mode retries (up to `iPacketMaxAttempts = 1000`), then perturbs, then falls back. A barely positive budget is also degenerate: at `maxISize` 1–2 the shrink loop reduces every named-template interval to the empty string (the `I1`–`I5` keys are then omitted from the client config) and at 3–4 to a 2-byte fragment. Intervals stay clipped until `maxISize` exceeds the template's largest interval — measured: the QUIC template renders unclipped from `MTU − S1 ≥ 264`, SIP from `MTU − S1 ≥ 511`.
:::

::: danger Defect: an omitted `network.mtu` collapses I1–I5 to `<t>`
`buildClientConfig` calls `GenerateCPS(protocol, manifest.Network.MTU, ...)` **before** defaulting the MTU to `1280`, so a manifest without `network.mtu` gets `maxISize < 0` and five bare `<t>` intervals, while the emitted client config still says `MTU = 1280`. The server config is unaffected (it generates no I-packets). Always set `network.mtu` explicitly; this is a currently-shipping defect, not intended behavior.
:::

`generate` also never re-parses the client configs, so any issue visible only in a client config (I-packet sizes included) is absent from its findings; `amnezigo validate` can be pointed at a client config, but it applies server-config rules to it — the client-only `I1`–`I5` keys are reported as unknown INI keys (`KEY001`) and `ListenPort` as missing (`FLD001`, an error) — and the I-packet-vs-padded-size leg is never checked, so that gap stays open.

## Choosing Parameters

The built-in [presets](/presets) cover the common cases; the heuristics below guide manual tuning. Run `amnezigo analyze` on a generated config to surface the RISK001–RISK009 findings referenced here.

**Size prefixes.** Keep `S4 ≥ 8` (RISK003) — below that, keepalive packets (`32 + S4` bytes) are trivially distinguishable. Larger `S4` masks data-plane sizes better but costs throughput (~`S4`/MTU per packet). `S1`–`S3` matter less (handshakes are rare) but should keep all four padded sizes ≥ 5 bytes apart (RISK004) and clear of the raw WG sizes `148`/`92`/`64`/`32` (RISK005). Note two RISK quirks: RISK004/RISK005 skip equal values (they require a non-zero difference), and under header protection the S floor of 12 already forces `S4 ≥ 12`, so RISK003 cannot fire. A large `S1` shrinks the I-packet budget (`maxISize = MTU − 198 − S1`), weakening protocol mimicry.

**Header ranges.** Without header protection each `Hn` range should span at least ~1 M values (RISK007) — a 2-value range is barely better than the fixed type-byte it replaces. RISK007 is **skipped entirely when header protection is active**, because the type byte is encrypted and the reference set is `1-1`…`4-4`. The four ranges must be pairwise non-overlapping (the receiver disambiguates message type by which range the header lands in) — but that rule is enforced only at generation: amnezigo's `validate` does not check overlap, so a partial explicit H set can mix a pinned range with freshly generated large ranges and be rejected by the engine (`headers must not overlap`) only at apply time. The `[1..4]` exclusion applies without header protection; under it, `1-1`…`4-4` is exactly what you want.

**Junk.** `Jc` controls noise density before each handshake; `Jmin`/`Jmax` control its size spread. Keep the range width ≥ 32 (RISK006) and entirely clear of all padded and raw WG sizes. A wider range (`Jmax − Jmin ≥ 500`) gives junk a less predictable size distribution; a higher `Jc` (≥ 5) buries the handshake more thoroughly but adds `Jc` packet-times of latency to each rekey. Remember that when all three junk fields are explicit, no collision check runs.

**Cover protocol (`I1`–`I5`).** Pick a UDP-based protocol common on your network — `dns`, `quic`, `stun`, `sip`, `dtls` are all good choices; `random` emits standalone random tags and is not a real protocol (a censor may flag unrecognised UDP). Keep I-packet sizes in the 100–500 B sweet spot, never above the ~1200 B MTU ceiling; RISK002 warns when a peer's five I-packet sizes span less than `iPacketClusterMinWidth = 20` B — since named templates leave `I5` empty (0 B), their span is simply the largest interval's size, so the check realistically targets compact `random` mode draws. Prefer named templates when you need stable configs; use `random` deliberately, knowing it redraws per run.

**MTU.** The default `1280` is safe everywhere (IPv6 minimum, avoids fragmentation on most links). `1420` (the classic WireGuard MTU) gives more I-packet headroom but can fragment on IPv6 links with a 1500-byte Ethernet MTU once obfuscation overhead is added — see below. Keep the budget healthy: `maxISize = MTU − 198 − S1` must exceed the template's largest interval for unclipped output (measured: QUIC needs `MTU − S1 ≥ 264`, SIP `≥ 511`; `maxISize` 1–4 yields empty or 2-byte intervals). Always set `network.mtu` explicitly (see the defect above).

**S4 + MTU fragmentation constraint.** `S4` is prepended to *every* transport-data packet, so the outer IP packet grows by `S4` bytes. For no IP fragmentation on a standard 1500-byte Ethernet link:

```text
tunnel_MTU + S4 ≤ 1440   (IPv4 outer transport: 20 IP + 8 UDP + 32 WG = 60 fixed)
tunnel_MTU + S4 ≤ 1420   (IPv6 outer transport: 40 IP + 8 UDP + 32 WG = 80 fixed)
```

Every MTU-1280 preset satisfies both with ≥ 100 bytes of headroom. `standard-1420` (`MTU 1420`, `S4 16`) is IPv4-safe (4-byte margin) but **exceeds the IPv6 budget by 16 bytes** — use it only when the outer transport is IPv4, or the physical link supports jumbo frames (≥ 1520 MTU). This is not specific to amnezigo: even vanilla WireGuard at MTU 1420 on IPv6 sits at the exact 1500-byte limit, so any obfuscation padding pushes it over.

## Manifest Reference — `obfuscation.*`

All `obfuscation.*` fields are optional. Omitting S/H/J fields triggers random generation bounded as above; explicit values are used verbatim (except zeros — see below). The 3.x fields default per `awg_version`.

::: tip Pointers: omit ≠ zero — and zero is not always a pin
`s1`–`s4`, `jc`, `jmin`, `jmax` decode to `*int` and `h1`–`h4` to `*HeaderRange`, so `nil` ("not set") is distinguishable from an explicit value. For the **S prefixes and `jc`**, zero is still treated as unset: `{"s1": 0}` is re-drawn as a generated non-zero value (`pickNonZero`), and `"jc": 0` is replaced unless `jmin` and `jmax` are also explicit. Explicit header ranges and 3.x ranges are used as written, including `{"min":0,"max":0}` (which disables a 3.x key but writes `H1 = 0-0` for a header range). Random fill bounds: S1–S3 ∈ `[minS, 64]`, S4 ∈ `[minS, 32]` with `minS = 12` under header protection and `0` otherwise; Jc ∈ `[0,10]`, redrawn when zero; Jmin/Jmax ∈ `[64,1024]`; H ranges as above.
:::

> `obfuscation.protocol`: string — **decorative**, not consumed by `generate`. Use the per-peer `protocol` to select I-packet templates.
> `obfuscation.s1`, `s2`, `s3`: int (nullable) — size prefixes, fixed value or random in `[minS, 64]` (min 12 under header protection)
> `obfuscation.s4`: int (nullable) — size prefix, fixed value or random in `[minS, 32]`
> `obfuscation.h1`–`h4`: `{min, max}` object (nullable) — header ranges, both `uint32`; defaults to `1-1`…`4-4` under header protection with all four unset
> `obfuscation.jc`: int (nullable) — junk packet count, fixed or random in `[0, 10]`
> `obfuscation.jmin`, `jmax`: int (nullable) — inclusive junk size range, fixed or random in `[64, 1024]`
> `obfuscation.awg_version`: string — `"2.0"`, `"3.0"` or `"3.1"` (default)
> `obfuscation.header_protection`: bool (nullable) — default true for `>= 3.0`
> `obfuscation.content_padding`, `rekey_after_time`, `rekey_timeout`, `reject_after_time`, `keepalive_timeout`, `max_handshake_attempts`: `{min, max}` `uint16` (nullable) — 3.0+; `nil` = default, `{0,0}` = key omitted
> `obfuscation.random_trailers`, `disable_cookies`: bool (nullable) — 3.1 only

Minimal manifest — every obfuscation field randomized (and `awg_version` defaults to `3.1`):

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "network": { "mtu": 1280 },
  "obfuscation": {},
  "peers": {
    "server": { "address": "10.99.0.1/24", "endpoint": "vpn.example.com", "listen_port": 51820 },
    "phone":  { "address": "10.99.0.2/24", "protocol": "quic" }
  }
}
```

Fully pinned S/H/J (matches the `home-balanced` preset). The pinned example deliberately shows only the S/H/J layer: the resolved output is still a 3.1 config, so it carries the nine 3.x keys at their defaults — `HeaderProtectionKey`, `ContentPaddingAddition = 2-10`, the five timer ranges, `RandomTrailers = on`, `DisableCookies = on` — and its unequal pinned S meets the enabled trailers with a `TRL001` warning:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "network": { "mtu": 1280 },
  "obfuscation": {
    "s1": 30, "s2": 35, "s3": 20, "s4": 12,
    "h1": { "min": 100,        "max": 5000000 },
    "h2": { "min": 10000000,   "max": 200000000 },
    "h3": { "min": 400000000,  "max": 800000000 },
    "h4": { "min": 1000000000, "max": 2100000000 },
    "jc": 5, "jmin": 250, "jmax": 750
  },
  "peers": {
    "server": { "address": "10.99.0.1/24", "endpoint": "vpn.example.com", "listen_port": 51820 }
  }
}
```

Note that this pinned set is **not** valid as written under header protection if any S drops below 12 — `s4: 12` is exactly at the floor and passes, but a hand-tuned `s4: 8` would abort generation. See [Built-in Presets](/presets) for seven ready-made parameter bundles (with their 3.1 `ContentPadding`/`RandomTrailers`/`DisableCookies` values) you can copy verbatim, and [Validation](/validation) for the `PSC001`/`PSC002`/`PSC003`/`HPK001`/`TRL001`/`JNK001` findings these parameters feed (`HDR001`/`HDR002` are library-level codes that the CLI's parser pre-empts with `PSE001`).
---
url: /transport-protection
---
# Transport Protection (AWG 3.x)

AmneziaWG 2.0 [obfuscation](/obfuscation) shapes the outside of a tunnel — junk packets (`Jc`, `Jmin`, `Jmax`), size prefixes (`S1`–`S4`), header ranges (`H1`–`H4`), and per-client custom packet strings (`I1`–`I5`). AWG 3.x adds a second, device-level layer on top of it:

- **Header protection** encrypts the 4-byte WireGuard message header with a symmetric ChaCha20 key, so the message type is no longer visible on the wire.
- **Content padding** and **random trailers** adjust packet sizes beyond the handshake padding the 2.0 layer already provides.
- **Timer ranges** jitter the WireGuard rekey, rekey-timeout, reject, keepalive, and handshake-attempt constants.
- **Cookie replies** can be disabled entirely.

Unlike the 2.0 parameters, these are device-level keys: they live in one `[Interface]` block, written verbatim — including one shared `HeaderProtectionKey` — to the server config and to every client config.

The target generation is selected per manifest by `obfuscation.awg_version`, and it is a hard output gate rather than a hint. Older engine builds reject INI keys they do not know (`Line unrecognized` in amneziawg-tools `src/config.c`), so a 3.x key must never appear in a config aimed at a lower generation.

| Generation | `awg_version` | Adds over the previous one |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AmneziaWG 2.0 | `"2.0"` | `Jc`/`Jmin`/`Jmax`, `S1`–`S4`, `H1`–`H4` ranges, `I1`–`I5` |
| AmneziaWG 3.0 | `"3.0"` | `HeaderProtectionKey`, `ContentPaddingAddition`, `RekeyAfterTime`, `RekeyTimeout`, `RejectAfterTime`, `KeepaliveTimeout`, `MaxHandshakeAttempts` |
| AmneziaWG 3.1 | `"3.1"` (default) | `RandomTrailers`, `DisableCookies` |

## Version Model

`version.go` models the selector as `type AWGVersion int`:

| Constant | Value | Label |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AWG20` | 1 | `2.0` |
| `AWG30` | 2 | `3.0` |
| `AWG31` | 3 | `3.1` |

- `DefaultAWGVersion = AWG31`; an unset (or empty) `obfuscation.awg_version` resolves to 3.1.
- `ParseAWGVersion` accepts exactly `""`, `"2.0"`, `"3.0"`, `"3.1"`. Anything else fails with `unsupported awg_version %q (expected "2.0", "3.0", or "3.1")` — including values such as `"2"`, `"4.0"`, `"3.10"`, `"v3.1"`, and `"latest"`. The `generate` CLI wraps the message: `Error: generating configs: resolve obfuscation: unsupported awg_version "3" (expected "2.0", "3.0", or "3.1")`.
- `AWGVersion.String()` returns the dotted label, or `AWGVersion(%d)` for out-of-range values such as the zero value.
- The resolved version is stored in `ServerObfuscationConfig.Version`, so the writer, parser, and validators never need the manifest. The **zero value** (`0`) sorts below `AWG20`, which is deliberate: a hand-built `ServerObfuscationConfig` that never sets `Version` emits exactly the legacy 2.0 key set and stays byte-compatible with existing library callers (see [Library API](/library-api)).

Two mechanisms enforce the gate:

- `checkObfuscationVersionGates` turns a 3.x manifest field under a lower `awg_version` into a hard error instead of silently dropping it.
- `writeTransportProtectionKeys` returns before emitting anything when `Version < AWG30`, so the entire nine-key block disappears for 2.0.

::: warning The gate is by field presence, not by value
Setting `header_protection: false` while `awg_version` is `"2.0"` still fails resolution with `obfuscation.header_protection requires awg_version 3.0 or later (got "2.0")`. A field that the target generation cannot express is an error even when the intended value would be a no-op.
:::

## Manifest Knobs

All ten knobs live in the manifest `obfuscation` object and are optional; the surrounding schema is documented in [Manifest Reference](/manifest-reference). `nil`/absent selects the version default, and the three booleans default to `true` for every version that understands them.

| JSON key | Go type | Absent resolves to | Minimum version |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `awg_version` | `string` | `3.1` | — |
| `header_protection` | `*bool` | `true` | 3.0 |
| `content_padding` | `*U16Range` | `{2, 10}` | 3.0 |
| `rekey_after_time` | `*U16Range` | `{120, 180}` | 3.0 |
| `rekey_timeout` | `*U16Range` | `{5, 8}` | 3.0 |
| `reject_after_time` | `*U16Range` | `{180, 240}` | 3.0 |
| `keepalive_timeout` | `*U16Range` | `{8, 12}` | 3.0 |
| `max_handshake_attempts` | `*U16Range` | `{16, 20}` | 3.0 |
| `random_trailers` | `*bool` | `true` | 3.1 |
| `disable_cookies` | `*bool` | `true` | 3.1 |

`U16Range` is `{"min": uint16, "max": uint16}`; both bounds are `uint16`, so JSON numbers above 65535 fail to unmarshal. Its semantics:

- An explicit `{"min": 0, "max": 0}` **disables** the key: the writer omits it and the engine keeps its own default.
- A missing bound decodes as `0`, so `{"min": 0}` is `{0, 0}` — disabled, not "0 as the lower bound". `{"min": 0, "max": 5}` is a hard error.
- Mixed zero bounds fail with `obfuscation.<field>: bounds must both be zero or both non-zero (got %d-%d)`.
- Inverted bounds fail with `obfuscation.<field>: max (%d) is below min (%d)`.

The three booleans follow the same pattern: `nil`/absent selects the version default (`true` for every version that understands the flag), an explicit `false` turns the behavior off, and any explicit value below the flag's minimum version is rejected by the presence-based version gate — `false` included.

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "network": { "mtu": 1280 },
  "obfuscation": {
    "awg_version": "3.1",
    "content_padding": { "min": 2, "max": 10 },
    "rekey_after_time": { "min": 120, "max": 180 },
    "random_trailers": true
  },
  "peers": {
    "server": { "address": "10.0.0.1/24", "endpoint": "vpn.example.com:51820", "listen_port": 51820 },
    "phone": { "address": "10.0.0.2/32" }
  }
}
```

Version gates run before any other resolution step and report the first offending field in declaration order:

| Field | Minimum | Exact error |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `header_protection` | 3.0 | `obfuscation.header_protection requires awg_version 3.0 or later (got "2.0")` |
| `content_padding` | 3.0 | `obfuscation.content_padding requires awg_version 3.0 or later (got "2.0")` |
| `rekey_after_time` | 3.0 | `obfuscation.rekey_after_time requires awg_version 3.0 or later (got "2.0")` |
| `rekey_timeout` | 3.0 | `obfuscation.rekey_timeout requires awg_version 3.0 or later (got "2.0")` |
| `reject_after_time` | 3.0 | `obfuscation.reject_after_time requires awg_version 3.0 or later (got "2.0")` |
| `keepalive_timeout` | 3.0 | `obfuscation.keepalive_timeout requires awg_version 3.0 or later (got "2.0")` |
| `max_handshake_attempts` | 3.0 | `obfuscation.max_handshake_attempts requires awg_version 3.0 or later (got "2.0")` |
| `random_trailers` | 3.1 | `obfuscation.random_trailers requires awg_version 3.1 or later (got "3.0")` |
| `disable_cookies` | 3.1 | `obfuscation.disable_cookies requires awg_version 3.1 or later (got "3.0")` |

The `(got "...")` suffix echoes the *resolved* version label. `generate` wraps every one of these with `generating configs: resolve obfuscation: ` and writes nothing.

::: tip The 3.x knobs are invisible to the projection helpers
`HasAnyValue()` and `ToSharedObfuscation()` still cover only `S1`–`S4`, `H1`–`H4`, `Jc`, `Jmin`, and `Jmax`. Library code that uses those helpers and then assumes the result carries `content_padding` or `header_protection` silently loses data — `resolveObfuscation` reads the 3.x fields directly.
:::

## Resolution Semantics

`resolveObfuscation` merges explicit manifest values with generated ones in a fixed order:

1. Parse `awg_version` (unset resolves to 3.1).
2. Run the version gates.
3. Derive `headerProtection`, `randomTrailers`, and `disableCookies` from the version, each overridden by its explicit pointer.
4. Seed explicit `S1`–`S4`.
5. Pick `minS`: `0` for 2.0, `headerProtectionNonceSize` (12) when header protection is on.
6. Decide whether S generation is uniform.
7. Fill missing S prefixes.
8. Check the S floor.
9. Fill missing header ranges.
10. Reuse or generate the header-protection key.
11. Apply the six 3.x ranges (version 3.0+ only).
12. Assign `RandomTrailers` and `DisableCookies`.
13. Fill missing junk parameters.

Because step 8 runs before steps 9–13, an S-floor violation is the error reported even when other fields are also wrong.

Resolution flags, before explicit overrides:

| Flag | 2.0 | 3.0 | 3.1 | Explicit field |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `headerProtection` | false | true | true | `header_protection` |
| `randomTrailers` | false | false | true | `random_trailers` |
| `disableCookies` | false | false | true | `disable_cookies` |

A flag can be turned off, but never forced on below its minimum version — the version gate rejects the field instead of ignoring it.

The same manifest resolves to different output per generation:

| Parameter | `"2.0"` | `"3.0"` | `"3.1"` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `header_protection` | off (field forbidden) | on (key generated) | on (key generated) |
| `content_padding` | off (no key) | `2-10` | `2-10` |
| five timer ranges | off (no keys) | defaults | defaults |
| `random_trailers` | off (field forbidden) | off (field forbidden) | on |
| `disable_cookies` | off (field forbidden) | off (field forbidden) | on |
| Emitted 3.x keys | none of the nine | key + six ranges | all nine |

### S-prefix floor: 12

Header protection encrypts the 4-byte header at offset `S{n}` with a ChaCha20 nonce built from the first 12 bytes of the packet, so the engine refuses `S < 12` whenever a header-protection key is present. Amnezigo encodes this as `headerProtectionNonceSize = 12` and enforces it during resolution:

```text
header protection requires S1-S4 >= 12 (got S3=8)
```

An explicit `s3: 8` under 3.1 makes `generate` exit 1 and write nothing:

```shell
amnezigo generate --project ./myproject
# Error: generating configs: resolve obfuscation: header protection requires S1-S4 >= 12 (got S3=8)
```

Generated values always respect the floor: `S1`–`S3` are drawn from `[minS, 65)` and `S4` from `[minS, 33)`, and the four padded handshake sizes (`S1+148`, `S2+92`, `S3+64`, `S4+32`) must be pairwise distinct. When header protection is off, `minS` is `0` and any `S` is legal — a 2.0 config can carry `S4 = 8`.

::: danger An explicit `S` of `0` does not pin zero
`fillMissingSPrefixes` only preserves non-zero values (`pickNonZero`), so `"s3": 0` behaves like "unset": the field is re-drawn in the floor-aware range. Under header protection that draw is never below 12, so a manifest cannot force `S < 12` — it can only trigger the floor error with a non-zero value such as `8`.
:::

### Uniform S under random trailers

When `random_trailers` resolves to `true` **and all four `S` fields are absent**, Amnezigo draws one value in `[minS, 33)` and uses it for `S1 = S2 = S3 = S4`. Equal size prefixes keep the four padded handshake sizes unambiguous for the receiver's size-based packet classification.

The uniform path is skipped as soon as **any** `S` field is explicit — the remaining fields are drawn independently (`S1`–`S3` from `[minS, 65)`, `S4` from `[minS, 33)`), which is exactly the case `TRL001` warns about. The rule also applies with header protection off, where `minS` is `0` and the drawn value can be as low as `1`.

### Header ranges under header protection

With header protection on and all four `H` fields absent, Amnezigo emits the reference ranges:

```ini
H1 = 1-1
H2 = 2-2
H3 = 3-3
H4 = 4-4
```

The message type is encrypted, so the WireGuard type-ids `1..4` are no longer observable and no longer have to be avoided. If even one `H` field is explicit, the remaining fields come from `GenerateHeaderRanges()` (wide random ranges that never intersect `1..4`) and the explicit values are kept verbatim. Amnezigo does not check whether the resulting ranges overlap; the engine does, at `awg setconf` time, with `headers must not overlap`. With header protection off, generated wide ranges are always used.

### Header-protection key lifecycle

`GenerateHeaderProtectionKey` draws 32 bytes from `crypto/rand` and base64-encodes them with `StdEncoding`: a 44-character string with one `=` pad. The key is deliberately **not clamped** — it is a symmetric ChaCha20 key, not a Curve25519 scalar.

- The key is recovered from the previous run's server config (`PersistedCredentials.HeaderProtectionKey`) and reused whenever `--full-reset` is not set and the persisted value is non-empty — see [Credentials & Key Reuse](/credentials).
- Otherwise a new key is generated. `--full-reset` rotates it together with every private key and PSK, so all previously distributed configs stop working.
- The same key is written to the server config and every client config, and it is the only 3.x value that is persisted between runs; the six ranges resolve to their defaults every time, while unpinned `S` values are still re-drawn.
- `--dry-run` still loads the persisted key (it does not rotate it); on a first run with no output tree it generates a fresh one that the next real run will not reuse.

::: danger The emitted server config is the only key store
A run that emits no key — target 2.0, or `header_protection: false` — drops it from the persisted state. Switching back to 3.x therefore generates a **new** key, and every client still holding the old one stops completing handshakes until it is re-imported. Regenerating with unpinned `S` values has the same re-import requirement, because the S prefixes change even though the key persists.
:::

## Emitted INI Keys

The nine keys are defined once in `transport_keys.go` — the exact spelling amneziawg-tools `src/config.c` parses — and that single definition is shared by the writer, the parser, and the validators.

| INI key | Value form | Emitted when | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `HeaderProtectionKey` | 44-char base64 of 32 bytes | header protection active and key non-empty | ChaCha20 key for the 4-byte message header |
| `ContentPaddingAddition` | `N` or `N-M` | range non-zero, version ≥ 3.0 | content-padding amount (bytes) |
| `RekeyAfterTime` | `N` or `N-M` | range non-zero, version ≥ 3.0 | seconds; jitter around WireGuard's 120 s rekey |
| `RekeyTimeout` | `N` or `N-M` | range non-zero, version ≥ 3.0 | seconds; around the 5 s rekey timeout |
| `RejectAfterTime` | `N` or `N-M` | range non-zero, version ≥ 3.0 | seconds; around the 180 s reject |
| `KeepaliveTimeout` | `N` or `N-M` | range non-zero, version ≥ 3.0 | seconds; around the 10 s keepalive |
| `MaxHandshakeAttempts` | `N` or `N-M` | range non-zero, version ≥ 3.0 | handshake attempts; around the 18-attempt constant |
| `RandomTrailers` | `on` / `off` | always at version ≥ 3.1 | random trailer padding |
| `DisableCookies` | `on` / `off` | always at version ≥ 3.1 | disable cookie replies |

Formatting rules:

- A range is written as a single decimal number when `Min == Max` and as `Min-Max` otherwise; the parser accepts both and a round trip normalises the same way (`RekeyAfterTime = 120` parses to `{120,120}` and is written back as `120`).
- Booleans are written `on`/`off`; the parser also accepts `1`/`0` case-insensitively and rejects anything else (`expected on/off/0/1, got "true"`). `RandomTrailers = true` is not valid engine input.
- `HeaderProtectionKey` is the only 3.x value with a decoded-content (length) check at load: it must decode to exactly 32 bytes, otherwise parsing aborts with `invalid HeaderProtectionKey "<value>": must be 44-char base64 of 32 bytes`. Because credential loading reuses the emitted config, a corrupt key blocks the next `generate` entirely.
- Malformed range or boolean values abort parsing too: `invalid <Key> "<value>": expected "N" or "N-M"`, `invalid <Key> "<value>": max (%d) is below min (%d)`, or the boolean message above.

Omission rules:

- `Version < AWG30` → nothing at all is emitted (2.0, and the zero-value `AWGVersion`).
- Empty `HeaderProtectionKey` → no key line. This is how `header_protection: false` appears in the output.
- A zero (`{0,0}`) range → that range key is omitted and the engine keeps its default.
- `Version < AWG31` → neither `RandomTrailers` nor `DisableCookies`; at 3.1 both are always emitted, `on` or `off`.

Emission order is fixed, and the block is written immediately after `H4`:

```text
HeaderProtectionKey        (only when non-empty)
ContentPaddingAddition     (skipped when zero)
RekeyAfterTime             (skipped when zero)
RekeyTimeout               (skipped when zero)
RejectAfterTime            (skipped when zero)
KeepaliveTimeout           (skipped when zero)
MaxHandshakeAttempts       (skipped when zero)
RandomTrailers             (3.1 only, on/off)
DisableCookies             (3.1 only, on/off)
```

In the **server** config the block is followed by the `#_` metadata comments (`#_ClientToClient`, `#_TunName`, ...). In a **client** config it is followed by the non-empty `I1`–`I5` lines, then a blank line and `[Peer]`. The full key order is documented in [Generated Output Format](/output-format).

A real server `[Interface]` tail from a live 3.1 run (keys elided):

```ini
Jc = 8
Jmin = 660
Jmax = 700
S1 = 31
S2 = 31
S3 = 31
S4 = 31
H1 = 1-1
H2 = 2-2
H3 = 3-3
H4 = 4-4
HeaderProtectionKey = /sdO3NVhpoC3drfkR/sz8xAG1lO9U10RwBHet0vPpDU=
ContentPaddingAddition = 2-10
RekeyAfterTime = 120-180
RekeyTimeout = 5-8
RejectAfterTime = 180-240
KeepaliveTimeout = 8-12
MaxHandshakeAttempts = 16-20
RandomTrailers = on
DisableCookies = on
#_ClientToClient = false
#_TunName = awg0
```

The client config repeats the same nine lines with the identical key, between `H4` and `I1` (`I1` shown; `I2`–`I4` follow for the default `quic` template):

```ini
H4 = 4-4
HeaderProtectionKey = /sdO3NVhpoC3drfkR/sz8xAG1lO9U10RwBHet0vPpDU=
ContentPaddingAddition = 2-10
RekeyAfterTime = 120-180
RekeyTimeout = 5-8
RejectAfterTime = 180-240
KeepaliveTimeout = 8-12
MaxHandshakeAttempts = 16-20
RandomTrailers = on
DisableCookies = on
I1 = <b 0xc0ff><b 0x00000001><b 0x08><r 8><b 0x00><b 0x00><b 0x0040><b 0x00><b 0x01><t><r 40>
```

## Engine Semantics

**Header cipher.** Header protection encrypts the 4-byte WireGuard message header at offset `S{n}` with ChaCha20; the nonce is the first 12 bytes of the packet (the start of the S-prefix), which is why `S >= 12` is a hard engine requirement and not a style preference. The key is 32 bytes shared by both ends.

**Key mismatch means no tunnel.** Two peers with different `HeaderProtectionKey` values never complete a handshake. The container e2e test replaces one client's key with a different valid 44-char key and attempts pings for 10 seconds: both `latest-handshakes` timestamps stay `0`, while an untouched control pair handshakes and pings in both directions.

**The header really is ciphertext.** For a handshake initiation the UDP payload is exactly `148 + S1` bytes; with header protection the little-endian `uint32` at offset `S1` is outside `1..4`, while with `header_protection: false` it lies inside the configured `H1` range.

**Header ranges.** The engine validates the four ranges itself:

- With a header-protection key, type-ids `1..4` are legal because they are encrypted — hence the `1-1`, `2-2`, `3-3`, `4-4` recommendation.
- Overlapping ranges are rejected by `awg setconf` with `headers must not overlap` in the daemon log; Amnezigo's validator does not check overlap at all.

**Random trailers.** A receiver with trailers enabled classifies packets by size and only accepts sizes above the expected base size. Equal `S` values keep the four padded handshake sizes unambiguous; unequal `S` values can misclassify padded handshake packets, which is what `TRL001` warns about.

**Timer ranges** are handed to the engine verbatim (the runtime dump uses the same `N`/`N-M` notation), and an explicit `rekey_after_time: {"min": 5, "max": 6}` really does force a rehandshake within seconds.

**Disable cookies** turns off the 3.1 cookie replies.

**Cross-version behaviour.** A 3.1 engine applies a 2.0 config unchanged: the runtime dump reports `header_protection_key` = `(none)` and both booleans `off`, and the tunnel comes up. The reverse does not hold: a pre-3.x engine (or a kernel implementation without the transport layer) refuses the unknown keys with `Line unrecognized`, so keep the runtime aligned. The Docker image and the e2e suite pin the same 3.1 engine (see below and [Installation](/installation)).

## Validation Findings

`validate` and `generate` share these codes. Conditions and exact messages:

| Code | Severity | Condition | Message |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `HPK001` | error | `HeaderProtectionKey` present and any of `S1`–`S4` < 12 | `header protection requires S1-S4 >= 12 (got S1=%d, S2=%d, S3=%d, S4=%d)` |
| `HPK003` | error | `HeaderProtectionKey` present but not base64 of exactly 32 bytes (library-built configs; the parser rejects malformed values at load) | `HeaderProtectionKey is not 44-char base64 of 32 bytes` |
| `TRL001` | warning | `RandomTrailers` is on and `S1..S4` are not all equal | `RandomTrailers is enabled while S1..S4 differ; the AWG 3.1 reference recommends equal S values to avoid packet-type misclassification` |
| `TRM001` | error | one of the six ranges has `Max < Min`, or exactly one bound is zero | `invalid <Key> range: max (%d) is below min (%d)` or `invalid <Key> range: bounds must both be zero or both non-zero (got %d-%d)` |

`TRM001` iterates `ContentPaddingAddition`, `RekeyAfterTime`, `RekeyTimeout`, `RejectAfterTime`, `KeepaliveTimeout`, `MaxHandshakeAttempts` and reports at most one structural problem per range; a disabled `{0,0}` range never produces a finding. Only the mixed-zero-bounds branch is reachable from the CLI — the parser pre-empts `Max < Min` with `PSE001` (`invalid RekeyAfterTime "10-5": max (5) is below min (10)`), so that branch surfaces when the validator is called on an already-parsed library config.

Two related codes change behaviour under header protection:

- `HDR001` (WG type-ids in an `H` range, `header range [%d-%d] contains forbidden WG type-id(s) in [1..4]`) is **suppressed** when `HeaderProtectionKey != ""` and `Max >= Min`, because `1..4` is the intended configuration. `HDR002` (`invalid header range: Max (%d) < Min (%d)`) still fires. Structurally, the parser accepts an `H` range containing `1..4` only when the file also carries a header-protection key — a key-less config with `H1 = 1-1` fails to parse as `PSE001`, regardless of line order.
- `RISK007` (`<Hn> range width is <n> (< 1M) — narrow header range reduces entropy`) is skipped entirely when a header-protection key is present, so `H1..H4 = 1-1..4-4` no longer looks like a defect. The size-based heuristics (`RISK001`, `RISK003`–`RISK006`, `RISK008`, `RISK009`) keep applying — for example `RISK003` still warns when `S4 < 8` in a header-protection-off config.

`generate` re-parses the bytes it is about to write and appends `ValidateServerConfig` findings, so 3.x recommendations reach the CLI as `Warnings: <n>` plus one line per finding:

```shell
amnezigo generate --project ./myproject
```

```text
Generated 2 config(s):
  server/awg0.conf (743 bytes)
  phone/awg0.conf (1027 bytes)

Warnings: 1
[WARNING TRL001]  (key=RandomTrailers): RandomTrailers is enabled while S1..S4 differ; the AWG 3.1 reference recommends equal S values to avoid packet-type misclassification
```

An existing config with several problems, checked with `validate`:

```shell
amnezigo validate server/awg0.conf
```

```text
[ERROR HPK001] server/awg0.conf (key=HeaderProtectionKey): header protection requires S1-S4 >= 12 (got S1=8, S2=25, S3=25, S4=25)
  Header protection encrypts the 4-byte message header at offset S{n}; the ChaCha20 nonce is the first 12 bytes of the packet.
[WARNING TRL001] server/awg0.conf (key=RandomTrailers): RandomTrailers is enabled while S1..S4 differ; the AWG 3.1 reference recommends equal S values to avoid packet-type misclassification
  The receiver classifies packets by size and only accepts size > expected when trailers are enabled, so unequal S values can misclassify padded handshake packets.
✗ server/awg0.conf: 1 errors, 1 warnings, 0 info
```

`validate` exits 1 when at least one error is present; warnings alone exit 0 unless `--strict` is set. Findings printed by `generate` describe the **server** config only. Running `validate` on a client config does surface its 3.x findings, but the file is still parsed as a server config, so expect `FLD001` (missing `ListenPort`) plus `KEY001` noise for `I1`–`I5`, `Endpoint`, and `PersistentKeepalive` alongside them. All findings and RISK codes are listed in [Validation & Analysis](/validation).

## Worked Example: 3.1 Defaults to 2.0 Pinned

A minimal manifest that accepts every 3.1 default:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "network": { "mtu": 1280 },
  "obfuscation": { "awg_version": "3.1" },
  "peers": {
    "server": { "address": "10.0.0.1/24", "endpoint": "vpn.example.com:51820", "listen_port": 51820 },
    "phone": { "address": "10.0.0.2/32" }
  }
}
```

::: warning Set `network.mtu` explicitly
If `network.mtu` is omitted, the emitted client config still says `MTU = 1280`, but its `I1`–`I5` collapse to the bare 4-byte `<t>` template, because the pipeline resolves the I-packets before applying the MTU default. See [Gotchas](/gotchas).
:::

Resolution result:

| Parameter | Resolved value |
| --- | --- |
| `awg_version` | `3.1` |
| Header protection | on; key generated (44-char base64) |
| `S1`–`S4` | one uniform draw in `[12, 33)` (this run: `31, 31, 31, 31`) |
| `H1`–`H4` | `1-1`, `2-2`, `3-3`, `4-4` |
| `ContentPaddingAddition` | `2-10` |
| `RekeyAfterTime` | `120-180` |
| `RekeyTimeout` | `5-8` |
| `RejectAfterTime` | `180-240` |
| `KeepaliveTimeout` | `8-12` |
| `MaxHandshakeAttempts` | `16-20` |
| `RandomTrailers` | `on` |
| `DisableCookies` | `on` |

The emitted `output/server/awg0.conf` (private keys elided):

```ini
[Interface]
PrivateKey = <44-char base64>
PublicKey = <44-char base64>
Address = 10.0.0.1/24
ListenPort = 51820
MTU = 1280
Jc = 8
Jmin = 660
Jmax = 700
S1 = 31
S2 = 31
S3 = 31
S4 = 31
H1 = 1-1
H2 = 2-2
H3 = 3-3
H4 = 4-4
HeaderProtectionKey = /sdO3NVhpoC3drfkR/sz8xAG1lO9U10RwBHet0vPpDU=
ContentPaddingAddition = 2-10
RekeyAfterTime = 120-180
RekeyTimeout = 5-8
RejectAfterTime = 180-240
KeepaliveTimeout = 8-12
MaxHandshakeAttempts = 16-20
RandomTrailers = on
DisableCookies = on
#_ClientToClient = false
#_TunName = awg0

[Peer]
#_Name = phone
PublicKey = <44-char base64>
PresharedKey = <44-char base64>
AllowedIPs = 10.0.0.2/32
```

Pinning the same manifest to `"obfuscation": { "awg_version": "2.0" }` removes all nine keys from both configs and returns `S`/`H` to free-form generation (`S < 12` is legal again):

```ini
S1 = 16
S2 = 13
S3 = 12
S4 = 3
H1 = 585749746-605219821
H2 = 978962065-1014433891
H3 = 1487655573-1946222480
H4 = 2041548459-2117327241
#_ClientToClient = false
```

Under `"awg_version": "3.0"` you get the key plus the six ranges, but neither `RandomTrailers` nor `DisableCookies`, and the S draws are independent (`36, 33, 47, 12` in a live run), because the uniform path is only active under trailers. Under `"3.1"` with `header_protection: false` only the key line is lost: the six ranges and both 3.1 booleans are still emitted, the `H` ranges switch to generated wide ranges, and because `minS` is `0` the uniform draw can go below 12.

### Verifying on a live node

After applying a config to a node running a 3.x engine, `awg show <if> dump` prints one tab-separated interface record whose fields are positional. In order they are `private_key`, `public_key`, `listen_port`, `jc`, `jmin`, `jmax`, `s1`–`s4`, `h1`–`h4`, `i1`–`i5`, then the nine 3.x values as 1-based fields **20–28** — `header_protection_key` (20), `content_padding_addition` (21), `rekey_after_time` (22), `rekey_timeout` (23), `reject_after_time` (24), `keepalive_timeout` (25), `max_handshake_attempts` (26), `random_trailers` (27), `disable_cookies` (28) — followed by `fwmark` (29). The positions are contract, not convenience: the e2e harness maps them by name (`dumpFieldNames` in `e2e/harness_test.go`) and its assertions fail if upstream reorders the record. To print just the nine values:

```shell
awg show awg0 dump | awk -F'\t' '{print $20, $21, $22, $23, $24, $25, $26, $27, $28}'
```

`awg show all dump` prefixes the interface name, shifting every position by one. A 2.0 config applied to a 3.1 engine reports `header_protection_key` = `(none)` and both booleans `off`.

## Ecosystem Integration

### vpn:// import links

With `--vpn-links`, the `last_config` object of each `vpn://` link carries the nine 3.x values as separate string fields whose JSON names equal the INI key names: `HeaderProtectionKey`, `ContentPaddingAddition`, `RekeyAfterTime`, `RekeyTimeout`, `RejectAfterTime`, `KeepaliveTimeout`, `MaxHandshakeAttempts`, `RandomTrailers`, `DisableCookies`. The values are copied verbatim from the client INI and omitted for pre-3.x configs; they live inside the obfuscation-enabled branch, which requires `Jc` to be present. See [VPN Import Links](/vpn-links).

### Presets

Preset data is 3.1 by construction: `Preset.ToServerObfuscation()` sets `Version: AWG31` and copies `ContentPadding`, `RandomTrailers`, and `DisableCookies`, leaving `HeaderProtectionKey` for the pipeline to fill. Because four presets pin unequal `S` values with trailers on (home-balanced `30/35/20/12`, mobile-aggressive `60/60/50/24`, stealth-paranoid `30/24/20/32`, standard-1420 `32/28/20/16`), `generate` prints a `TRL001` warning for them. See [Built-in Presets](/presets).

### Container e2e proof

The `e2e` suite drives the real engine through Docker, pinned to amneziawg-go `v3.1.20260828` and amneziawg-tools `v3.1.20260812`:

```shell
go test -tags=e2e ./e2e/...
```

The suite needs a reachable Docker daemon and a working `/dev/net/tun` inside containers; it builds the CLI and a local `amnezigo-e2e-awg:31` image once, skips when Docker or TUN is unavailable, and fails when the CLI or image build breaks. Against the real engine it proves the 3.1 defaults end to end (with a byte-identical `HeaderProtectionKey` on both ends), that a mismatched key never handshakes, that the wire header is ciphertext, that a 2.0 config still tunnels on the 3.1 engine, that an explicit rekey range forces a rehandshake, and that overlapping `H` ranges are rejected by `awg setconf`.

### Runtime alignment

The generated 3.x keys are engine features, so the runtime must be 3.x. The shipped Docker image is pinned to `amneziavpn/amneziawg-go:3.1.20260828`; an older runtime (or a kernel implementation without the transport layer) cannot load the keys. The release artifacts and the image are amd64-only. See [Installation](/installation) for the image and release matrix.
---
url: /presets
---
# Built-in Presets

Amnezigo ships seven **named bundles of obfuscation parameters** in `presets.go`, each tuned for a network environment: `lan-conservative`, `home-balanced`, `mobile-aggressive`, `stealth-paranoid`, `standard-1420`, `low-overhead` and `test-minimal` — `ListPresets()` returns them in exactly that order. A preset is plain data: a `Preset` value holding `S1`–`S4`, `H1`–`H4`, `Jc`/`Jmin`/`Jmax`, the three AWG 3.1 knobs (`ContentPadding`, `RandomTrailers`, `DisableCookies`), an `MTU` and a suggested cover protocol. `generate` never resolves a preset by name.

Every preset is structurally valid by construction:

- Its `S1`–`S4` produce four pairwise-distinct AWG-padded handshake sizes (`S1+148`, `S2+92`, `S3+64`, `S4+32`).
- Its junk range `[Jmin..Jmax]` excludes all padded sizes and all raw WireGuard sizes (148/92/64/32).
- Its `H1`–`H4` ranges are non-overlapping, ascending, and above the WireGuard type-id window `[1..4]`.
- Its `S1`–`S4` all stay at or above the 12 B header-protection floor.

"Valid by construction" is not "warning-free": four presets deliberately emit a `TRL001` warning on every `generate`, and `analyze` can still report heuristic findings (see the AWG 3.1 Behaviour and Analyze Findings Per Preset sections below).

::: danger Presets are DATA — there is NO `preset` manifest field
There is no `preset` key in the manifest schema and no `--preset` flag on any command. The removed imperative CLI (`init`/`add`/`edit`/`remove`/`export`/`list`) and the `Manager` API no longer exist — any documentation mentioning them is stale. The CLI has exactly four commands today: `generate`, `validate`, `analyze` and `version`. `GetPreset`/`ListPresets` are library-only helpers with no non-test callers, and the manifest schema carries resolved parameters only: presets are resolved at the Jsonnet level before JSON is produced. To use a preset, **copy its values into `obfuscation.*`** — including the three 3.1 knobs `content_padding`, `random_trailers` and `disable_cookies` — and its `MTU` into `network.mtu` (or emit them from a Jsonnet lib you write — amnezigo ships none). See [Jsonnet](/jsonnet) and [Manifest Reference](/manifest-reference).
:::

## Preset Table

Six presets use **MTU 1280** (IPv6-safe, avoids fragmentation); `standard-1420` uses **1420** for more I-packet headroom. `H1`–`H4` are shown as `min–max`; `ContentPadding` is a `U16Range` written as `{min, max}` in the manifest, and `{0, 0}` **disables** the engine key (`ContentPaddingAddition` is omitted from the config).

| Name | MTU | S1 | S2 | S3 | S4 | H1 | H2 | H3 | H4 | Jc | Jmin | Jmax | DefaultProtocol | ContentPadding | RandomTrailers | DisableCookies | When to use |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `lan-conservative` | 1280 | 12 | 12 | 15 | 12 | 10–1000000 | 2000000–100000000 | 200000000–500000000 | 700000000–2000000000 | 3 | 161 | 240 | `random` | `{0, 0}` (off) | false | true | Corporate LANs with minimal DPI; low overhead preferred over deep obfuscation. |
| `home-balanced` | 1280 | 30 | 35 | 20 | 12 | 100–5000000 | 10000000–200000000 | 400000000–800000000 | 1000000000–2100000000 | 5 | 250 | 750 | `quic` | `{2, 10}` | true | true | Good default for home internet where some DPI may exist but is not aggressive. |
| `mobile-aggressive` | 1280 | 60 | 60 | 50 | 24 | 50–10000000 | 50000000–500000000 | 700000000–1200000000 | 1500000000–2147000000 | 8 | 500 | 1000 | `dns` | `{2, 10}` | true | true | Carrier networks with heavy DPI inspection (MTS, Beeline, etc.). Maximum entropy. |
| `stealth-paranoid` | 1280 | 30 | 24 | 20 | 32 | 50–50000000 | 100000000–600000000 | 700000000–1300000000 | 1500000000–2147000000 | 10 | 300 | 1100 | `quic` | `{4, 12}` | true | true | Hostile DPI / national firewalls. Large `S4` pads every transport packet; wide junk, wide headers. Highest per-packet cost (~2.5%). |
| `standard-1420` | 1420 | 32 | 28 | 20 | 16 | 100–5000000 | 10000000–200000000 | 400000000–800000000 | 1000000000–2100000000 | 5 | 250 | 800 | `quic` | `{2, 8}` | true | true | Balanced profile at the classic WG MTU 1420 — more I-packet headroom (`maxISize` 1190). Requires an IPv4 outer transport or a jumbo-frame link: `S4`+`MTU` exceeds the IPv6 Ethernet budget by 16 B. |
| `low-overhead` | 1280 | 12 | 12 | 12 | 12 | 50–50000000 | 100000000–400000000 | 500000000–900000000 | 1100000000–2100000000 | 2 | 180 | 320 | `dns` | `{2, 4}` | false | true | Bandwidth-constrained links (satellite, metered). `S` values at the 12 B header-protection floor; minimal junk. Trades masking for throughput. |
| `test-minimal` | 1280 | 12 | 13 | 12 | 12 | 5–10000 | 20000–50000 | 100000–500000 | 1000000–5000000 | 1 | 200 | 250 | `random` | `{0, 0}` (off) | false | false | Smallest valid parameter set — integration testing and CI **only**. NOT for production. |

::: warning DefaultProtocol is metadata only
`Preset.DefaultProtocol` is informational. `generate` does not read it — it uses each peer's `peers.<name>.protocol`, which defaults to `quic` when empty. The `obfuscation.protocol` manifest field is a separate trap: it exists in the schema but is never read by the pipeline either. To actually select a cover template, set `peers.<name>.protocol`; valid names are `quic`, `dns`, `dtls`, `stun`, `sip`, `rtp` and `random`.
:::

## AWG 3.1 Behaviour

All seven presets are AWG 3.1 data by construction: `Preset` has **no `Version` field**, and `ToServerObfuscation()` hardcodes `Version: AWG31`. Copying a preset into a manifest that leaves `obfuscation.awg_version` unset (the default `"3.1"`) yields the full 3.x device layer: header protection on with a generated key, `ContentPaddingAddition`, the five timer ranges, `RandomTrailers` and `DisableCookies`. See [Transport Protection](/transport-protection) for the layer itself and [Obfuscation](/obfuscation) for the S/H/J semantics.

- **S-prefix floor**: every preset keeps `S1`–`S4` >= 12, so none of them can trip the header-protection floor — neither the pipeline abort (`header protection requires S1-S4 >= 12`) nor the `HPK001` finding.
- **`TRL001` is expected for four presets**: `home-balanced` (30/35/20/12), `mobile-aggressive` (60/60/50/24), `stealth-paranoid` (30/24/20/32) and `standard-1420` (32/28/20/16) pin deliberately unequal `S` values while `RandomTrailers` is enabled. Every `generate` prints `Warnings: 1` with `TRL001` (`RandomTrailers is enabled while S1..S4 differ; the AWG 3.1 reference recommends equal S values to avoid packet-type misclassification`) — the configs are still written and this is not a preset defect. To silence it, set `"random_trailers": false` or equalize the `S` values.
- **The uniform-S shortcut never runs for a copied preset**: `GenerateUniformSPrefixes` is chosen only when `random_trailers` is on *and* all four `S` manifest fields are nil. Presets pin all four, so each `S` is used verbatim and `TRL001` follows whenever the values differ.
- **`low-overhead` is the only preset with uniform `S` values** (12/12/12/12) and, together with `lan-conservative` and `test-minimal`, has trailers off — those three emit no `TRL001`. `low-overhead` is also the only preset with all four `S` at the 12 B floor.
- **`test-minimal` is the only preset with `DisableCookies: false`** — copying it into a production manifest silently leaves cookie replies enabled. It is explicitly not intended for production.
- **Content padding is disabled in `lan-conservative` and `test-minimal`** (`{0, 0}`): the `ContentPaddingAddition` key is omitted from their configs. A 3.1 preset does not have to enable every knob.
- **No preset overrides the five timer ranges.** `rekey_after_time`, `rekey_timeout`, `reject_after_time`, `keepalive_timeout` and `max_handshake_attempts` are not part of the `Preset` struct, so a copied preset always runs on the version defaults (`{120,180}`, `{5,8}`, `{180,240}`, `{8,12}`, `{16,20}`).

## Analyze Findings Per Preset

`generate` and `validate` run the structural checks; `analyze` runs heuristics (`RISK001`–`RISK009`) and can still report findings for a preset. Measured over the preset values analyzed as a config with no header-protection key and no peers:

| Preset | `analyze` findings | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| `lan-conservative` | `RISK007` (warning) | `H1` width 999,991 < 1,000,000 (`10–1000000`). |
| `home-balanced` | none | — |
| `mobile-aggressive` | `RISK005` (info) | Padded Response 152 is within 4 B of the raw WireGuard initiation size 148 (the raw response size is 92); `checkRISK005` compares every padded size against every raw WG size, so this is a cross-class near-collision. |
| `stealth-paranoid` | none | Padded Transport 64 equals the raw cookie-reply size 64; `RISK005` requires a strictly non-zero difference, so this exact collision is silently not flagged. |
| `standard-1420` | none | — |
| `low-overhead` | none | — |
| `test-minimal` | `RISK007` x3 (warning) | `H1` width 9,996, `H2` width 30,001, `H3` width 400,001 — all below 1,000,000. |

Three caveats when reading this table:

- `RISK007` is skipped entirely when the analyzed config carries a `HeaderProtectionKey`. Any config generated from a default 3.1 manifest has one, so `lan-conservative` and `test-minimal` do **not** report the H-width warnings there; `mobile-aggressive`'s `RISK005` appears in both cases.
- The measurement config had no peers, which adds the `RISK008` info (`no peers defined — I-packet analysis skipped`); that is an artifact of the measurement, not a preset result.
- `analyze` regenerates I-packet sizes on every run, so I-packet-based heuristics (`RISK002`) vary with the peer's protocol template; the table lists the checks derived from each preset's own parameters. See [Validation](/validation) for both finding families.

## Padded Handshake Sizes

For reference, the AWG-padded handshake sizes each preset produces (`S1+148`, `S2+92`, `S3+64`, `S4+32`) — all pairwise distinct within each preset:

| Preset | S1+148 | S2+92 | S3+64 | S4+32 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `lan-conservative` | 160 | 104 | 79 | 44 |
| `home-balanced` | 178 | 127 | 84 | 44 |
| `mobile-aggressive` | 208 | 152 | 114 | 56 |
| `stealth-paranoid` | 178 | 116 | 84 | 64 |
| `standard-1420` | 180 | 120 | 84 | 48 |
| `low-overhead` | 160 | 104 | 76 | 44 |
| `test-minimal` | 160 | 105 | 76 | 44 |

## Quick Pick

| Your situation | Preset |
|---|---|
| Just want it to work — home broadband, light DPI | `home-balanced` |
| On mobile carrier with active DPI (MTS, Beeline, Megafon) | `mobile-aggressive` |
| Behind a national firewall / hostile censor (GFW, Iran) | `stealth-paranoid` |
| Corporate LAN, barely any DPI, want low overhead | `lan-conservative` |
| Link allows MTU 1420 (IPv4 outer) and you want richer cover packets | `standard-1420` |
| Satellite / metered / very slow — every byte counts | `low-overhead` |
| Writing a test or CI pipeline | `test-minimal` |

When in doubt, start with `home-balanced`, run `amnezigo analyze` on the generated config, and escalate to `mobile-aggressive` or `stealth-paranoid` only if RISK findings or real-world blocking warrant it.

## How To Use A Preset

Presets are resolved at the **authoring level** — you copy the preset's values into `obfuscation.*` (and `network.mtu`) in `amnezigo.json`, or expose them through a `.amnezigo.jsonnet` lib. The manifest never carries a preset name.

Manifest mapping, using `home-balanced`:

> `network.mtu`: int — from `Preset.MTU` (1280 for six presets, 1420 for `standard-1420`).
> `obfuscation.s1`, `s2`, `s3`, `s4`: int (nullable) — from `Preset.S1`–`S4`.
> `obfuscation.h1`–`h4`: `{min, max}` objects — from `Preset.H1`–`H4`.
> `obfuscation.jc`, `jmin`, `jmax`: int (nullable) — from `Preset.Jc`/`Jmin`/`Jmax`.
> `obfuscation.content_padding`: `{min, max}` (`uint16`, nullable) — from `Preset.ContentPadding`; write `{"min": 0, "max": 0}` to disable the key.
> `obfuscation.random_trailers`, `obfuscation.disable_cookies`: bool (nullable) — from `Preset.RandomTrailers`/`Preset.DisableCookies`.
> `obfuscation.awg_version`: string — optional; defaults to `"3.1"`, the generation all presets target.
> `peers.<name>.protocol`: string — from `Preset.DefaultProtocol`; optional (empty defaults to `quic`).

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "network": { "mtu": 1280 },
  "obfuscation": {
    "awg_version": "3.1",
    "s1": 30,
    "s2": 35,
    "s3": 20,
    "s4": 12,
    "h1": { "min": 100,        "max": 5000000 },
    "h2": { "min": 10000000,   "max": 200000000 },
    "h3": { "min": 400000000,  "max": 800000000 },
    "h4": { "min": 1000000000, "max": 2100000000 },
    "jc": 5,
    "jmin": 250,
    "jmax": 750,
    "content_padding": { "min": 2, "max": 10 },
    "random_trailers": true,
    "disable_cookies": true
  },
  "peers": {
    "server": { "address": "10.0.0.1/24", "endpoint": "vpn.example.com:51820", "listen_port": 51820 },
    "laptop": { "address": "10.0.0.2/32", "protocol": "quic" }
  }
}
```

::: warning Omitting a 3.1 knob cannot reproduce these presets
The three 3.1 knobs are not neutral when omitted: an omitted `content_padding` resolves to the 3.1 default `{2, 10}`, and omitted `random_trailers`/`disable_cookies` resolve to `true`. Every preset deviation must therefore be written explicitly:

- `"random_trailers": false` for `lan-conservative`, `low-overhead` and `test-minimal`.
- `"disable_cookies": false` for `test-minimal`.
- `"content_padding": { "min": 0, "max": 0 }` for `lan-conservative` and `test-minimal` (the key is then omitted from the config), `{4, 12}` for `stealth-paranoid`, `{2, 8}` for `standard-1420`, `{2, 4}` for `low-overhead`.

Only `home-balanced` and `mobile-aggressive` happen to coincide with the 3.1 defaults on all three knobs (`{2, 10}`, `true`, `true`) — copy the whole block anyway.
:::

::: tip Setting a non-zero number pins it; omitting it does not
The S/H/J fields are nullable in the manifest. Copying a preset makes every value an explicit number, so it is used verbatim. If you instead omit (say) `s1`, `generate` fills it with a generated value; under header protection the S draws respect the 12 B floor. An explicit `"s1": 0` is **not** a fixed zero either — it is treated as missing and re-drawn. Copy the whole block.
:::

::: warning Copy the preset's MTU — do not rely on the default
`ToServerObfuscation()` does not carry `MTU`, and omitting `network.mtu` is a known defect: the client config is written with `MTU = 1280` while its `I1`–`I5` collapse to the `<t>` placeholder (the client path passes the raw, still-zero MTU to the I-packet generator before the 1280 default is applied). Set `network.mtu` explicitly — every preset value in the tables above assumes it.
:::

The same values can be exposed from a Jsonnet lib so manifests stay DRY — see the [Jsonnet](/jsonnet) page.

## Go API

The preset library is plain Go data in package `amnezigo` — the unexported `presetRegistry` slice plus two accessors and one projection method (from `presets.go`):

| Symbol | Signature | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `GetPreset` | `func GetPreset(name string) (Preset, error)` | Returns the preset with the given name. On a miss: `unknown preset %q; available presets: [...]` listing all seven names in registry order. |
| `ListPresets` | `func ListPresets() []Preset` | Returns a **copy** of the registry slice (safe to mutate). |
| `Preset.ToServerObfuscation` | `func (p Preset) ToServerObfuscation() ServerObfuscationConfig` | Projects the preset onto the generator's `ServerObfuscationConfig`: copies `Jc`/`Jmin`/`Jmax`, `S1`–`S4`, `H1`–`H4`, `ContentPadding`, `RandomTrailers`, `DisableCookies`, and hardcodes `Version: AWG31`. |

```go
type Preset struct {
    Name            string
    Description     string
    DefaultProtocol string
    H1, H2, H3, H4  HeaderRange
    MTU             int
    S1, S2, S3, S4  int
    Jc, Jmin, Jmax  int

    ContentPadding U16Range // AWG 3.1; {0,0} disables the key
    RandomTrailers bool     // AWG 3.1
    DisableCookies bool     // AWG 3.1
}
```

There is **no `Version` field** on `Preset` — the AWG target lives only in `ToServerObfuscation()`, which hardcodes `AWG31`.

```go
import "github.com/Arsolitt/amnezigo"

for _, p := range amnezigo.ListPresets() {
    fmt.Println(p.Name, p.MTU)
}

home, err := amnezigo.GetPreset("home-balanced")
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
// ToServerObfuscation projects Jc/Jmin/Jmax, S1-S4, H1-H4 and the three
// 3.1 knobs into the config the generator consumes, with Version AWG31.
cfg := home.ToServerObfuscation()
```

::: tip What `ToServerObfuscation()` does and does not carry
It copies `Jc`/`Jmin`/`Jmax`, `S1`–`S4`, `H1`–`H4`, `ContentPadding`, `RandomTrailers` and `DisableCookies`, and sets `Version: AWG31`. It intentionally leaves `HeaderProtectionKey` empty because the `generate` pipeline supplies and persists that key separately; a library caller building a `ServerConfig` by hand must set a key itself to get header protection. It also does not carry `MTU`, `Name`, `Description` or `DefaultProtocol` (wire `MTU` into `network.mtu` yourself), and it never sets the five timer ranges.
:::
---
url: /validation
---
# Validation & Analysis

Amnezigo ships two diagnostic commands that operate on an **already-generated server config** (`awg0.conf`):

- **`amnezigo validate`** — enforces the S-prefix, junk-range, header-range and AWG 3.x transport-protection invariants. Findings are classified `error` / `warning` / `info` and drive the exit code.
- **`amnezigo analyze`** — runs heuristic *weakness* checks and profiles handshake/junk/header/I-packet parameters. Purely advisory; always exits `0`.

Both read an AmneziaWG server INI file — they do **not** consume a manifest. To check a manifest, run [`amnezigo generate`](/quick-start) first (or with `--dry-run`) and validate the produced `awg0.conf`. The rules themselves live in exported library functions (`ValidatePacketSizes`, `ValidateHeaderRange`, `ValidateServerConfig`), documented on [Library API](/library-api); the CLI is a thin wrapper that adds parse-warning findings and an exit code.

::: tip
`validate`'s text output and `generate`'s warning list share one line convention: `[<SEVERITY> <CODE>] <file>:<line> (key=<key>): <message>`, with empty file/line/key segments omitted — a key-only finding therefore shows a double space after the closing bracket. `analyze` does **not** use it: its findings are embedded in the report as `  [<severity>] <CODE>: <message>` (lowercase severity, no location), e.g. `  [info] RISK005: padded Cookie (94) is within ±4 B of raw WG size 92 — may confuse naive DPI`.
:::

## amnezigo validate

```shell
amnezigo validate <config> [--output text|json] [--strict] [--quiet]
```

`validate` takes exactly one positional argument — the path to a server config file — and runs the full rule set: required fields, S-prefix collisions, junk-range sanity, header ranges, header protection, random trailers, and the six AWG 3.x transport ranges. It parses with strict mode **unconditionally**, so unknown keys and raw `<c>` tags always surface as findings.

### Flags

| Flag | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--output` | `text` | no | Output format: `text` or `json`. Anything else returns `unknown --output format "<value>" (want: text|json)`. |
| `--strict` | `false` | no | Treat warnings as errors for the exit code. |
| `--quiet` | `false` | no | Suppress the summary line; print findings only. |

::: tip
`--output` here is an output **format**; `generate --output <dir>` is an output **directory**. Do not share one variable between the commands.
:::

::: warning Validate is built for server configs
Strict parsing runs regardless of `--strict`, so client-only keys (`I1`–`I5`, `Endpoint`, `PersistentKeepalive`, …) each become a `KEY001` warning. `--strict` only controls whether those warnings fail the exit code.
:::

### What validate checks

`ValidateServerConfig` runs its rule groups in a fixed order: required fields (`FLD001`), S-prefixes (`PSC001`/`PSC002`/`PSC003`), junk range (`JNK001`), header ranges (`HDR001`/`HDR002`), header protection (`HPK001`/`HPK003`), random trailers (`TRL001`), transport ranges (`TRM001`). Immediately before that, strict-mode parse warnings (`CPS001`, `KEY001`) are converted into `warning` findings. A structural parse error produces a single `PSE001` error instead of the rule results.

| Code | Severity | Trigger |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `FLD001` | error | A required server field is missing: `PrivateKey`, `Address`, or `ListenPort` (one finding per missing field, `key=` set to the field name). Message `required field "<name>" is missing`; detail `server configs require PrivateKey, Address, and ListenPort to function.` |
| `PSC001` | error | **S-pair collision** — two of the four S-padded handshake sizes are equal (`S1+148`, `S2+92`, `S3+64`, `S4+32`). Message `packet size collision (s-pair): S1+148 vs S2+92 at 148 bytes`. |
| `PSC002` | error | **Junk-range collision** — `[Jmin..Jmax]` contains one of the four padded sizes **or** one of the four raw WireGuard sizes (`148`, `92`, `64`, `32`). Message `packet size collision (junk-range): [Jmin..Jmax] contains 148 at 148 bytes`. |
| `PSC003` | error | **I-packet collision** — an I-packet length equals one of the four padded sizes. Not reachable from `ValidateServerConfig`; see the scope note below. |
| `PSC000` | error | Fallback for a `ValidatePacketSizes` error that is neither a `*PacketSizeCollisionError` nor `ErrEmptyJunkRange`. An unrecognised `PacketSizeCollisionError.Kind` does not produce `PSC000` — the code map lookup yields an empty `code` string. Reserved; no current code path produces it. |
| `JNK001` | error | Junk range is empty: `Jmin > Jmax`. Message `junk range Jmin (<Jmin>) > Jmax (<Jmax>)`. A single inverted range is reported **twice**, because both the S-prefix rule group (via the empty-range sentinel) and the junk-range rule group fire. |
| `HDR001` | error | An `H1`–`H4` range intersects a standard WireGuard message type-id (`1..4`), which would let vanilla WireGuard packets be accepted. Message `header range [<min>-<max>] contains forbidden WG type-id(s) in [1..4]`. **Suppressed** when `HeaderProtectionKey` is set **and** `Max >= Min`: under AWG 3.x header protection `H1..H4 = 1-1/2-2/3-3/4-4` is the legitimate reference configuration. |
| `HDR002` | error | An `H1`–`H4` range is structurally inverted: `Max < Min`. Message `invalid header range: Max (<max>) < Min (<min>)`. Fires even when header protection is active. |
| `HPK001` | error | `HeaderProtectionKey` is set and any of `S1`–`S4` is below `12` (`headerProtectionNonceSize`). Message `header protection requires S1-S4 >= 12 (got S1=<n>, S2=<n>, S3=<n>, S4=<n>)`, `key=HeaderProtectionKey`. The detail explains that header protection encrypts the 4-byte header at offset `S{n}` and the ChaCha20 nonce is the first 12 bytes of the packet — hence the floor. |
| `HPK003` | error | `HeaderProtectionKey` is non-empty but is not base64 `StdEncoding` of exactly 32 bytes. Message `HeaderProtectionKey is not 44-char base64 of 32 bytes`. |
| `TRL001` | warning | `RandomTrailers` is enabled while `S1`–`S4` are not all equal. Message `RandomTrailers is enabled while S1..S4 differ; the AWG 3.1 reference recommends equal S values to avoid packet-type misclassification`, `key=RandomTrailers`. Four shipped presets trigger this deliberately — see [Presets](/presets). Silencing it requires `random_trailers: false` or equal S values. |
| `TRM001` | error | One of the six AWG 3.x `uint16` ranges (`ContentPaddingAddition`, `RekeyAfterTime`, `RekeyTimeout`, `RejectAfterTime`, `KeepaliveTimeout`, `MaxHandshakeAttempts`) has `Max < Min` — message `invalid <key> range: max (<max>) is below min (<min>)` — or exactly one zero bound — message `invalid <key> range: bounds must both be zero or both non-zero (got <min>-<max>)`. `{0,0}` (the key is disabled) is valid and silent, and only the first structural problem per range is reported. |
| `KEY001` | warning | Unknown INI key encountered during strict parse: `unknown INI key "<key>" in <section> section`. |
| `CPS001` | warning | A raw `<c>` tag literal is present in the config: `raw <c> tag detected; rejected by amneziawg-go and AmneziaVPN clients`. Emitted for comment lines too. |
| `PSE001` | error | A structural parse error aborted loading (emitted instead of the rule checks above). |

WireGuard raw message sizes (before S-padding): Initiation `148`, Response `92`, Cookie Reply `64`, Transport `32`. These four constants, plus the four `S{n}`-padded totals, are the eight integers the junk range must avoid. The padded-size labels used in diagnostics are `S1+148`, `S2+92`, `S3+64`, `S4+32`.

::: warning Parse errors are not findings
Structural problems abort parsing and reach the CLI as one `PSE001` error carrying the parser's message: a malformed `HeaderProtectionKey` (`invalid HeaderProtectionKey "<v>": must be 44-char base64 of 32 bytes`), a range value that is not `N` or `N-M`, a `Max < Min` range, a boolean that is not `on`/`off`/`0`/`1`, or an H range intersecting `1..4` while no header-protection key is present. Semantic problems (`HPK001`, `TRL001`, `TRM001`, packet-size collisions) are findings on an otherwise-parsed config. Keep the two apart when documenting or scripting.
:::

::: warning Codes the CLI cannot reach
- `PSC003` is **library-only**: `validateSPrefixes` calls `ValidatePacketSizes` with a nil I-packet list, so `validate` can never report an I-packet collision — only a direct library call can.
- `HDR001` and `HDR002` are effectively **parse-blocked** on the CLI path, because the parser calls `ValidateHeaderRange` on all four ranges after scanning (with the same header-protection suppression for the type-id variant) and aborts first. They are reachable only when validating an already-parsed config through the library.
- `HPK003` likewise matters mainly to library-built configs; a malformed key in a file is rejected structurally first.
- `TRM001`'s `Max < Min` variant is also parse-blocked (`invalid RekeyTimeout "10-5": max (5) is below min (10)` → `PSE001`); only the mixed-zero-bound form reaches the validator.
- Overlapping H ranges are **not** a validator rule at all — the engine rejects them at `awg setconf` time (`headers must not overlap`).
:::

::: warning `{0,0}` header ranges pass validation
`ValidateHeaderRange` accepts a zero range, so `{0,0}` produces no finding — but it will trip the generator/engine. Full zero-range hardening is out of scope for the validator.
:::

### Severity and exit codes

| Condition | Exit code |
| --- | --- |
| No errors (warnings/info may still print) | `0` |
| At least one error | `1` |
| `--strict` set **and** at least one warning | `1` |

`info`-level findings **never** affect the exit code. Without `--strict`, warnings are reported but do not fail validation; with `--strict`, any warning flips the exit code to `1`. The validator itself only ever produces `error` and `warning` findings; `info` exists for the analyze heuristics. On a CLI failure (unreadable file, unknown `--output`) the command returns an error instead of exiting: Cobra prints `Error: <err>`, then the usage block, then `Execute` prints `Error: <err>` again, and the process exits with status `1`.

### Output formats

**Text** (default) — one line per finding using the canonical `OneLine` format, followed by an optional summary:

```text
[<SEVERITY> <CODE>] <file>:<line> (key=<key>): <message>
```

- `SEVERITY` is uppercased (`ERROR` / `WARNING` / `INFO`).
- The `:line` segment is omitted when the finding has no line number; the `(key=…)` segment is omitted when the finding has no key.
- If a finding carries a `Detail`, it is printed indented beneath the line.
- Unless `--quiet` is set, a trailing summary line is printed:

```text
<marker> <path>: <E> errors, <W> warnings, <I> info
```

`marker` is `✓` when there are no errors, `✗` otherwise.

Example text output for a config missing `Address`:

```text
[ERROR FLD001] awg0.conf (key=Address): required field "Address" is missing
  server configs require PrivateKey, Address, and ListenPort to function.
✗ awg0.conf: 1 errors, 0 warnings, 0 info
```

Example of a 3.x semantic finding (unequal S values with random trailers enabled):

```text
[WARNING TRL001] awg0.conf (key=RandomTrailers): RandomTrailers is enabled while S1..S4 differ; the AWG 3.1 reference recommends equal S values to avoid packet-type misclassification
```

**JSON** (`--output json`) — a single object:

```json
{
  "file": "awg0.conf",
  "findings": [
    {
      "message": "required field \"Address\" is missing",
      "detail": "server configs require PrivateKey, Address, and ListenPort to function.",
      "code": "FLD001",
      "severity": "error",
      "location": { "file": "awg0.conf", "key": "Address" }
    }
  ],
  "summary": { "errors": 1, "warnings": 0, "info": 0 }
}
```

`findings` is never `null` — a clean config yields `"findings": []`. Each finding has `message`, optional `detail`, `code`, `severity`, and an optional `location` object (`file`, `line`, `key` are each omitted when empty; the CLI stamps `file` with the argument path).

### Examples

```shell
amnezigo validate /etc/amnezia/awg0.conf
amnezigo validate awg0.conf --output json
amnezigo validate awg0.conf --strict --quiet
```

Typical workflow after generating from a manifest:

```shell
amnezigo generate
amnezigo validate output/<server-peer>/awg0.conf --strict
```

## amnezigo analyze

```shell
amnezigo analyze [--config awg0.conf] [--protocol random|quic|dns|dtls|stun|sip|rtp]
                 [--peer <name>] [--samples <n>] [--seed <n>]
                 [--output text|json]
```

`analyze` loads a server config (non-strict parsing, so a config the parser rejects aborts the command before any heuristics run) and runs the heuristic weakness checks (`RISK001`–`RISK009`), profiling the four S-padded handshake sizes, junk-packet parameters, the four header ranges, and freshly generated I-packet sizes per peer.

### Flags

| Flag | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | `awg0.conf` | no | Server config file path (CWD-relative). Must be a server config. |
| `--protocol` | `random` | no | Protocol used to generate I-packets for analysis: `random`, `quic`, `dns`, `dtls`, `stun`, `sip`, `rtp`. An unknown value is **not** rejected — it silently falls through to a random named template. |
| `--peer` | _(empty)_ | no | Analyze only this peer (empty = all peers). |
| `--samples` | `0` | no | Number of I-packet generations for distribution analysis. `0` = snapshot only. |
| `--seed` | `0` | no | Declared as a PRNG seed for reproducible I-packet generation — **currently inert** (see Reproducibility below). |
| `--output` | `text` | no | Output format: `text` or `json`. Anything else returns `invalid output format "<value>": must be text or json`. |

::: warning
The default `--config` is `awg0.conf` in the **current working directory**, not the generated output path. Point it at a server config explicitly, e.g. `--config output/<server-peer>/awg0.conf`.
:::

::: tip Two defaults that disagree
A peer with no `protocol` field gets QUIC I-packets during `generate` (the pipeline defaults to QUIC), while `analyze` defaults `--protocol` to `random`. Pass the protocol explicitly to compare like with like.
:::

### Snapshot vs distribution mode

I-packet sizes (`I1`–`I5`) are **freshly regenerated** from the config parameters on every run, not read from disk — the report always carries a `sample_note` saying so. This means the numbers describe what the parameters *can* produce, not the strings stored in the config file:

- `analyze` calls the same `GenerateCPS` entry point the CLI generator uses, with an empty forbidden set — it does not avoid the four padded handshake sizes, exactly as generated client configs do not (only the library `GenerateConfig` performs collision avoidance). A reported size can therefore equal a padded size without any command rejecting it.
- The reported sizes are derived from the config's `protocol`/MTU/`S1` parameters, not the `I1`–`I5` values in the file.

The two sampling modes:

- **Snapshot** (`--samples 0`, the default) — one generation per peer. Each peer reports single values for `I1`–`I5`.
- **Distribution** (`--samples N`, `N > 0`) — generates I-packets `N` times per peer and reports statistics for each of `I1`–`I5`:

> `mean`: float64 (rounded to 2 decimals) · `min`: int · `max`: int · `median`: int · `samples`: int

### Reproducibility

::: danger `--seed` is currently ineffective
The CLI builds a seeded `math/rand/v2` PCG reader and assigns it to `AnalyzeOptions.Rand`, but no code path in the package reads that field — I-packet generation goes straight to `crypto/rand`. Two runs of `amnezigo analyze --config <cfg> --output json --seed 42 --samples 5` produce different distributions despite the flag's help text promising otherwise. Treat snapshot and distribution numbers as samples that change between invocations; there is currently no way to make `analyze` output reproducible.
:::

Because the sampling is non-deterministic, `RISK002` (which measures the span of generated I-packet sizes) can appear or disappear between runs on the same config. Run `--samples` with a reasonably large `N` before drawing conclusions about cluster width, and read the closing `Note:` line as the authoritative caveat.

### Heuristic checks

All findings are advisory — `warning` or `info`, never `error` (a test asserts `Analyze` cannot emit an `error` finding). `analyze` exits `0` on success regardless of how many fire; only a config-load failure or an invalid `--output` value makes it exit non-zero. A CI gate must parse `--output json`, not the exit status.

| Code | Severity | Trigger (threshold) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `RISK001` | warning | Junk range `[Jmin..Jmax]` contains a raw WireGuard size (`148`/`92`/`64`/`32`) — junk packets may be misclassified. One finding per colliding size. |
| `RISK002` | warning | A peer's I-packet cluster span (`max(I1..I5) − min`) is `< 20` B — a narrow cluster is easier to fingerprint. Computed from the freshly generated snapshot, so it varies between runs. |
| `RISK003` | warning | `S4 < 8` — small transport padding makes keepalive packets distinguishable. |
| `RISK004` | warning | Two padded handshake sizes differ by `1–4` B (`< 5`) — close sizes weaken classification. |
