and `#_GenKeyTime` in `[Peer]`. They are parsed back for identity and credential
reuse but are not engine keys. A hand-edited config that drops them loses
credential reuse and peer names.

Two further traps: `#_ClientToClient = yes` silently means **false** (the
parser compares the raw value to the string `"true"`), and the pipeline never
populates `#_EndpointV4`/`#_EndpointV6`, peer `#_PrivateKey`, or `#_GenKeyTime`
— the writer and parser support them, but generated output does not contain
them.

**Fix:** do not strip `#_` lines in post-processing; write `true`/`false` in
hand-edited configs.

### Client-only fields are ignored, and `awg setconf` cannot apply the whole config

On a client peer, `tun_name`, `main_iface`, `endpoint`, `listen_port` and
`display_name` have no effect: client configs take the endpoint from the server
peer and never carry the other fields. `display_name` appears only in `vpn://`
links, so setting it without `--vpn-links` produces no visible effect.

Separately, `awg setconf` rejects the wg-quick-style keys — `Address`, `MTU`,
`DNS`, `PublicKey`, `PostUp`, `PostDown`, `PersistentKeepalive` — so the
generated server config cannot be applied in one go: only the crypto and
obfuscation keys plus `ListenPort` go through `setconf`; the address, MTU and
routes are configured with `ip`.

**Fix:** set interface fields on the server peer only, and apply generated
configs the way the e2e harness does.

### Release artifacts and images are amd64 only

GoReleaser builds `linux/amd64` and `darwin/amd64` only, the container image
publishes `linux/amd64` only, and the runtime base image is amd64-only — there
are no arm64 artifacts or images.

**Fix:** on Apple Silicon use `--platform linux/amd64` for the image, or build
the binary from source.

### The published image has no default user

There is deliberately no `USER` directive in either Dockerfile: the CLI reads
and writes configs in the mounted working directory. Runs without `--user`
produce root-owned output files.

**Fix:** pass `--user $(id -u):$(id -g)` on every `docker run`.

### CLI and toolchain traps

- **`--output` means two different things.** For `generate` it is an output
  directory; for `validate` and `analyze` it is an output format (`text` or
  `json`, case-sensitive, and an unknown value is a CLI error). Keep separate
  flag variables per command.
- **Output paths are never printed.** `generate` prints relative paths and
  sizes only (`  server/awg0.conf (743 bytes)`), so the destination is implicit
  in `--output` (default `<project>/output`).
- **Findings from `generate` have no location.** In-memory configs carry an
  empty `Location`, so a finding renders with a double space
  (`[WARNING TRL001]  (key=RandomTrailers): ...`); `validate` re-stamps the
  file path. Use `validate --output json` when you need structured locations.
- **`generate` re-parses only its own server config — and ignores parse
  errors.** Findings are appended only when the generated bytes parse, and
  client configs are never re-parsed at all; point `validate` at the file to
  close the gap. A clean `generate` is not proof the config is parseable.
- **`--vpn-links` writes an extra file per client** (`<peer>/amnezigo.vpn`,
  one link each), which shows up in the generated count and in the output
  tree.
- **Bare `amnezigo` prints help and exits `0`.** An unknown subcommand prints
  `Error: unknown command ...` twice and exits `1`; assert on output, not on
  the exit code of a bare invocation.
- **Release pipeline:** promoting an `-rc.N` to a final tag on the same commit
  makes GoReleaser resolve the RC tag first and fail every asset upload with
  `422 already_exists` (the workflow pins `GORELEASER_CURRENT_TAG` to avoid
  this); `NOTICE` and `licenses/` are regenerated by `hack/noticegen` and CI
  fails when the checked-in copies are stale; the e2e suite self-skips without
  Docker or `/dev/net/tun`, so a green local run does not prove the container
  tests executed.
- **Version strings depend on the build.** `amnezigo version` prints
  `amnezigo <Version> (<Commit>)`; releases strip the tag's leading `v`,
  `make build` stamps `git describe` (for example `v0.3.0-5-g81451b7-dirty`),
  and a plain source build reports `amnezigo dev (none)`.
- **`awg show dump` field positions are a contract.** The 3.x data lands at
  1-based fields 20-28 of the interface record (`header_protection_key` 20,
  `content_padding_addition` 21, the five timers 22-26, `random_trailers` 27,
  `disable_cookies` 28; the interface fwmark follows at 29). `awg show all
  dump` additionally prefixes the interface name.

## Validation Pitfalls

### `validate` checks INI server configs, not manifests

The command parses an **AmneziaWG server `.conf`** with strict options and
reports findings; it never loads a `amnezigo.json` or `.amnezigo.jsonnet`. To
check a manifest, generate with `--dry-run` to catch load-time errors, then
validate the emitted server config.

**Fix:** `amnezigo generate --dry-run` for manifest and load errors;
`amnezigo validate output/<server>/awg0.conf` for INI-level findings.

### Parsing is always strict; `--strict` only sets the exit code

`validate` calls `ParseServerConfigWithOptions` with `Strict: true`
unconditionally, so client-only keys (`I1`-`I5`, `Endpoint`,
`PersistentKeepalive`) and any other unknown key become `KEY001` warnings. A
client config also lacks `ListenPort`, which is an `FLD001` error. Verified
live on a generated client config: 1 error and 6 warnings with the default
quic template (the named templates define no `I5`), 7 warnings when all five
I-keys are present — exit 1 even though the file is valid for the engine.
Without `--strict`, warnings print but the process exits `0`.

**Fix:** validate the server config. Use `--strict` in CI gates to fail on
warnings; treat `validate` on a client config as expected to fail.

### An H range covering WireGuard type-ids `1-4` is a parse error — unless a header-protection key is present

Any `H1`-`H4` range that overlaps the standard WireGuard message type-ids
(`1`-`4`) is structurally rejected at parse time and surfaces as `PSE001`
(`invalid H1: header range [1-10] contains forbidden WG type-id(s) in [1..4]`)
— **unless** the config also carries a header-protection key, because then the
type-ids are encrypted and `1-1`..`4-4` is the legitimate reference set. The
check runs after the whole file is read, so line order does not matter.

**Fix:** without a header key, keep every H range above `4` (for example
`100-1000`). With a header key, the reference set is expected.

### Structural failures are `PSE001`; semantic problems are findings

Malformed structures — an invalid `HeaderProtectionKey`, a non-range value, a
bad boolean, a structurally invalid H range — abort parsing and surface in the
CLI as a single `PSE001` finding. Semantic problems (`HPK001`, `HPK003`,
`TRL001`, `TRM001`, `PSC*`, `HDR*`, `JNK001`) are findings on an otherwise
parsed config.

**Fix:** fix the structural error first; expect the semantic findings on the
next run.

### Junk range bounds are inclusive, and pinned junk skips generation-time checks

`ValidatePacketSizes` treats `[jmin..jmax]` as inclusive on both ends: a bound
exactly equal to a forbidden size is a collision —
`[ERROR PSC002] ...: packet size collision (junk-range): [Jmin..Jmax] contains
64 at 64 bytes`, exit 1. Forbidden sizes are the four padded sizes
(`S1+148`, `S2+92`, `S3+64`, `S4+32`) and the raw WireGuard sizes
`148`/`92`/`64`/`32`. Explicit `jc`/`jmin`/`jmax` values skip that collision
check during generation (`fillMissingJunk` short-circuits when all three are
explicit) and are caught only by `validate`/`ValidatePacketSizes` afterwards.
Note the padded-size invariant has **six** pair comparisons, not one; older
guidance mentioning only `S1+56 != S2` understates it. `jmin > jmax` is a
structural error (`ErrEmptyJunkRange`), reported as `JNK001`. Generation itself
panics rather than returning an error when it exhausts its 1000-attempt budgets
(`GenerateConfig`, `GenerateServerConfig`, `GenerateSPrefixes`,
`GenerateHeaderRanges`, junk-range generation) — give the generator room or pin
values it can use.

**Fix:** run `validate` after pinning J values and keep the range clear of the
padded and raw sizes. See [Obfuscation](/obfuscation).

### `<c>` is not a usable tag, `<rc>` is letters only, and unknown tags count 0 bytes

`BuildCPSTag("c", ...)` returns an empty string — the same sentinel as any
unknown tag — and `CPSLength` counts it as 0 bytes, so size accounting cannot
catch it. The tag is recognised only by the kernel module; amneziawg-go and
every AmneziaVPN client reject it, and a raw `<c>` literal in a config is
flagged as `CPS001` (`raw <c> tag detected; rejected by amneziawg-go and
AmneziaVPN clients`). The supported tags are exactly `<b>`, `<t>`, `<r>`,
`<rc>`, `<rd>` and `<d>`; anything else renders as 0 bytes and shrinks the
interval silently — that covers `<ds>`/`<dz>`, which the amneziawg-go 3.1
engine accepts but amnezigo does not recognise, and plain typos. Numeric parse
failures inside a tag also become 0 (`strconv.Atoi` error ignored). Two sizing
quirks: an interval whose computed length exactly equals the max I-size is
rejected (`n >= maxSize`) and shrunk, and the SIP template's byte budgets in
its comment (~360/240/170/120) are approximate — measured I1-I4 render at
312/203/140/87.

::: warning `<rc>` is letters-only
The alphabet is the 52 ASCII letters `[a-zA-Z]`, not the commonly cited
`[a-zA-Z0-9]`; there is no alphanumeric tag. Mixed fields need concatenation,
for example `<rc 4><rd 2>`. `<d>` is a zero-byte passthrough that requires AWG
2.0 userspace (the kernel module rejects it) and is never emitted by random
mode because a standalone random interval has no earlier interval to source it
from. `<t>` is 4 bytes (a `uint32`), not 8, and at most one `<t>` is allowed
per interval.
:::

**Fix:** use `<rd>` for digits and `<rc>` for letters, combine tags when you
need mixed content, and target userspace engines for `<d>`.

### Header and range checks have blind spots

- `HDR001` (WG type-ids in H ranges) is suppressed whenever a header-protection
  key is present; overlapping H ranges are not a validator rule at all.
- `HDR002` (`Max < Min`) fires even under header protection.
- `HPK003` (`HeaderProtectionKey` is not 44-char base64 of 32 bytes) is
  library-only: a malformed key in a file is a `PSE001` parse failure.
- `TRM001` reports only the first structural problem per range (inverted ranges
  are checked before mixed-zero ones), and `{0,0}` — the disabled state — never
  produces a finding.
- A `U16Range` with one zero bound is a hard error: `{"min": 0}` decodes to
  `{0,0}` (disabled), while `{"min": 0, "max": 5}` fails with
  `obfuscation.<field>: bounds must both be zero or both non-zero (got 0-5)`.
  Bounds are `uint16`, so values above 65535 fail to unmarshal.
- `JNK001` can be emitted twice for the same defect (`jmin > jmax`), once via
  `ErrEmptyJunkRange` and once from the dedicated rule — deduplicate by code.
- `PSC003` (I-packet vs padded-size collision) is unreachable from
  `ValidateServerConfig`, which passes a nil i-packet slice; it is
  library-only.
- `ValidatePacketSizes` is generic and accepts an out-of-range S4 (for example
  `116`) as long as padded sizes differ, while generation caps S4 at 32 and
  S1-S3 at 64.
- `RandomTrailers` accepts only case-insensitive `on`/`1`/`off`/`0`; a
  hand-edited `RandomTrailers = true` fails with `expected on/off/0/1, got
  "true"`.
- INI parsing is agnostic to the key set's version: `validate` accepts all nine
  3.x keys regardless of the engine the config is meant for (INI files carry
  no version), so it cannot tell you that a 2.0 engine will refuse the file.

### `analyze` always exits 0 on findings

No matter how many `RISK001`-`RISK009` findings fire, `analyze` exits `0` on
success; findings are advisory. A non-zero exit happens only on a config-load
or output-format error.

**Fix:** gate CI on parsed `--output json`, not on the exit status.

### `analyze --seed` is inert

::: danger Shipping defect — `--seed` does not make output reproducible
The CLI builds a seeded `math/rand/v2` PCG reader and assigns it to
`AnalyzeOptions.Rand`, but no code path in the package reads that field;
I-packet generation goes straight to `crypto/rand`. Verified live: two runs of
`analyze --config <cfg> --output json --seed 42 --samples 5` produced different
distributions, despite the flag's help text promising reproducible output.
:::

**Fix:** do not rely on `--seed` for repeatable reports; compare distributions,
not exact numbers.

### `analyze` profiles regenerated I-packets, not your stored I1-I5

`Analyze` calls `GenerateCPS` with an empty forbidden set and its own protocol,
so the snapshot and distribution are fresh samples. The report even says so:
`Note: I-packet sizes are freshly generated from config parameters and may
differ on each run.`

**Fix:** read I1-I5 from the config file itself when exact values matter.

### `generate` defaults to `quic`, `analyze` defaults to `random`

A peer with no `protocol` gets QUIC I-packets during generation, while
`analyze` defaults its `--protocol` flag to `random`. The two commands describe
the same config with different I-packet shapes unless you pass `--protocol`
explicitly.

**Fix:** pass the same `--protocol` to both commands; remember that an unknown
protocol name is not rejected and falls through to a random named template.

### `RISK004`, `RISK005` and `RISK007` have thresholds that hide problems

`RISK004` and `RISK005` require `0 < diff < 5`, so two identical padded sizes
produce no `RISK004` and a padded size exactly equal to a raw WireGuard size
(for example `stealth-paranoid` S4=32 → 64) produces no `RISK005`. Treat a
clean section as "no near-misses in the band," not "no collisions." `RISK007`
fires only for H widths below 1,000,000 and is skipped entirely under header
protection, so `lan-conservative`'s H1 (width 999,991) trips it while a
header-protected config never will.

### `validate` exits through `os.Exit`, and usage errors print twice

A failed lint calls `os.Exit(1)` inside the command, so no usage text is
printed and deferred cleanup does not run. A CLI-level failure (unreadable
file, unknown `--output`) returns a cobra error instead, which prints the usage
block and then `Error: ...` a second time from `Execute`.

**Fix:** script on exit codes and stdout findings; expect doubled `Error:`
lines for usage-level failures.

## VPN Import Links

The `--vpn-links` flag generates `amnezigo.vpn` files containing `vpn://`
import links for the AmneziaVPN app. These links use a proprietary envelope
format with specific structural requirements; the pitfalls below cover the
common traps when working with or hand-crafting them. See
[VPN Import Links](/vpn-links) for the envelope structure.

::: danger `vpn://` links target AmneziaVPN, not standalone AmneziaWG
The link is an AmneziaVPN-specific envelope: a JSON payload wrapped in
`qCompress` (4-byte big-endian length header + zlib), then
`base64.RawURLEncoding` (no padding), prefixed with `vpn://`. The container
type is `amnezia-awg`. The standalone AmneziaWG client and the kernel module
cannot import these links — they only read `.conf` files.

**Fix:** use the AmneziaVPN app to import `vpn://` links; for standalone AWG,
use the generated `awg0.conf` directly.
:::

::: warning The server peer never gets a `.vpn` file
`appendVPNLink` is called only for client peers inside the filtered-clients
loop; the server config is added to the output set without any link. This is by
design — the link is a client-side import artifact.

**Fix:** none needed. Read `output/<server>/awg0.conf` for the server's
connection details.
:::

::: danger `allowed_ips` is a JSON array — and can be null
In the envelope, `last_config.allowed_ips` is a JSON **array** of strings
(`["0.0.0.0/0", "::/0"]`), built by splitting the INI `AllowedIPs` value. The
field has no `omitempty`, so a client INI without `AllowedIPs` serializes
`"allowed_ips": null` — exactly the `JSONException` → error 1000 failure mode
the encoder comments warn about.

**Fix:** never represent `allowed_ips` as a comma-separated string in a
hand-crafted link, and do not strip `AllowedIPs` from a client INI before
generating links.
:::

::: danger All AWG obfuscation fields in `last_config` are strings
`Jc`, `Jmin`, `Jmax`, `S1`-`S4`, `H1`-`H4` and `I1`-`I5` are typed as `string`,
not numbers; only `port` is an integer (and the envelope's `awg.port` is a
string while `last_config.port` is a number, so do not assume one type across
both). Passing `"Jc": 4` instead of `"Jc": "4"` causes a `JSONException` on
import.

**Fix:** quote every AWG field value when hand-crafting an envelope; type-switch
on `port` depending on where it appears.
:::

::: danger `last_config` is a stringified JSON object — inlining it causes error 1000
The structured fields are marshaled to JSON bytes first, those bytes are
embedded as a **string** value in the outer envelope, and the envelope is
marshaled again. Inlining the structured fields directly into the envelope
produces the `JSONException` → error 1000 path.

**Fix:** always nest the structured fields inside a stringified JSON object
assigned to `last_config`. The app reads them via `getString()` /
`getJSONArray()`; the raw INI in the envelope's `config` field is for display
only, and a missing structured field fails on the first `getString()` call.
:::

::: warning `isObfuscationEnabled` is derived from the `Jc` line
The encoder sets `isObfuscationEnabled = (Jc != "")` by checking the client INI
for a `Jc` line; without it the app will not enable AWG extension parameters.
The nine 3.x fields are inside the same `Jc`-gated branch, so a `Jc`-less
config silently loses `HeaderProtectionKey` and the other eight 3.x keys from
`last_config`. The 3.x mapping is comment-documented but not pinned by a test,
so verify it against the app before relying on it.

**Fix:** keep `Jc` in the client config, and validate generated links in the
AmneziaVPN app when 3.x fields matter.
:::

::: warning DNS is limited to two slots
The envelope has only `dns1` and `dns2`; everything beyond the second entry of
`network.dns` is silently dropped.

**Fix:** configure additional DNS servers in the app after importing; the first
two come from the manifest.
:::

::: warning CPS tag strings (I1-I5) are preserved verbatim, not expanded
The I1-I5 values in `last_config` are copied as literal CPS tag strings (for
example `<b 0x12><r 16>`) — not expanded to hex bytes. This is intentional: the
engine parses the tags at connect time, so expanding them at config time would
freeze random bytes and reduce obfuscation quality. `I5` is omitted when empty.

**Fix:** pass CPS tags as literal strings when hand-crafting an envelope.
:::

::: warning qCompress format is Qt-specific
The payload is Qt's `qCompress` format: a 4-byte big-endian `uint32`
uncompressed-length header followed by zlib-compressed data, then
`base64.RawURLEncoding` (no `=` padding). **Manual decoding:** strip the
`vpn://` prefix, base64url-decode, skip the first 4 bytes, then zlib-inflate
the remainder.
:::

::: warning Endpoint resolution falls back to `listen_port`
`resolveEndpoint` tries `net.SplitHostPort` first; if the endpoint string lacks
a port (`vpn.example.com`), it falls back to the server peer's `listen_port`.
So `endpoint = "vpn.example.com"` with `listen_port = 55424` resolves to
`vpn.example.com:55424`.

**Fix:** you may omit the port from `endpoint`; include it only when the public
port differs from the listen port.
:::

::: danger `.vpn` files are credentials
`last_config.config` contains the verbatim client INI (private key, PSK) plus
the same secrets as structured fields. A `.vpn` file is as sensitive as the
client config itself. No SSH credentials appear in the envelope — that part is
by design.

**Fix:** treat `.vpn` files like private keys; do not paste them into tickets
or chat.
:::

## FAQ

### Why do my keys change on every `generate`?

They should not — unless the `output/` directory is missing, a peer directory
was deleted or renamed, a peer's `#_Name` comment was stripped, or you passed
`--full-reset`. Keys and PSKs are recovered from the previous output and reused.
The exception is the header-protection key: it lives only in the emitted server
config, so any run without a 3.x key (an `awg_version: "2.0"` run, or
`header_protection: false`) drops it, and the next 3.1 run rotates it. Note
that obfuscation values change every run even when keys do not — see
*Key reuse is asymmetric* above.

### I set `obfuscation.protocol` but my client uses a different one. Why?

The top-level `obfuscation.protocol` is dead configuration. Template selection
is per-peer: set `protocol` inside each peer object. An empty `protocol`
defaults to `quic`, and an unknown name silently picks a random named template.

### How do I pin an obfuscation value instead of letting it randomize?

Write the value — omitting a numeric field means "random"; including a value
means "use this". Zero is special: a `0` is always replaced for S (`{"s1": 0}`
becomes a generated value) and for Jc unless `jmin` and `jmax` are also pinned
(with all three explicit, `Jc = 0` stays `0`). S itself cannot be pinned to
zero. Under header protection, pinned S values must be ≥ 12 or generation
aborts with `header protection requires S1-S4 >= 12 (got S<n>=<value>)` — the
floor exists because the header cipher's ChaCha20 nonce is built from the first
12 bytes of the S-prefix. If you leave all four S unset with `random_trailers` on, the
generator draws one uniform value for all four; pinning any one S switches the
other three to independent draws and normally triggers `TRL001`. For the header
fields, `h1`-`h4` are objects (`{"min": int, "max": int}`); pin all four or
none.

### Why does `generate` print `Warnings: 1` with `TRL001`?

`TRL001` means `RandomTrailers is enabled while S1..S4 differ; the AWG 3.1
reference recommends equal S values to avoid packet-type misclassification`. It
is a warning, not an error, and it is expected whenever you pin unequal S
values with `random_trailers` on — including four of the seven presets
(`home-balanced`, `mobile-aggressive`, `stealth-paranoid`, `standard-1420`).
Equalize the S values or set `random_trailers: false` to silence it.

### `amnezigo analyze` says `awg0.conf` not found — but I generated configs

`analyze --config` defaults to `awg0.conf` in your current working directory,
not the generated output path. Pass it explicitly:
`amnezigo analyze --config output/<server>/awg0.conf`.

### Can I validate my manifest before generating?

Not directly with `validate` (it only reads INI configs). Use
`amnezigo generate --dry-run` to catch load-time errors (bad `version`, zero or
multiple server peers, Jsonnet failures) without writing files; remember that a
dry run neither previews the keys a real run will write nor creates anything on
the first run. After generating, run `validate` on the server config.

### How do I use a preset?

Copy the preset's `s1`-`s4`, `h1`-`h4`, `jc`, `jmin`, `jmax`, `content_padding`,
`random_trailers`, `disable_cookies` and MTU values into your manifest's
`obfuscation.*` and `network.mtu`, and set the protocol per client peer — there
is no `preset` field and no `--preset` flag. See [Presets](/presets) for the
exact values.

### How do I make `analyze` output reproducible?

You cannot today: `--seed` is accepted but inert, because `AnalyzeOptions.Rand`
is assigned and never read. Treat the report as a fresh sample each run and
compare distributions rather than exact numbers.

### Which engine do I need for a 3.1 config?

An AmneziaWG 3.x userspace engine — the transport-protection keys are engine
features, not decoration. The published image pins
`amneziavpn/amneziawg-go:3.1.20260828`; 2.0/3.0 builds reject the nine 3.x
keys with `Line unrecognized`, and kernel implementations without the
transport-protection layer cannot use them either.

### Can I run amnezigo on arm64 or Apple Silicon?

Not from the published artifacts: the release matrix and container images are
amd64 only, and the runtime base image is amd64-only. Use
`--platform linux/amd64` for the image, or build the binary from source.

### How do I avoid root-owned files from the Docker image?

The image has no `USER` directive, so pass `--user $(id -u):$(id -g)` on every
`docker run` that writes into a mounted directory.
